import { boardCode, SEED_MAX } from '../deck.ts';

const UINT32_RANGE = 2 ** 32;
const RANDOM_LIMIT = Math.floor(UINT32_RANGE / SEED_MAX) * SEED_MAX;

export function freshBoardCode(size: number, previousSeed?: number): string {
  const buffer = new Uint32Array(1);
  for (;;) {
    crypto.getRandomValues(buffer);
    const draw = buffer[0];
    if (draw === undefined || draw >= RANDOM_LIMIT) continue;
    const seed = (draw % SEED_MAX) + 1;
    if (seed !== previousSeed) return boardCode(size, seed);
  }
}
# Randomness policy

This page explains the boundary between choosing a fresh deal and reproducing a deal in Neon Pairs.

A new board needs an unpredictable seed. A board code, restart, imported snapshot and replay need the opposite property: a particular code always reconstructs the same deck. The implementation keeps those two tasks separate rather than letting a shuffle consult ambient state. [Deck generation](../gameplay/deck-generation.md) covers the deal algorithm as a format; this page concentrates on its source ownership and integration.

## One boundary for fresh input

`src/game/session/fresh-board.ts` exports `freshBoardCode(size, previousSeed?)`. It obtains a seed and returns the normal board-code representation through `boardCode` from `deck.ts`. Only src/game/session/fresh-board.ts may call a random source. Everything else that needs randomness imports it from there. The session controller uses that exported operation when initializing a session or asking for a new game.

The distinction is visible in the imports. `use-game.ts` imports `freshBoardCode` for fresh deals and `createGame` for constructing a game from a code. `game.ts` imports `generateBoard`, which works from supplied data. Nothing in a card component needs to choose a seed, and no deck is shuffled merely because React rendered it.

## Two finite ranges

The fresh-board module uses a one-element `Uint32Array` and `crypto.getRandomValues`. Its possible raw values span the unsigned 32-bit range, with `UINT32_RANGE` set to `2 ** 32`. The allowed seed range is defined in `deck.ts` by `SEED_MAX = 2_147_483_646`. Valid codes use positive seeds, so the transformation adds one after taking a remainder.

The module computes `RANDOM_LIMIT = Math.floor(UINT32_RANGE / SEED_MAX) * SEED_MAX`. With the current values the limit is `4_294_967_292`. A draw below that limit is accepted; one at or above it is retried. Thus each allowed remainder has the same number of accepted raw values. The last four unsigned values do not enter the modulo mapping.

The seed is `(draw % SEED_MAX) + 1`. Its endpoints are therefore 1 and `SEED_MAX`; zero is not produced. The code also checks that `buffer[0]` is defined, which matches the project's checked-index TypeScript setting even though the buffer length is deliberately one. It loops until it can return a valid code.

This is rejection sampling, not rounding a floating-point draw. Applying a plain remainder to all `2 ** 32` possible values would assign a few seeds one more source value than the others. The difference is small numerically, but a reproducible format benefits from an implementation whose range treatment can be described exactly.

## Excluding the immediately previous seed

When `previousSeed` is supplied, a candidate equal to it is discarded. `use-game.ts` passes the current game's seed when creating a new game, including when a different grid size is selected. This means the next seed differs from the immediately preceding seed even across a size change.

That check is narrower than a history of every generated deal. The implementation does not keep a seed registry, does not persist a sequence of fresh codes and does not exclude every seed seen earlier in the session. A code can reappear after intervening games. Nor does the initial call pass an earlier browser session's seed; preferences retain size and best moves, not the last active deal.

The retry loop also does not claim a bounded number of calls. It retries out-of-range draws and an excluded candidate. There is no time-based fallback in this module. A browser crypto failure is not caught here. The storage module's tolerant behavior should not be mistaken for a universal fallback around every browser API.

## Construction after selection

Once the seed is selected, `boardCode(size, seed)` validates the representation. Its format is `np1-SIZE-SEED`, with the supported sizes supplied by `GRID_SIZES`. The parser accepts exactly the seven sizes 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16. It also checks that the seed is a safe integer within the allowed maximum.

`createGame(code)` calls `generateBoard(code)` and adds the initial progress fields. The starting deck is already determined by that point. The game starts with no matched positions, a closed selection, zero moves, zero elapsed milliseconds and `started: false`.

The code-producing function can throw for an invalid size or seed. The session's `newGame` action checks the requested size with `isValidSize` before requesting a fresh code. Its normal UI callers use the native select populated from `GRID_SIZES`. These checks protect the application path without adding a second size list to the form.

## Deterministic state is not ambient entropy

`deck.ts` exports `nextRandomState(state)`, but this function is arithmetic over an explicit argument. It computes `(state * 16_807) % 2_147_483_647`. Repeating a call with the same state returns the same result. The name describes a pseudorandom sequence; it does not imply a browser read.

For a valid seed, the generator advances that sequence inside a descending Fisher–Yates shuffle. The initial deck contains two copies of every integer face from zero to `size ** 2 / 2 - 1`, arranged as adjacent duplicates before shuffling. For a 4 by 4 board, it starts as `0, 0, 1, 1` and so on through face 7.

At shuffle position `index`, the number of choices is `index + 1`. The implementation computes a divisible acceptance limit from `SEED_MAX`, advances its local generator state, subtracts one to form the draw, rejects values outside the limit and uses the accepted remainder as the swap position. Both the raw seed selection and the shuffle use rejection, but they operate on different ranges and have different owners.

The maximum multiplication in the sequence is below JavaScript's safe integer limit. The independent browser-test oracle uses BigInt arithmetic, providing a separate expression of the same documented deal rather than calling the production generator to predict itself. [Purity guide](purity-guide.md) explains why explicit state makes these checks possible.

## A concrete stable example

The fixture code `np1-4-1` produces this row-major deck:

```text
6 7 0 5
2 2 0 5
3 7 1 6
4 4 1 3
```

Positions are zero based in rules and formats. Positions 2 and 6 are a pair; positions 0 and 11 are another. The fixture's `EXAMPLE_DECK` stores the whole literal sequence, while `EXAMPLE_PAIRS` lists the matching positions. Those are test facts, not attributes added to hidden cards in the shipped DOM.

Changing the shuffle traversal, recurrence, rejection condition or starting deck would change this example and potentially every shared code. Such a change is therefore observable through board codes, snapshots and replays, even if the interface still looks like a memory game. The generator's determinism connects implementation detail to a public format.

## Every action that chooses or reuses a deal

| Path | Seed behavior in the current implementation |
| --- | --- |
| Initial `useGame` state | Fresh seed using the saved valid size or default size |
| New Game | Fresh seed excluding the current seed |
| Grid-size selection | Fresh seed for the selected size, excluding the current seed |
| Restart | Existing board code passed to `createGame` |
| Load board | Submitted code trimmed, parsed and reconstructed |
| Load snapshot | Decoder validates its code and reconstructs its deck |
| Replay | Reader validates the supplied code and starts from it |

This table is useful when a bug report says that “a new board changed.” A new game is expected to change the seed. A restart or imported code is expected to repeat the existing deal. A size selection is a fresh deal rather than a geometric rearrangement of the old cards.

`newGame` also resets the clock and replaces the session game. Seed choice alone does not clear progress or focus; session replacement and the generation key supply those lifetimes. [Session module](session-module.md) covers that process.

## Evidence and blind spots

`deck.test.ts` covers board-code parsing, generated structure and known vectors. `deck-rejection.test.ts` reads independent BigInt vectors for an over-limit draw and a draw exactly on the shuffle limit. The equality boundary matters because accepting it would break the uniform mapping and alter the deterministic result for that seed.

The browser suite loads documented codes through actual controls and uses `specDeal` from `tests/deal-oracle.ts` when it needs an independent deal. `lifecycle.e2e.test.ts` checks that New Game changes the current code and that a size change chooses a different seed from the previous deal. A complete all-size journey checks that the resulting decks remain playable.

The fresh-board module has no adjacent unit test. Deterministic deck tests establish format behavior and known sequences, rather than statistical properties of the browser entropy source. The raw seed boundary is short enough to inspect directly, but inspection is a different kind of evidence.

The source audit's core list rejects browser entropy references in the named core files. It does not implement a whole-program information-flow proof or a general scanner for every possible source of variation. [Source audit notes](source-audit-notes.md) describes precisely what it scans.

## Diagnosing an unexpected deck

The most useful reproduction is the board code, not the time the game started. Parsing that code reveals both size and seed. Calling `generateBoard` with it establishes the expected deck without involving React or browser state. An imported snapshot reconstructs that same deck and then validates progress against it.

If the code differs, investigate which action replaced the session. If the code agrees but the deck differs, compare the shuffle against the literal vector and independent oracle. If the deck agrees but the wrong art appears, investigate `faceDesign`, reveal state and card props. These are distinct failures with different evidence.

A hidden card deliberately receives `null` as its face prop. Looking for all face identities in its DOM is not a valid debugging strategy for this application boundary. Tests already have the code and can derive a deck independently. [React boundaries](react-boundaries.md) describes that presentation decision in context.
# Acceptance
Acceptance is a set of journeys that checks whether Neon Pairs meets its product requirements.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Finish a game, then start another one during a mismatch. The first journey checks play and completion. The second checks that an earlier timer can't change a new game.

## Play

Use these journeys with the requirements in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md):

- Finish every supported size with complete pairs.
- Reveal one card twice, then reveal a different card. Check the exact move count.
- Match a pair, then miss a pair. Check the immediate match and the 800ms active mismatch interval.
- Hide the page during a mismatch, then return and finish its remaining interval.
- Start and restart during a mismatch. Check the cleared state and later timer updates.
- Finish games with better, equal and worse move counts. Reload and check the current size's best.

## Controls

Use pointer, touch and keyboard to follow [Input](../interface/input.md) and [Controls](../interface/controls.md). Check control labels, row movement, edge stops, native Tab exit and focus after each action. Check that hidden cards reveal no identity in the DOM.

Follow the keyboard journey in I17 and check its accessibility tree. During user acceptance, confirm spoken results with a screen reader, including consecutive identical results and the final match with its win.

## Appearance

Measure the layout and review all 128 faces against [Visuals](../visuals/visuals.md). Use a 44px grayscale face sheet to distinguish shape, marker and fill. Check 16x16 boards at both stated viewport sizes, full focus outlines and the equivalent zoom layout. Check reduced motion and the static completion banner after its single pulse.

Play through completion and reset while checking [Sound](../sound/sound.md). Every action stays silent.

## Reproduction

Check [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) with its example deck and replay. Check snapshot round trips and malformed input. Check the exact mismatch timeout before an equal-time replay action.

Load an unfinished snapshot, attempt input while paused, then Resume. Check its remaining active time and focus. Load a completed snapshot and check its static banner and unchanged best score.

## Delivery

Use a locked install, type check, unit tests and a fresh browser build as defined in [Technology](../architecture/technology.md). Open the resulting HTML directly from disk with network access blocked. Use a local HTTP origin for saved preferences.

Review the pure game functions, browser effects, file sizes and behavior placement against [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md).

Back to [Neon Pairs](../README.md).
# Focus policy

This page records focus behavior in the current game and the policy for a feature that changes the main screen.

Focus tells a keyboard user where input will go next. It is related to game selection but is not stored as part of a turn or snapshot. The current interface deliberately keeps deal-action focus, remembered board focus and card reveal state as distinct things.

## Existing page and future screens

`Game.tsx` currently renders one main area with an h1, deal controls, statistics, instructions, turn output, the Board and reproduction controls. It has no alternate-screen branch or screen-level h2 focus target. Replacing a deal remounts the board within that page; it does not replace the page with a different screen.

A feature that introduces a screen replacement has a different orientation problem from resetting a deck. When a feature replaces what the main area shows, focus moves to that screen's h2, which has tabindex="-1". This gives the new screen a programmatic landing place without adding that heading to ordinary Tab traversal. The current deal and load callbacks can still be understood on their own terms; they are not evidence that such a screen transition already exists.

The policy applies to the feature-level replacement described here. Expanding native details, updating statistics, closing a mismatch or displaying the completed-game paragraph does not currently create a new screen. Those operations retain the page structure and follow the existing behavior below. [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) covers a separate interaction with its own opening focus.

## Initial load is quiet

The hook `useBoardFocus(size)` initializes `focused` to zero. Board gives index 0 a tab index of zero and the other card buttons a tab index of minus one. This makes the first card available on entry, but no mount effect calls its focus method.

The browser's current focus therefore remains where it is at initial load. The page does not jump down to the board before a player has found Grid size or New Game. The board help paragraph describes how to enter and operate it. Its region uses `aria-describedby="board-help"` to associate those instructions with the board.

A remembered entry point is often described casually as “focus on the first card.” In this code that wording is incomplete. There is an entry point ready at the first card, while actual focus may be on the document, a deal button or another native control. Keeping those concepts separate prevents accidental mount-time focus stealing.

## Deal actions retain their location

New Game and Restart are native buttons that call the session controller. Neither callback moves focus into the board. After either action, a keyboard user remains on the button they used and can repeat the action or Tab toward the board. The size select uses its native interaction and likewise does not issue a board focus call.

The replacement increments `session.generation`, used as Board's React key. The newly mounted hook begins with a remembered index of zero. Thus the next board entry goes to the first card, even if the previous deal's memory was near its end. Actual action focus and future board entry are updated through different mechanisms.

A valid board-code load also increments generation. BoardCodeForm focuses its Load board ref on successful submission because its input is keyed by generation and will be replaced. That is especially important when the action was Enter in the input. An invalid submission keeps the input node and does not call the button ref, so correction can continue in place.

Clicking the load button starts with focus on that button, and an invalid click leaves it there. The distinction is based on the action's origin and successful input replacement, not on a general rule that all errors move focus into a field. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) follows those cases in detail.

## Remembered board focus

Board focus memory is a local hook state containing a card index. The `onFocus` callback updates it whenever a card receives focus. Board renders exactly that index with `tabIndex={0}`. All other cards remain programmatically focusable with `tabIndex={-1}`.

Arrow movement uses the DOM order of the deck and never changes game selection on its own. Tab and Shift+Tab are left to the browser, so the board is one stop in the page sequence rather than a trap. Returning to it finds the last focused card, even if that card is now matched.

Matched positions stay in the navigation geometry. A player does not need to relearn how many arrow presses separate two coordinates after a match. During a mismatch, focus can also move while activation is blocked. The same is true while imported unfinished progress waits for Resume. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) provides the calculations and edge behavior.

## Resume transfers before removal

Resume is the current exception to retaining focus on the action button. It exists only while `session.paused` is true. Clearing that flag removes the button, so leaving focus there would leave a disappearing target.

In `Game.tsx`, the local `resume()` function first calls `board.current?.focusRemembered()` and then `controller.resume()`. Board's imperative method focuses the remembered card with `preventScroll: true` and then brings it into view. Only after that does the controller clear the paused state and notices.

The ordering is observable. `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` installs a focus listener and confirms that Resume is still present when the card receives focus. A visual assertion after the fact would not establish this timing. The focus-entry test also remembers a far card on a large imported board, scrolls away and confirms that Resume returns to that location with nearest alignment.

The remembered location after import is initially the first card because the import replaced the board. The player can change it while paused. Resume uses that current memory rather than the snapshot's revealed index or a hard-coded first card. A snapshot stores game progress, not the browser's last navigation location.

## Visible focus and scroll clearance

`game.css` defines `:focus-visible` as a `3px` white outline with a `2px` offset. `card.css` gives cards `scroll-margin: 6px`. This combination accommodates the ring when the card is brought to the edge of the scroll area.

The focus hook uses `card.matches(':focus-visible')` before scrolling in `cardFocused`. Keyboard movement can scroll immediately; pointer focus avoids moving a card under a held press. Board scrolls a clicked card after the click completes. The timing is part of reliable focus behavior, not only a visual polish detail.

`useNearestScroll` stores the board's last reported scroll position, restores it and then invokes `scrollIntoView` with nearest alignment. The source records the Chromium-specific reason: Tab or Shift+Tab can center a newly focused card before the handler runs. Starting from the prior view preserves the player's location as much as possible.

The helper leaves the outer page's scrolling to the browser. A review therefore measures both the card inside the board viewport and its visibility inside the window. A ring can be uncut by the board yet still sit partly below the window if the outer document did not move appropriately.

## Focus is not completion feedback

Winning does not move focus to the completion paragraph in GameStatus. The final card stays the current control, and the completed summary becomes available in document order. The final turn's feedback is published through the game's event output. The component does not force the player to leave the board simply because all pairs are now matched.

Likewise, a mismatch closing does not restore focus to either of its cards. Focus may have moved elsewhere while the pair was visible. The game-state update closes the faces while the user's navigation choice survives. An ordinary clock tick also leaves focus untouched.

These examples are useful when evaluating a proposed effect that focuses something whenever `game` changes. Game changes for elapsed time, first reveals, turn results and resets. An effect tied to that broad object would combine very different events and could interrupt typing or navigation. The existing code places its explicit focus operations at narrower action boundaries.

## Review evidence

The keyboard browser check covers Tab exit, remembered re-entry and matched-card focus. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` covers Enter submission from Board code. `tests/focus-entry.e2e.test.ts` covers nearest alignment and the switch from pointer use to keyboard arrows. `tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` checks outline clearance on large boards, including an interior card where container padding alone cannot protect the ring.

A useful focus report names the source control, action, destination and whether the source remains mounted. For example: “Enter in Board code loads 6x6, replaces the input and leaves Load board focused.” That is more precise than “load focuses correctly,” and it exposes why failure has a different result. [Interface review checklist](interface-review-checklist.md) gathers these journeys with layout and input checks.

For new screen work, the source review begins by locating the actual replacement boundary. For changes within the existing game page, it begins with the current action-specific behavior above. Screen replacement and the established board lifecycle have separate focus behavior.
# Disabled state guide

This page explains why some card activations have no effect while the controls remain focusable and usable for navigation.

The game separates control semantics, focus and game eligibility. A matched card exposes an unavailable state, but it stays in the board. A mismatching pair temporarily blocks further activation, yet arrows can still explore the same coordinates. These are deliberate differences rather than one universal disabled flag.

## Matched cards use ARIA state

`Card.tsx` sets `aria-disabled={matched}` on its native button. It does not set the HTML `disabled` attribute. When matched is true, the button remains available to programmatic focus and the board's remembered tab-stop mechanism.

The card's accessible name includes `matched`, along with its coordinate and face description. Its face remains visible, its border becomes the green palette color and a corner check mark appears. Matched cards retain full opacity. The state is communicated through text, semantics and visual treatment rather than by dimming the card until it is difficult to identify.

The click handler still calls `activate(index)` for a matched card. ARIA describes the state; it does not suppress native events. The actual game guard in `activateCard` checks `state.matched.includes(index)` and returns the same state. The session sees that identity and returns without publishing a new result.

This is an important code-reading boundary. Removing the guard because a button “is already disabled” would mistake an accessibility attribute for an event blocker. Conversely, adding native disabled would change focus behavior even if ignored activation still produced no move.

## Why focus remains available

The board uses one remembered card in the page's tab sequence. Arrow movement traverses coordinates without skipping solved positions. A match can therefore leave focus on its second card, and the next arrow still means the adjacent row or column.

If matched buttons became natively disabled, they would no longer participate in the same focus behavior. Remembered entry could point to an unavailable native focus target, and movement would need a different policy for skipping positions. The current input specification instead keeps the rectangular geometry stable.

A player can leave with Tab and return to the remembered matched card. Activating it again has no game effect. This is covered in `tests/keyboard.e2e.test.ts`, which checks the disabled attribute, continued focus and unchanged move count after another Space activation.

[Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) explains the tab-index pattern and edge clamping. The disabled state does not create a second movement algorithm or change the size of the board.

## A revealed first card is different

The first revealed card has state `revealed` and is not matched. It therefore exposes `aria-disabled="false"`. Activating it again is nevertheless ignored by the game's `SelectionKind.one` branch because `first === index`.

This is not inconsistent with the matched-card treatment. The first reveal is an intermediate turn state. The game waits for a different eligible position to complete the attempt, while the first card remains readable and focusable. The button name describes what the player can know, and the core determines whether this particular activation advances the turn.

There is no separate “selected but disabled” CSS class or native disabling operation for that card. A repeated click may keep focus there and apply completed-click scrolling, but it does not add a move, restart elapsed time or produce a turn result.

The same separation lets a player navigate away from the first card and return without changing selection. Focus is not stored in the `selection` union. A review that derives reveal state from the currently focused element would collapse two independent parts of the interface.

## Mismatch blocking is in the game

After two different faces are revealed, selection becomes `mismatch` with a remaining active interval. The core's mismatch branch returns unchanged state for every attempted activation until advancement closes the pair. The unmatched card buttons do not all acquire ARIA disabled state during this interval.

Movement and focus remain available. A player can inspect coordinates or prepare a next choice while the pair stays visible. Closing the mismatch does not force focus back to either revealed position. The game-state change removes their faces, while navigation memory remains where the player moved it.

The controller synchronizes active time before processing a card action. An activation arriving when the mismatch has already expired can therefore be processed after closure rather than being rejected against stale rendered state. The guard operates on current synchronized game state, not a CSS class observed a moment earlier.

The interval pauses while the document is hidden. That is a clock lifecycle behavior, not a mass change to card attributes. [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) and [Clock design](../architecture/clock-design.md) describe the timing model.

## Imported pause is in the session

Loading unfinished progress sets `session.paused`. `activateSession` returns immediately while that flag is true, before calling the core activation function. `tickSession` also rejects advancement while paused.

The Board does not receive paused as a prop. It continues rendering the loaded game's visible faces, matched states and navigation callbacks. Unmatched buttons remain semantically unmatched rather than becoming a new paused-card class. The load notice and Resume explain the paused session state outside the board.

A player can move focus while paused. Resume returns to the current remembered card before clearing the pause and removing its button. A snapshot with a pending mismatch then continues its remaining interval. A completed import is not paused and has no Resume button; all of its cards are already matched.

The automated accessibility journey explicitly checks that a paused unfinished import does not mark unmatched cards disabled. This is stronger than assuming paused and disabled are interchangeable words. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) describes the visible continuation controls.

## Deal and text controls stay usable

New Game and Restart are available during ordinary play, mismatch waiting and imported pause. Their controller operations replace the game and clear the old session context. There is no busy-state branch disabling them while a timer is active.

The reproduction actions also remain available. An invalid draft is submitted for validation rather than causing its load button to become disabled before the user can request a result. Export reads current progress without replacing the game. A valid load can replace a paused or active position through the same validated boundary.

The current forms do not use `required`, a disabled submit button or `aria-invalid` as their validation mechanism. Their native length limits constrain editing, and the controller reports invalid content on action. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) traces those outcomes and the preservation of drafts.

This describes the existing controls, not a new general rule that every possible action in a future feature is always enabled. The relevant question in review is which layer owns the reason an action cannot change state, and whether the element's semantics and focus behavior match that reason.

## Rendering, counters and no-op actions

Core activation returns the original object for invalid indices, matched positions, repeated first positions and mismatch blocking. The session preserves identity when the core does. That lets the surrounding controller avoid committing a new state for an ignored action.

Synchronization can still advance elapsed time before the ignored activation is considered. Seeing Time change around a no-op click does not mean the click added a move. The move count changes only when a second eligible card resolves an attempt, subject to its cap.

At completion, every index is matched, so further card activation follows the matched guard. The final clock stays stopped because advancement checks `isWon`. There is no extra completed-overlay element that captures clicks above the board.

These details help distinguish a correct ignored action from a lost input. A click on a hidden eligible card in a closed active game should reveal it. A click on a matched card should not change the turn. Both can deliver the same native event; their game-state eligibility differs.

## Review evidence

The useful checks pair an input with both its state effect and its focus effect. The keyboard test checks matched inactivity while focus remains. The input-contract test checks hidden controls' exact ARIA attributes. The accessibility journey checks matched disabled exposure and paused unmatched exposure. Session unit tests check paused activation and advancement independently of the DOM.

A defect report can name the card coordinate, its visible state, session pause status, selection kind and expected counter change. That information reveals whether the problem belongs to native focus, ARIA exposure, controller timing or core eligibility. Treating every ignored input as the same disabled-control problem would hide those distinctions.
# ADR 003: Distribute one HTML file

This record explains the single HTML distribution and the distinction between delivery and source organization.

## Context

A player should be able to save the game, open it later and still have the complete board, artwork and controls. A directory full of scripts, images and fonts creates several opportunities for a copied game to become incomplete. Moving just the HTML can lose a stylesheet; a remote font or sprite can stop loading away from the network. The original distribution discussion therefore focused on what a player actually receives.

The chosen artifact is `dist/index.html`. It contains the script, styles and artwork needed for play and can open directly from disk. The source remains a set of focused TypeScript, TSX and CSS files. Single-file delivery was never an argument for putting the whole implementation into one authored module. [Source layout](../architecture/source-layout.md) documents the source arrangement.

## Build decision

Vite combines React transformation with `vite-plugin-singlefile`. The main configuration sets the target to `es2023` and disables module preload. A preload helper would have no useful chunks to fetch in the final inline page. The source comment records that reason, and `build-output.e2e.test.ts` inspects the HTML for the unwanted fetch and preload code.

The source `index.html` is an entry document containing a root element and a module reference to `src/main.tsx`. It is not itself the final self-contained game. Copying it before a build would preserve a development entry path rather than deliver the playable artifact. This distinction matters when reporting that an offline test passed.

## What the choice buys

An offline copy is straightforward to archive and pass between machines. Inline SVG faces need no image directory. The system font needs no font request. There is no runtime account or service configuration to carry alongside the file. These choices reinforce the artifact boundary; see [ADR 004](adr-004-no-backend.md), [ADR 007](adr-007-svg-faces.md) and [ADR 027](adr-027-offline-first.md).

Browser tests cover the built artifact, including opening from a file URL with network access blocked. This is more informative than observing that a development server happened to have everything cached. The browser test command builds current source before running, so its distribution evidence refers to the current implementation.

## Tradeoffs

A single HTML file gives up separate long-lived asset caches. An update replaces the complete artifact rather than just a changed script. For a small game with generated artwork and no remote resources, that cost was accepted in exchange for reliable copying and local opening. The bundle is still a real bundle, so package size and build output remain relevant; [ADR 040](adr-040-file-size-aim.md) discusses the compact-artifact aim.

Saved preferences are a separate concern. Storage behavior for file URLs varies between browsers. The project uses a local HTTP origin when checking persistence, while direct disk opening checks that the game plays. A usable offline artifact does not promise that every browser treats its file storage like a stable web origin.

The diagnostic face sheet and session harness also have single-file builds, but they are separate outputs under `.art` and `.session`. They are not extra files a player needs, and they are not embedded debugging routes inside the shipped page. [ADR 051](adr-051-test-artifacts.md) explains why that separation is useful.

## The distribution configuration

The same configuration used by the build keeps development watcher exclusions separate from the offline output settings.

```ts
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react';
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
import { viteSingleFile } from 'vite-plugin-singlefile';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react(), viteSingleFile()],
  // One inline file has no chunks to preload, so leave out the preload helper and its fetch call.
  build: { target: 'es2023', modulePreload: false },
  server: {
    watch: {
      ignored: ['**/.browser-work/**', '**/.playwright-browsers/**', '**/.npm-cache/**'],
    },
  },
});
```
# ADR 057: Split the view by behavior

This record explains the component boundaries and the targeted rendering work that keeps large boards responsive.

## Context

A single game component could contain the select, status, 256 buttons, snapshot editor, timers and storage effects. That would be quick to start and difficult to review once input, import and visibility interact. The project instead separates the view by behavior while keeping the composition easy to follow.

`Game.tsx` is the assembly point. `Controls` owns deal actions, `GameStatus` renders progress and completion, `Board` renders and navigates cards, and `Reproduction` owns the disclosure and drafts. Browser session behavior lives behind `useGame`. These boundaries correspond to real responsibilities rather than a generic component taxonomy.

## Small does not mean responsibility-free

`Card` is a leaf button with the state descriptor, face renderer and event callbacks it needs. `Board` calculates face-up and matched membership and supplies positional props. `useBoardFocus` owns remembered focus and navigation. The session controller decides how an activation changes the game and when browser time is synchronized.

This arrangement prevents a card from reading storage or deciding whether a snapshot load should pause. It also prevents the controller from querying every button to paint its revealed state. Each layer can be understood in terms of the data or browser effect it actually owns. [React boundaries](../architecture/react-boundaries.md) explains those connections.

## A concrete rendering concern

The active clock can update often, and a 16x16 board contains many buttons. The board memoizes the face-up set from matched positions and selection, and separately memoizes matched membership. It passes a stable activation callback that reads the latest handler through a ref. `Card` is memoized.

A pure clock tick that preserves selection and matched arrays therefore does not force every unchanged card to render again. The optimization follows an observed repeating update. It is not a reason to make every value global or to hide the data flow behind a subscription framework.

## Styles and tests follow the boundary

Card styles sit with `Card`, board layout with `Board`, status styles with `GameStatus`, and control styles with controls. The diagnostic face sheet renders the actual card outside the main controls to verify that its appearance does not depend on unrelated parent styling. That is useful evidence that the component owns its own presentation.

Focused tests sit near the associated behavior, while browser journeys span the assembled application. The source-size specification aims for 100 lines per TypeScript file and limits authored files to 200 lines. The audit checks that ceiling. These constraints keep authored files reviewable.

## Alternatives

A monolithic component would reduce imports but mix unrelated reasons to change. Splitting every few lines into a new component would create indirection without a stable behavior boundary. A generic reusable-control framework could add configuration for cases this game does not have. The chosen middle ground uses small named pieces with concrete jobs.

Props do repeat some data, but that repetition is visible and type checked. A reviewer can trace how a closed card receives `null` instead of a face ID. Hiding that relationship behind an ambient store would make the information boundary harder to inspect.

## Consequences

More files mean more navigation, so direct imports and meaningful ownership matter. The payoff is that a focus bug, parser fix or status-layout change usually has an identifiable home. [ADR 001](adr-001-react.md), [ADR 016](adr-016-no-state-library.md), [CSS organization](../architecture/css-organization.md) and [Source layout](../architecture/source-layout.md) are the companion pages. The aim is understandable behavior with targeted rendering work, not file count as an end in itself.

## Stable card inputs in the board

The board keeps membership calculations and callback identity stable across clock-only renders, while the latest controller callback remains reachable.

```tsx
const { size, deck, matched, selection } = game;
  const { viewport, element, focused, focusRemembered, navigate, cardFocused } =
    useBoardFocus(size);
  useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({ focusRemembered }), [focusRemembered]);
  // A clock tick keeps both arrays, so the cards' props stay equal and no card renders again.
  const faceUp = useMemo(() => faceUpCards({ matched, selection }), [matched, selection]);
  const matchedCards = useMemo(() => new Set(matched), [matched]);
  // The game passes a new handler on each render. Cards keep one callback that calls the latest.
  const latestActivate = useRef(activate);
  useLayoutEffect(() => {
    latestActivate.current = activate;
  });
  const activateCard = useCallback((index: number) => latestActivate.current(index), []);
  const style: BoardStyle = { '--grid-size': size };
```
# React boundaries

This page explains where React participates in Neon Pairs and where ordinary data functions remain independent of rendering.

React mounts the application, holds the session for presentation, owns local UI state and manages browser-effect lifetimes. The game rules are callable outside React. That separation lets the browser UI and replay CLI share behavior without teaching the core about components, effects or DOM events.

## The mounted tree

`src/main.tsx` calls `createRoot` after checking the `root` element and renders `Game` inside `StrictMode`. `Game.tsx` composes deal controls, status, feedback, board and reproduction controls. It calls `useGame` once to obtain the current session and actions.

The component tree is intentionally direct. There is no React context carrying a global game store and no router coordinating separate screens. `Controls` receives size and two actions. `GameStatus` receives a game, an optional best and a celebration flag. `Board` receives the game and activation action. `Reproduction` receives current code context, exchange actions and pause-related presentation.

These props describe the existing contracts. A component can render data it does not own without gaining responsibility for deciding a turn. The core still computes matches, move counts, elapsed advancement and victory.

## The data-only side

`deck.ts`, `game.ts`, `selection.ts`, `elapsed-time.ts`, `saved-format.ts`, `snapshot.ts`, `snapshot-selection.ts` and `replay.ts` do not import React. They accept values and return values. `session/session.ts` is also a data transformation module, although it lives beside hooks that import React.

The board has data-only helpers too. `keyboard.ts` computes a target from keys and coordinates. `card-state.ts` computes a state description. `face-design.ts` maps an integer identity to design values. These helpers can be tested without rendering `Board` or building a synthetic browser tree.

This is the meaningful interpretation of the React boundary: importing a rule in a CLI does not start an effect or require a mounted component. It is not a claim that every file ending in `.ts` is independent of React. `use-board-focus.ts`, `nearest-scroll.ts` and the session hooks are TypeScript modules with hooks and browser behavior.

## React imports in application code

| Module | React mechanisms used |
| --- | --- |
| `main.tsx` | `StrictMode`; root rendering through React DOM |
| `Game.tsx` | Ref for the board's focus interface |
| `Board.tsx` | Memoized derivations, refs, stable callback, layout effect and imperative handle |
| `Card.tsx` | `memo` and a keyboard event type |
| `use-board-focus.ts` | Local state, refs and callbacks |
| `nearest-scroll.ts` | Ref, effect and callback |
| `BoardCodeForm.tsx` | Ref for the successful-load focus target |
| `Reproduction.tsx` | Local snapshot draft state |
| `use-game.ts` | Session state and current-value ref |
| `use-session-clock.ts` | Clock/visibility refs and timer effect |
| `use-saved-preferences.ts` | Persistence effect |

`Controls`, `GameStatus` and `Face` contain JSX without importing a React runtime object. The compiler uses `jsx: react-jsx`, so those files do not need the older `import React` pattern. JSX participation and explicit hook imports are related but different observations.

The diagnostic entries also use React DOM. The face sheet renders real cards, while the session harness mounts and unmounts the real game. Their entrypoints are outside `src` and built separately, so they do not become extra runtime controls in the distributed game.

## One action path for activation

`Card` renders a native button and invokes its supplied activation callback from `onClick`. Native keyboard activation and ordinary pointer activation therefore reach the same controller action. The keydown handler delegates navigation; it does not implement another matching algorithm.

The controller synchronizes active time and calls `activateSession`, which calls `activateCard`. Components receive the resulting state and render it. A class such as `matched` is an outcome of the data, not the authoritative record of a matched pair. Reading CSS classes back into the core would reverse that relationship.

Matched buttons use `aria-disabled`, keeping them in the board's focus model. The rule function still rejects activating matched positions. During a mismatch, the session does not mark every other button disabled; the core rejects new activations while that selection is pending. Semantic presentation and transition legality are both visible, with legality centralized in the rules.

## Latest values without another store

`useGame` keeps React state for rendering and a ref for immediate event-time access. `commit` updates the ref before setting React state. A clock synchronization can therefore commit a new game, and the immediately following activation can consume that new game in the same task.

The board has a similar but narrower pattern for callback identity. `Game` supplies a new activation function as it renders. `Board` stores that function in `latestActivate`, updates the ref in a layout effect and passes a stable `useCallback` wrapper to cards. Memoized cards see a stable function prop while it calls the latest controller closure.

These refs do not bypass the rules. They keep the correct data/action visible across render scheduling. The data transition still returns a new immutable description, and React still receives the committed session. [Session module](session-module.md) explains why the current ref matters for export and activation boundaries.

## Render cost on a large board

A 16 by 16 board has 256 cards. Active time can update on the 40ms observation cadence, but most ticks do not change any card's appearance. `advanceGame` retains the deck and matched array and, outside a mismatch change, retains the selection object. `Board` memoizes face-up and matched sets from those references.

`Card` is wrapped in `memo`. Its props are primitive presentation values and stable callbacks. On an elapsed-only update, face, matched, tabIndex, size and handlers stay equal, so the cards do not all need to rerender. The parent can still update the statistic.

A pending mismatch changes selection as its remainder decreases, so the face-up set can be recomputed. The resulting card props can nevertheless remain equal until the selection actually closes. This distinction explains why immutable reference stability is useful even though the board's parent renders more often than its cards.

Memoization is not a substitute for correct state ownership. Mutating the matched array in place could keep its reference stable while changing its meaning, causing derived sets to miss an update. The transition code returns a new matched array when a pair is found, matching the assumptions of the board's memoization.

## Concealed identity is a prop boundary

`Board` knows the immutable deck, but it passes `face={null}` for every position outside the derived face-up set. `Card` then renders only a decorative back. It does not mount `Face` and hide it with CSS. Its accessible description omits face design when the supplied face is null.

When revealed or matched, a card gets the face number and renders inline SVG. `Face` marks the SVG as decorative, while the button's label describes the visible design. The board can therefore hold authoritative identity without exposing concealed identity through every child element.

This behavior is also why tests use documented board codes rather than a diagnostic global. A test can reconstruct a deal independently and activate matching positions through the public interface. There is no application solver endpoint that a production user or test needs to query.

## Local focus and DOM work

`useBoardFocus` holds a focused index initialized to zero and refs to the viewport and grid. Arrow handling calls `navigationTarget`; a non-null result prevents the browser default and focuses the target button with `preventScroll: true`. Focus events update the remembered index.

`useNearestScroll` listens to the board viewport's scroll events and remembers the reported position. For keyboard focus it restores that position before calling `scrollIntoView` with nearest alignment. This accounts for Chromium's automatic centering on focus. A click scrolls after activation so the pressed card is not moved under a held pointer before release.

These browser operations belong with the board presentation, not `GameState`. A replay contains positions and logical times, not a scroll offset. A snapshot can load into a differently sized viewport. Keeping focus and scrolling local preserves that independence.

## Replacement and imperative focus

`Game` gives `Board` a ref typed as `BoardFocus`. The board exposes only `focusRemembered()` through `useImperativeHandle`. The parent does not receive the whole grid DOM or a collection of card nodes.

Resume uses that limited operation, then calls the controller's resume action. A replacement instead increments generation and changes the board key, remounting its local focus state. `BoardCodeForm` keys its uncontrolled input by that same generation, so successful loading replaces the old draft with the current code.

A generation is consequently a lifecycle boundary shared by adapters and components. It is not a reason to put DOM state in the session core. The rule functions remain unaware of keyed mounts, refs or focus methods.

## Effects and cleanup

Browser effects pair setup with cleanup: the clock removes its listener and timeout, and nearest scrolling removes its viewport listener. The separate session harness lets tests unmount the real game and measure that cleanup. [Clock design](clock-design.md) details the active flag, generation checks and scheduling lifetime.

## Keeping a change on the right side

An incorrect pair count starts in the game state and derivation, not in JSX text. An incorrect load-pause state starts in session replacement, not a disabled style. An incorrect arrow stop starts in the numerical navigation helper, while an incorrect scroll alignment starts in the DOM hook. The boundary narrows where an explanation should begin.

The architecture specification permits shared support when two actual behaviors need the same meaning. It does not introduce a generic hooks or utilities layer merely because several files use React. Current direct imports keep ownership legible, and the module policy describes feature placement. Together they make small components useful without making rendering the owner of the game rules.

# Randomness policy

This page explains the boundary between choosing a fresh deal and reproducing a deal in Neon Pairs.

A new board needs an unpredictable seed. A board code, restart, imported snapshot and replay need the opposite property: a particular code always reconstructs the same deck. The implementation keeps those two tasks separate rather than letting a shuffle consult ambient state. [Deck generation](../gameplay/deck-generation.md) covers the deal algorithm as a format; this page concentrates on its source ownership and integration.

## One boundary for fresh input

`src/game/session/fresh-board.ts` exports `freshBoardCode(size, previousSeed?)`. It obtains a seed and returns the normal board-code representation through `boardCode` from `deck.ts`. Only src/game/session/fresh-board.ts may call a random source. Everything else that needs randomness imports it from there. The session controller uses that exported operation when initializing a session or asking for a new game.

The distinction is visible in the imports. `use-game.ts` imports `freshBoardCode` for fresh deals and `createGame` for constructing a game from a code. `game.ts` imports `generateBoard`, which works from supplied data. Nothing in a card component needs to choose a seed, and no deck is shuffled merely because React rendered it.

## Two finite ranges

The fresh-board module uses a one-element `Uint32Array` and `crypto.getRandomValues`. Its possible raw values span the unsigned 32-bit range, with `UINT32_RANGE` set to `2 ** 32`. The allowed seed range is defined in `deck.ts` by `SEED_MAX = 2_147_483_646`. Valid codes use positive seeds, so the transformation adds one after taking a remainder.

The module computes `RANDOM_LIMIT = Math.floor(UINT32_RANGE / SEED_MAX) * SEED_MAX`. With the current values the limit is `4_294_967_292`. A draw below that limit is accepted; one at or above it is retried. Thus each allowed remainder has the same number of accepted raw values. The last four unsigned values do not enter the modulo mapping.

The seed is `(draw % SEED_MAX) + 1`. Its endpoints are therefore 1 and `SEED_MAX`; zero is not produced. The code also checks that `buffer[0]` is defined, which matches the project's checked-index TypeScript setting even though the buffer length is deliberately one. It loops until it can return a valid code.

This is rejection sampling, not rounding a floating-point draw. Applying a plain remainder to all `2 ** 32` possible values would assign a few seeds one more source value than the others. The difference is small numerically, but a reproducible format benefits from an implementation whose range treatment can be described exactly.

## Excluding the immediately previous seed

When `previousSeed` is supplied, a candidate equal to it is discarded. `use-game.ts` passes the current game's seed when creating a new game, including when a different grid size is selected. This means the next seed differs from the immediately preceding seed even across a size change.

That check is narrower than a history of every generated deal. The implementation does not keep a seed registry, does not persist a sequence of fresh codes and does not exclude every seed seen earlier in the session. A code can reappear after intervening games. Nor does the initial call pass an earlier browser session's seed; preferences retain size and best moves, not the last active deal.

The retry loop also does not claim a bounded number of calls. It retries out-of-range draws and an excluded candidate. There is no time-based fallback in this module. A browser crypto failure is not caught here. The storage module's tolerant behavior should not be mistaken for a universal fallback around every browser API.

## Construction after selection

Once the seed is selected, `boardCode(size, seed)` validates the representation. Its format is `np1-SIZE-SEED`, with the supported sizes supplied by `GRID_SIZES`. The parser accepts exactly the seven sizes 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16. It also checks that the seed is a safe integer within the allowed maximum.

`createGame(code)` calls `generateBoard(code)` and adds the initial progress fields. The starting deck is already determined by that point. The game starts with no matched positions, a closed selection, zero moves, zero elapsed milliseconds and `started: false`.

The code-producing function can throw for an invalid size or seed. The session's `newGame` action checks the requested size with `isValidSize` before requesting a fresh code. Its normal UI callers use the native select populated from `GRID_SIZES`. These checks protect the application path without adding a second size list to the form.

## Deterministic state is not ambient entropy

`deck.ts` exports `nextRandomState(state)`, but this function is arithmetic over an explicit argument. It computes `(state * 16_807) % 2_147_483_647`. Repeating a call with the same state returns the same result. The name describes a pseudorandom sequence; it does not imply a browser read.

For a valid seed, the generator advances that sequence inside a descending Fisher–Yates shuffle. The initial deck contains two copies of every integer face from zero to `size ** 2 / 2 - 1`, arranged as adjacent duplicates before shuffling. For a 4 by 4 board, it starts as `0, 0, 1, 1` and so on through face 7.

At shuffle position `index`, the number of choices is `index + 1`. The implementation computes a divisible acceptance limit from `SEED_MAX`, advances its local generator state, subtracts one to form the draw, rejects values outside the limit and uses the accepted remainder as the swap position. Both the raw seed selection and the shuffle use rejection, but they operate on different ranges and have different owners.

The maximum multiplication in the sequence is below JavaScript's safe integer limit. The independent browser-test oracle uses BigInt arithmetic, providing a separate expression of the same documented deal rather than calling the production generator to predict itself. [Purity guide](purity-guide.md) explains why explicit state makes these checks possible.

## A concrete stable example

The fixture code `np1-4-1` produces this row-major deck:

```text
6 7 0 5
2 2 0 5
3 7 1 6
4 4 1 3
```

Positions are zero based in rules and formats. Positions 2 and 6 are a pair; positions 0 and 11 are another. The fixture's `EXAMPLE_DECK` stores the whole literal sequence, while `EXAMPLE_PAIRS` lists the matching positions. Those are test facts, not attributes added to hidden cards in the shipped DOM.

Changing the shuffle traversal, recurrence, rejection condition or starting deck would change this example and potentially every shared code. Such a change is therefore observable through board codes, snapshots and replays, even if the interface still looks like a memory game. The generator's determinism connects implementation detail to a public format.

## Every action that chooses or reuses a deal

| Path | Seed behavior in the current implementation |
| --- | --- |
| Initial `useGame` state | Fresh seed using the saved valid size or default size |
| New Game | Fresh seed excluding the current seed |
| Grid-size selection | Fresh seed for the selected size, excluding the current seed |
| Restart | Existing board code passed to `createGame` |
| Load board | Submitted code trimmed, parsed and reconstructed |
| Load snapshot | Decoder validates its code and reconstructs its deck |
| Replay | Reader validates the supplied code and starts from it |

This table is useful when a bug report says that “a new board changed.” A new game is expected to change the seed. A restart or imported code is expected to repeat the existing deal. A size selection is a fresh deal rather than a geometric rearrangement of the old cards.

`newGame` also resets the clock and replaces the session game. Seed choice alone does not clear progress or focus; session replacement and the generation key supply those lifetimes. [Session module](session-module.md) covers that process.

## Evidence and blind spots

`deck.test.ts` covers board-code parsing, generated structure and known vectors. `deck-rejection.test.ts` reads independent BigInt vectors for an over-limit draw and a draw exactly on the shuffle limit. The equality boundary matters because accepting it would break the uniform mapping and alter the deterministic result for that seed.

The browser suite loads documented codes through actual controls and uses `specDeal` from `tests/deal-oracle.ts` when it needs an independent deal. `lifecycle.e2e.test.ts` checks that New Game changes the current code and that a size change chooses a different seed from the previous deal. A complete all-size journey checks that the resulting decks remain playable.

The fresh-board module has no adjacent unit test. Deterministic deck tests establish format behavior and known sequences, rather than statistical properties of the browser entropy source. The raw seed boundary is short enough to inspect directly, but inspection is a different kind of evidence.

The source audit's core list rejects browser entropy references in the named core files. It does not implement a whole-program information-flow proof or a general scanner for every possible source of variation. [Source audit notes](source-audit-notes.md) describes precisely what it scans.

## Diagnosing an unexpected deck

The most useful reproduction is the board code, not the time the game started. Parsing that code reveals both size and seed. Calling `generateBoard` with it establishes the expected deck without involving React or browser state. An imported snapshot reconstructs that same deck and then validates progress against it.

If the code differs, investigate which action replaced the session. If the code agrees but the deck differs, compare the shuffle against the literal vector and independent oracle. If the deck agrees but the wrong art appears, investigate `faceDesign`, reveal state and card props. These are distinct failures with different evidence.

A hidden card deliberately receives `null` as its face prop. Looking for all face identities in its DOM is not a valid debugging strategy for this application boundary. Tests already have the code and can derive a deck independently. [React boundaries](react-boundaries.md) describes that presentation decision in context.
# Acceptance
Acceptance is a set of journeys that checks whether Neon Pairs meets its product requirements.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Finish a game, then start another one during a mismatch. The first journey checks play and completion. The second checks that an earlier timer can't change a new game.

## Play

Use these journeys with the requirements in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md):

- Finish every supported size with complete pairs.
- Reveal one card twice, then reveal a different card. Check the exact move count.
- Match a pair, then miss a pair. Check the immediate match and the 800ms active mismatch interval.
- Hide the page during a mismatch, then return and finish its remaining interval.
- Start and restart during a mismatch. Check the cleared state and later timer updates.
- Finish games with better, equal and worse move counts. Reload and check the current size's best.

## Controls

Use pointer, touch and keyboard to follow [Input](../interface/input.md) and [Controls](../interface/controls.md). Check control labels, row movement, edge stops, native Tab exit and focus after each action. Check that hidden cards reveal no identity in the DOM.

Follow the keyboard journey in I17 and check its accessibility tree. During user acceptance, confirm spoken results with a screen reader, including consecutive identical results and the final match with its win.

## Appearance

Measure the layout and review all 128 faces against [Visuals](../visuals/visuals.md). Use a 44px grayscale face sheet to distinguish shape, marker and fill. Check 16x16 boards at both stated viewport sizes, full focus outlines and the equivalent zoom layout. Check reduced motion and the static completion banner after its single pulse.

Play through completion and reset while checking [Sound](../sound/sound.md). Every action stays silent.

## Reproduction

Check [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) with its example deck and replay. Check snapshot round trips and malformed input. Check the exact mismatch timeout before an equal-time replay action.

Load an unfinished snapshot, attempt input while paused, then Resume. Check its remaining active time and focus. Load a completed snapshot and check its static banner and unchanged best score.

## Delivery

Use a locked install, type check, unit tests and a fresh browser build as defined in [Technology](../architecture/technology.md). Open the resulting HTML directly from disk with network access blocked. Use a local HTTP origin for saved preferences.

Review the pure game functions, browser effects, file sizes and behavior placement against [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md).

# Focus policy

This page records focus behavior in the current game and the policy for a feature that changes the main screen.

Focus tells a keyboard user where input will go next. It is related to game selection but is not stored as part of a turn or snapshot. The current interface deliberately keeps deal-action focus, remembered board focus and card reveal state as distinct things.

## Existing page and future screens

`Game.tsx` currently renders one main area with an h1, deal controls, statistics, instructions, turn output, the Board and reproduction controls. It has no alternate-screen branch or screen-level h2 focus target. Replacing a deal remounts the board within that page; it does not replace the page with a different screen.

A feature that introduces a screen replacement has a different orientation problem from resetting a deck. When a feature replaces what the main area shows, focus moves to that screen's h2, which has tabindex="-1". This gives the new screen a programmatic landing place without adding that heading to ordinary Tab traversal. The current deal and load callbacks can still be understood on their own terms; they are not evidence that such a screen transition already exists.

The policy applies to the feature-level replacement described here. Expanding native details, updating statistics, closing a mismatch or displaying the completed-game paragraph does not currently create a new screen. Those operations retain the page structure and follow the existing behavior below. [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) covers a separate interaction with its own opening focus.

## Initial load is quiet

The hook `useBoardFocus(size)` initializes `focused` to zero. Board gives index 0 a tab index of zero and the other card buttons a tab index of minus one. This makes the first card available on entry, but no mount effect calls its focus method.

The browser's current focus therefore remains where it is at initial load. The page does not jump down to the board before a player has found Grid size or New Game. The board help paragraph describes how to enter and operate it. Its region uses `aria-describedby="board-help"` to associate those instructions with the board.

A remembered entry point is often described casually as “focus on the first card.” In this code that wording is incomplete. There is an entry point ready at the first card, while actual focus may be on the document, a deal button or another native control. Keeping those concepts separate prevents accidental mount-time focus stealing.

## Deal actions retain their location

New Game and Restart are native buttons that call the session controller. Neither callback moves focus into the board. After either action, a keyboard user remains on the button they used and can repeat the action or Tab toward the board. The size select uses its native interaction and likewise does not issue a board focus call.

The replacement increments `session.generation`, used as Board's React key. The newly mounted hook begins with a remembered index of zero. Thus the next board entry goes to the first card, even if the previous deal's memory was near its end. Actual action focus and future board entry are updated through different mechanisms.

A valid board-code load also increments generation. BoardCodeForm focuses its Load board ref on successful submission because its input is keyed by generation and will be replaced. That is especially important when the action was Enter in the input. An invalid submission keeps the input node and does not call the button ref, so correction can continue in place.

Clicking the load button starts with focus on that button, and an invalid click leaves it there. The distinction is based on the action's origin and successful input replacement, not on a general rule that all errors move focus into a field. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) follows those cases in detail.

## Remembered board focus

Board focus memory is a local hook state containing a card index. The `onFocus` callback updates it whenever a card receives focus. Board renders exactly that index with `tabIndex={0}`. All other cards remain programmatically focusable with `tabIndex={-1}`.

Arrow movement uses the DOM order of the deck and never changes game selection on its own. Tab and Shift+Tab are left to the browser, so the board is one stop in the page sequence rather than a trap. Returning to it finds the last focused card, even if that card is now matched.

Matched positions stay in the navigation geometry. A player does not need to relearn how many arrow presses separate two coordinates after a match. During a mismatch, focus can also move while activation is blocked. The same is true while imported unfinished progress waits for Resume. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) provides the calculations and edge behavior.

## Resume transfers before removal

Resume is the current exception to retaining focus on the action button. It exists only while `session.paused` is true. Clearing that flag removes the button, so leaving focus there would leave a disappearing target.

In `Game.tsx`, the local `resume()` function first calls `board.current?.focusRemembered()` and then `controller.resume()`. Board's imperative method focuses the remembered card with `preventScroll: true` and then brings it into view. Only after that does the controller clear the paused state and notices.

The ordering is observable. `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` installs a focus listener and confirms that Resume is still present when the card receives focus. A visual assertion after the fact would not establish this timing. The focus-entry test also remembers a far card on a large imported board, scrolls away and confirms that Resume returns to that location with nearest alignment.

The remembered location after import is initially the first card because the import replaced the board. The player can change it while paused. Resume uses that current memory rather than the snapshot's revealed index or a hard-coded first card. A snapshot stores game progress, not the browser's last navigation location.
