# ADR 003: Distribute one HTML file

This record explains the single HTML distribution and the distinction between delivery and source organization.

## Context

A player should be able to save the game, open it later and still have the complete board, artwork and controls. A directory full of scripts, images and fonts creates several opportunities for a copied game to become incomplete. Moving just the HTML can lose a stylesheet; a remote font or sprite can stop loading away from the network. The original distribution discussion therefore focused on what a player actually receives.

The chosen artifact is `dist/index.html`. It contains the script, styles and artwork needed for play and can open directly from disk. The source remains a set of focused TypeScript, TSX and CSS files. Single-file delivery was never an argument for putting the whole implementation into one authored module. [Source layout](../architecture/source-layout.md) documents the source arrangement.

## Build decision

Vite combines React transformation with `vite-plugin-singlefile`. The main configuration sets the target to `es2023` and disables module preload. A preload helper would have no useful chunks to fetch in the final inline page. The source comment records that reason, and `build-output.e2e.test.ts` inspects the HTML for the unwanted fetch and preload code.

The source `index.html` is an entry document containing a root element and a module reference to `src/main.tsx`. It is not itself the final self-contained game. Copying it before a build would preserve a development entry path rather than deliver the playable artifact. This distinction matters when reporting that an offline test passed.

## What the choice buys

An offline copy is straightforward to archive and pass between machines. Inline SVG faces need no image directory. The system font needs no font request. There is no runtime account or service configuration to carry alongside the file. These choices reinforce the artifact boundary; see [ADR 004](adr-004-no-backend.md), [ADR 007](adr-007-svg-faces.md) and [ADR 027](adr-027-offline-first.md).

Browser tests cover the built artifact, including opening from a file URL with network access blocked. This is more informative than observing that a development server happened to have everything cached. The browser test command builds current source before running, so its distribution evidence refers to the current implementation.

## Tradeoffs

A single HTML file gives up separate long-lived asset caches. An update replaces the complete artifact rather than just a changed script. For a small game with generated artwork and no remote resources, that cost was accepted in exchange for reliable copying and local opening. The bundle is still a real bundle, so package size and build output remain relevant; [ADR 040](adr-040-file-size-aim.md) discusses the compact-artifact aim.

Saved preferences are a separate concern. Storage behavior for file URLs varies between browsers. The project uses a local HTTP origin when checking persistence, while direct disk opening checks that the game plays. A usable offline artifact does not promise that every browser treats its file storage like a stable web origin.

The diagnostic face sheet and session harness also have single-file builds, but they are separate outputs under `.art` and `.session`. They are not extra files a player needs, and they are not embedded debugging routes inside the shipped page. [ADR 051](adr-051-test-artifacts.md) explains why that separation is useful.

## The distribution configuration

The same configuration used by the build keeps development watcher exclusions separate from the offline output settings.

```ts
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react';
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
import { viteSingleFile } from 'vite-plugin-singlefile';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react(), viteSingleFile()],
  // One inline file has no chunks to preload, so leave out the preload helper and its fetch call.
  build: { target: 'es2023', modulePreload: false },
  server: {
    watch: {
      ignored: ['**/.browser-work/**', '**/.playwright-browsers/**', '**/.npm-cache/**'],
    },
  },
});
```
# ADR 057: Split the view by behavior

This record explains the component boundaries and the targeted rendering work that keeps large boards responsive.

## Context

A single game component could contain the select, status, 256 buttons, snapshot editor, timers and storage effects. That would be quick to start and difficult to review once input, import and visibility interact. The project instead separates the view by behavior while keeping the composition easy to follow.

`Game.tsx` is the assembly point. `Controls` owns deal actions, `GameStatus` renders progress and completion, `Board` renders and navigates cards, and `Reproduction` owns the disclosure and drafts. Browser session behavior lives behind `useGame`. These boundaries correspond to real responsibilities rather than a generic component taxonomy.

## Small does not mean responsibility-free

`Card` is a leaf button with the state descriptor, face renderer and event callbacks it needs. `Board` calculates face-up and matched membership and supplies positional props. `useBoardFocus` owns remembered focus and navigation. The session controller decides how an activation changes the game and when browser time is synchronized.

This arrangement prevents a card from reading storage or deciding whether a snapshot load should pause. It also prevents the controller from querying every button to paint its revealed state. Each layer can be understood in terms of the data or browser effect it actually owns. [React boundaries](../architecture/react-boundaries.md) explains those connections.

## A concrete rendering concern

The active clock can update often, and a 16x16 board contains many buttons. The board memoizes the face-up set from matched positions and selection, and separately memoizes matched membership. It passes a stable activation callback that reads the latest handler through a ref. `Card` is memoized.

A pure clock tick that preserves selection and matched arrays therefore does not force every unchanged card to render again. The optimization follows an observed repeating update. It is not a reason to make every value global or to hide the data flow behind a subscription framework.

## Styles and tests follow the boundary

Card styles sit with `Card`, board layout with `Board`, status styles with `GameStatus`, and control styles with controls. The diagnostic face sheet renders the actual card outside the main controls to verify that its appearance does not depend on unrelated parent styling. That is useful evidence that the component owns its own presentation.

Focused tests sit near the associated behavior, while browser journeys span the assembled application. The source-size specification aims for 100 lines per TypeScript file and limits authored files to 200 lines. The audit checks that ceiling. These constraints keep authored files reviewable.

## Alternatives

A monolithic component would reduce imports but mix unrelated reasons to change. Splitting every few lines into a new component would create indirection without a stable behavior boundary. A generic reusable-control framework could add configuration for cases this game does not have. The chosen middle ground uses small named pieces with concrete jobs.

Props do repeat some data, but that repetition is visible and type checked. A reviewer can trace how a closed card receives `null` instead of a face ID. Hiding that relationship behind an ambient store would make the information boundary harder to inspect.

## Consequences

More files mean more navigation, so direct imports and meaningful ownership matter. The payoff is that a focus bug, parser fix or status-layout change usually has an identifiable home. [ADR 001](adr-001-react.md), [ADR 016](adr-016-no-state-library.md), [CSS organization](../architecture/css-organization.md) and [Source layout](../architecture/source-layout.md) are the companion pages. The aim is understandable behavior with targeted rendering work, not file count as an end in itself.

## Stable card inputs in the board

The board keeps membership calculations and callback identity stable across clock-only renders, while the latest controller callback remains reachable.

```tsx
const { size, deck, matched, selection } = game;
  const { viewport, element, focused, focusRemembered, navigate, cardFocused } =
    useBoardFocus(size);
  useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({ focusRemembered }), [focusRemembered]);
  // A clock tick keeps both arrays, so the cards' props stay equal and no card renders again.
  const faceUp = useMemo(() => faceUpCards({ matched, selection }), [matched, selection]);
  const matchedCards = useMemo(() => new Set(matched), [matched]);
  // The game passes a new handler on each render. Cards keep one callback that calls the latest.
  const latestActivate = useRef(activate);
  useLayoutEffect(() => {
    latestActivate.current = activate;
  });
  const activateCard = useCallback((index: number) => latestActivate.current(index), []);
  const style: BoardStyle = { '--grid-size': size };
```
# React boundaries

This page explains where React participates in Neon Pairs and where ordinary data functions remain independent of rendering.

React mounts the application, holds the session for presentation, owns local UI state and manages browser-effect lifetimes. The game rules are callable outside React. That separation lets the browser UI and replay CLI share behavior without teaching the core about components, effects or DOM events.

## The mounted tree

`src/main.tsx` calls `createRoot` after checking the `root` element and renders `Game` inside `StrictMode`. `Game.tsx` composes deal controls, status, feedback, board and reproduction controls. It calls `useGame` once to obtain the current session and actions.

The component tree is intentionally direct. There is no React context carrying a global game store and no router coordinating separate screens. `Controls` receives size and two actions. `GameStatus` receives a game, an optional best and a celebration flag. `Board` receives the game and activation action. `Reproduction` receives current code context, exchange actions and pause-related presentation.

These props describe the existing contracts. A component can render data it does not own without gaining responsibility for deciding a turn. The core still computes matches, move counts, elapsed advancement and victory.

## The data-only side

`deck.ts`, `game.ts`, `selection.ts`, `elapsed-time.ts`, `saved-format.ts`, `snapshot.ts`, `snapshot-selection.ts` and `replay.ts` do not import React. They accept values and return values. `session/session.ts` is also a data transformation module, although it lives beside hooks that import React.

The board has data-only helpers too. `keyboard.ts` computes a target from keys and coordinates. `card-state.ts` computes a state description. `face-design.ts` maps an integer identity to design values. These helpers can be tested without rendering `Board` or building a synthetic browser tree.

This is the meaningful interpretation of the React boundary: importing a rule in a CLI does not start an effect or require a mounted component. It is not a claim that every file ending in `.ts` is independent of React. `use-board-focus.ts`, `nearest-scroll.ts` and the session hooks are TypeScript modules with hooks and browser behavior.

## React imports in application code

| Module | React mechanisms used |
| --- | --- |
| `main.tsx` | `StrictMode`; root rendering through React DOM |
| `Game.tsx` | Ref for the board's focus interface |
| `Board.tsx` | Memoized derivations, refs, stable callback, layout effect and imperative handle |
| `Card.tsx` | `memo` and a keyboard event type |
| `use-board-focus.ts` | Local state, refs and callbacks |
| `nearest-scroll.ts` | Ref, effect and callback |
| `BoardCodeForm.tsx` | Ref for the successful-load focus target |
| `Reproduction.tsx` | Local snapshot draft state |
| `use-game.ts` | Session state and current-value ref |
| `use-session-clock.ts` | Clock/visibility refs and timer effect |
| `use-saved-preferences.ts` | Persistence effect |

`Controls`, `GameStatus` and `Face` contain JSX without importing a React runtime object. The compiler uses `jsx: react-jsx`, so those files do not need the older `import React` pattern. JSX participation and explicit hook imports are related but different observations.

The diagnostic entries also use React DOM. The face sheet renders real cards, while the session harness mounts and unmounts the real game. Their entrypoints are outside `src` and built separately, so they do not become extra runtime controls in the distributed game.

## One action path for activation

`Card` renders a native button and invokes its supplied activation callback from `onClick`. Native keyboard activation and ordinary pointer activation therefore reach the same controller action. The keydown handler delegates navigation; it does not implement another matching algorithm.

The controller synchronizes active time and calls `activateSession`, which calls `activateCard`. Components receive the resulting state and render it. A class such as `matched` is an outcome of the data, not the authoritative record of a matched pair. Reading CSS classes back into the core would reverse that relationship.

Matched buttons use `aria-disabled`, keeping them in the board's focus model. The rule function still rejects activating matched positions. During a mismatch, the session does not mark every other button disabled; the core rejects new activations while that selection is pending. Semantic presentation and transition legality are both visible, with legality centralized in the rules.

## Latest values without another store

`useGame` keeps React state for rendering and a ref for immediate event-time access. `commit` updates the ref before setting React state. A clock synchronization can therefore commit a new game, and the immediately following activation can consume that new game in the same task.

The board has a similar but narrower pattern for callback identity. `Game` supplies a new activation function as it renders. `Board` stores that function in `latestActivate`, updates the ref in a layout effect and passes a stable `useCallback` wrapper to cards. Memoized cards see a stable function prop while it calls the latest controller closure.

These refs do not bypass the rules. They keep the correct data/action visible across render scheduling. The data transition still returns a new immutable description, and React still receives the committed session. [Session module](session-module.md) explains why the current ref matters for export and activation boundaries.

## Render cost on a large board

A 16 by 16 board has 256 cards. Active time can update on the 40ms observation cadence, but most ticks do not change any card's appearance. `advanceGame` retains the deck and matched array and, outside a mismatch change, retains the selection object. `Board` memoizes face-up and matched sets from those references.

`Card` is wrapped in `memo`. Its props are primitive presentation values and stable callbacks. On an elapsed-only update, face, matched, tabIndex, size and handlers stay equal, so the cards do not all need to rerender. The parent can still update the statistic.

A pending mismatch changes selection as its remainder decreases, so the face-up set can be recomputed. The resulting card props can nevertheless remain equal until the selection actually closes. This distinction explains why immutable reference stability is useful even though the board's parent renders more often than its cards.

Memoization is not a substitute for correct state ownership. Mutating the matched array in place could keep its reference stable while changing its meaning, causing derived sets to miss an update. The transition code returns a new matched array when a pair is found, matching the assumptions of the board's memoization.

## Concealed identity is a prop boundary

`Board` knows the immutable deck, but it passes `face={null}` for every position outside the derived face-up set. `Card` then renders only a decorative back. It does not mount `Face` and hide it with CSS. Its accessible description omits face design when the supplied face is null.

When revealed or matched, a card gets the face number and renders inline SVG. `Face` marks the SVG as decorative, while the button's label describes the visible design. The board can therefore hold authoritative identity without exposing concealed identity through every child element.

This behavior is also why tests use documented board codes rather than a diagnostic global. A test can reconstruct a deal independently and activate matching positions through the public interface. There is no application solver endpoint that a production user or test needs to query.

## Local focus and DOM work

`useBoardFocus` holds a focused index initialized to zero and refs to the viewport and grid. Arrow handling calls `navigationTarget`; a non-null result prevents the browser default and focuses the target button with `preventScroll: true`. Focus events update the remembered index.

`useNearestScroll` listens to the board viewport's scroll events and remembers the reported position. For keyboard focus it restores that position before calling `scrollIntoView` with nearest alignment. This accounts for Chromium's automatic centering on focus. A click scrolls after activation so the pressed card is not moved under a held pointer before release.

These browser operations belong with the board presentation, not `GameState`. A replay contains positions and logical times, not a scroll offset. A snapshot can load into a differently sized viewport. Keeping focus and scrolling local preserves that independence.

## Replacement and imperative focus

`Game` gives `Board` a ref typed as `BoardFocus`. The board exposes only `focusRemembered()` through `useImperativeHandle`. The parent does not receive the whole grid DOM or a collection of card nodes.

Resume uses that limited operation, then calls the controller's resume action. A replacement instead increments generation and changes the board key, remounting its local focus state. `BoardCodeForm` keys its uncontrolled input by that same generation, so successful loading replaces the old draft with the current code.

A generation is consequently a lifecycle boundary shared by adapters and components. It is not a reason to put DOM state in the session core. The rule functions remain unaware of keyed mounts, refs or focus methods.

## Effects and cleanup

Browser effects pair setup with cleanup: the clock removes its listener and timeout, and nearest scrolling removes its viewport listener. The separate session harness lets tests unmount the real game and measure that cleanup. [Clock design](clock-design.md) details the active flag, generation checks and scheduling lifetime.

## Keeping a change on the right side

An incorrect pair count starts in the game state and derivation, not in JSX text. An incorrect load-pause state starts in session replacement, not a disabled style. An incorrect arrow stop starts in the numerical navigation helper, while an incorrect scroll alignment starts in the DOM hook. The boundary narrows where an explanation should begin.

The architecture specification permits shared support when two actual behaviors need the same meaning. It does not introduce a generic hooks or utilities layer merely because several files use React. Current direct imports keep ownership legible, and the module policy describes feature placement. Together they make small components useful without making rendering the owner of the game rules.

# Native controls guide

This page explains the native HTML elements used by Neon Pairs and the behavior they supply to the interface.

The source combines React event wiring with browser controls. It does not draw input controls on canvas or implement a replacement select menu. The resulting code leaves common editing, activation and disclosure behavior with the browser while keeping game decisions in the session and core.

## The current element choices

| Element | Use in the game | Application responsibility around it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `button` | Cards and actions | Decide what the activation changes |
| `select` with `option` | Grid size | Supply supported sizes and start a deal |
| `label` | Grid size and text fields | Associate visible names with field ids |
| `input` | Board-code draft | Read and validate the submitted code |
| `textarea` | Snapshot draft and export | Hold text and pass it to the snapshot decoder |
| `form` | Board-code submission | Prevent navigation and handle the result |
| `details` with `summary` | Reproduction disclosure | Supply content and layout |
| `dl` with `dt` and `dd` | Current game statistics | Derive the displayed values |

These choices describe the current DOM. Policies for other kinds of content are documented in [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) and [Tables policy](tables-policy.md), without implying that those elements already appear in Game.

## Buttons unify activation

Card renders a native button with `type="button"`. Its `onClick` sends an index to the shared activation path. Enter and Space can activate the same control through normal button behavior, so there is no separate keydown implementation of reveal.

The board's keydown handler only handles plain arrows with a navigation target. It does not call activation for Enter or Space and then also allow a native click. That avoids two paths processing one keyboard action. The game's pure activation guard still decides whether the card is eligible.

Action buttons outside the board use explicit types too. The Board code loader is `type="submit"` inside its form. New Game, Restart, Export snapshot, Load snapshot and Resume are `type="button"`. This makes submission intent visible in JSX rather than relying on where the browser happens to find an enclosing form.

A native button's semantics do not automatically implement ARIA-disabled behavior. Card uses `aria-disabled={matched}` while remaining focusable, and the game ignores matched activations. [Disabled state guide](disabled-state-guide.md) explains that deliberate split.

## The select keeps its native interaction

Controls renders a labeled select whose value comes from `game.size`. Each option comes from `GRID_SIZES` and has a numeric side length value with `NxN` display text. The browser supplies its dropdown interaction and option-selection behavior.

The component handles change by converting the selected value to a number and calling `newGame`. There is no local menu-open flag, active-option state or custom pointer hit testing. The controller still checks supported sizes, because native options are an interface aid rather than the only trust boundary.

The select inherits the shared font and panel colors through `.control`. Styling the border and background does not replace its role or its label relationship. The current CSS does not remove it in favor of an invisible field beneath a separately focusable drawn menu.

A successful board-code or snapshot load changes the actual game size, which flows back into this controlled select. The visible selected option therefore follows the model rather than a second UI-only size state. [Control bar](control-bar.md) covers that data flow.

## Text editing remains text editing

Board code is an input, and Snapshot JSON is a textarea. They retain selection, caret movement and browser editing operations. The textarea can resize vertically and receives readable export text without a clipboard permission dependency.

The card's `user-select: none` styling is scoped to `.card`. It does not disable selecting an exported snapshot. The code-field spell-check and autocomplete settings reflect its format-oriented use; the snapshot field disables spell checking as well. None of those attributes validates the entered data.

BoardCodeForm uses FormData and prevents the form's default navigation in `onSubmit`. Pressing Enter in the input reaches that same submission path. The snapshot tools instead use local React state and explicit action buttons, preserving multiline Enter behavior in the textarea.

Controlled and uncontrolled fields both appear here. Reproduction controls the textarea value with state. BoardCodeForm uses `defaultValue` on an input keyed by generation. Native element choice does not determine which React state pattern is appropriate. The intended draft lifecycle does; see [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md).

## A disclosure is already an interaction

The reproduction panel uses details with a summary, starts collapsed and relies on native expansion. There is no handler toggling an `expanded` variable or emulating summary key activation. The CSS styles the panel and summary without changing their source order.

The summary's visible text supplies its purpose. The load notice and Resume live outside the collapsible body, so closing it does not hide the pause continuation action. This is a layout and component-boundary decision around the native disclosure, not a custom disclosure implementation.

A disclosure leaves the surrounding document operable and expands in flow. It is not equivalent to a modal overlay. That distinction matters when reading a feature description: choosing a different native element changes more than a border shape or animation.

## DOM cards and artwork

Board is a CSS grid of DOM buttons, and each visible face is an inline SVG child. Hidden cards omit the face component entirely. The button name comes from position, state and, when available, face description; the SVG is hidden from accessibility and cannot receive focus.

The face drawing is therefore not the input surface's semantic replacement. A user activates the button, not an independently focusable path inside the SVG. This keeps the artwork and interaction connected without requiring canvas coordinate mapping or an invisible parallel button list.

The matched check mark is also an aria-hidden, nonfocusable SVG. It reinforces state visually while the button name and disabled property express it through the control. [Card artwork](../visuals/card-artwork.md) and [Screen reader notes](screen-reader-notes.md) describe those channels more fully.

## Native elements still need application work

The browser does not know that a pair matches, that a snapshot import is paused or that a game replacement invalidates an old timer. Those decisions remain in `game.ts`, `session.ts` and `use-game.ts`. A correct native element can still call the wrong controller action.

Nor does a button automatically implement the board's remembered entry point. `useBoardFocus` supplies the tab-index pattern and arrows, while the browser supplies basic focus and activation. The scroll helper addresses a specific Chromium centering behavior rather than replacing all browser scrolling.

Labels and descriptions also need correct associations. A visible label next to an input is not sufficient if its `htmlFor` points elsewhere. A load notice remains useful because the buttons reference its actual id. Native semantics reduce custom behavior, but they do not excuse checking the JSX relationships.

The same applies to CSS. Minimum height, shrinking fields, wrapping rows and visible outlines are explicit styles. A native input can still overflow a narrow page if its sizing constraints are wrong. [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md) and [Target size policy](target-size-policy.md) cover those aspects.

## Why alternatives would carry more work

Replacing the select with a drawn menu would move option navigation, expansion, selection and focus handling into application code. Replacing summary with a styled generic container would require recreating its activation and expanded-state exposure. Those are concrete costs even if the replacement initially resembles the current design.

A canvas board would also need a separate way to expose each card's position, name, state and focus behavior. The current DOM makes those properties inspectable directly. This is the benefit behind the existing choice, not a claim that native elements alone solve every accessibility issue.

The source does not contain a component library or a custom form abstraction that all new controls must use. Shared labels and CSS are small local tools. [ADR 006](../decisions/adr-006-native-controls.md) is the decision reference, while [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md) explains the separation between browser effects and pure game behavior.

## Evidence in review

The controls tests locate fields and buttons by names and roles, inspect native option values and check selectable export text. Keyboard tests rely on normal Tab exit and native button activation. The accessibility journey captures the browser's exposed control roles and states.

These checks are more informative than asserting only that a div has the right class. They verify the interaction surface that the player receives. At the same time, they remain browser and tree evidence, with spoken confirmation assigned to user acceptance in the repository README.

For a refactor, compare element type, explicit button type, field association, key handling and callback as a connected path. If a visual wrapper is the only intended change, those details reveal whether it also changed submission, tab order or mobile flex behavior. The native structure makes the comparison concrete.
# Purity guide

This page explains the data-oriented core of Neon Pairs and the practical value of keeping rules independent of rendering and browser effects.

The core receives a board code, state, activation index, logical time amount or serialized text. Its results depend on those inputs. React, storage, event listeners and scheduling enter through adapters. This separation supports browser play and command-line replay with the same transition functions.

## Purity is about observable decisions

`createGame(code)` reconstructs the deck and initializes progress. `activateCard(state, index)` decides whether an activation is ignored, opens one card, matches a pair or creates a mismatch. `advanceGame(state, milliseconds)` applies supplied logical time. None needs to know which button was pressed or when a browser timeout was requested.

`isWon(state)` derives victory from matched and deck lengths. `faceUpCards` derives presentation positions from matched positions and selection. These functions avoid a second mutable record of facts that are already available in the state.

The session also contains pure operations. `activateSession` adds feedback and completion preferences to a core transition, while `tickSession` gates a logical advance by generation and pause. Pure does not mean “must be in the top-level game directory”; it means the decision can be evaluated from explicit data without performing an external effect.

## A concrete activation sequence

For `np1-4-1`, positions 2 and 6 both contain face 0. Starting from `createGame`, activating 2 returns a game with `started: true` and a one-card selection. Moves remain zero. Activating 6 returns a game with both positions appended to `matched`, selection closed and moves equal to one.

Activating position 0 and then 1 instead opens a mismatch because the example deck has faces 6 and 7 there. The second activation adds one move and sets `remainingMs` to 800. Activating another position while that mismatch is pending returns the same object.

The same sequence can be used by a pointer journey, a keyboard journey or replay. Their input acquisition differs, but the rule decision does not. A UI-only correction to the move text would leave these other clients inconsistent; a correction in the transition reaches them all.

## Local mutation can produce a pure result

`generateBoard` constructs a local array and swaps elements while generating the seeded deck. That local mutation does not mutate an input deck or expose intermediate state. The completed board description and deck are frozen before return.

Similarly, `readMatched` constructs a local array and map while validating input. Its decision depends on supplied data, and callers do not observe the intermediate accumulation. Purity here does not require expressing every loop as a chain of array combinators.

What matters for shared game state is that transitions do not mutate the state given to them. A new match creates a new matched array; a new selection creates a new selection object. An ignored activation returns the old state. These reference relationships are meaningful to the session commit function and board memoization.

## Readonly types and runtime behavior

The `Board` and `GameState` interfaces expose readonly fields, and arrays are typed readonly. This prevents ordinary TypeScript callers from assigning into them. The generator adds runtime freezing for the board description and deck.

Not every returned progress object is recursively frozen. The code's immutability discipline is expressed through readonly types and functional transitions, with explicit freeze at the stable board boundary. Describing the whole state as deeply frozen at runtime would overstate the implementation.

`faceUpCards` returns a `ReadonlySet<number>` but constructs an ordinary Set internally. The type communicates the consumer contract. `Board` memoizes that derived set rather than storing it in the serialized game. This distinction keeps a convenient rendering index from becoming another authoritative state field.

## Logical time is an argument

`advanceGame` ignores nonfinite or nonpositive deltas and returns unchanged data before start or after victory. For active unfinished games it caps elapsed total and decreases mismatch remainder. An advance that expires a mismatch closes selection in the same call.

Replay uses this property by advancing from the previous timestamp to the next action before activating. Equal timestamps produce a zero advance and preserve array order. A timeout boundary is therefore a numerical question that can be tested without waiting for browser scheduling.

The browser controller supplies measured active deltas through the session clock. Its effect lifecycle determines which intervals are active. The core does not infer hidden periods from a timestamp history or attempt to compensate for browser throttling itself. [Clock design](clock-design.md) follows the adapter side.

## Validation is a pure boundary too

Serialized text is untrusted input even when produced by another copy of the game. `parseJson` returns unknown data or an undefined malformed marker. `isJsonObject`, integer checks and exact-key checks narrow it before any state is installed.

The snapshot decoder checks the code, bounds, matched positions and selection against a newly reconstructed deck. It checks a minimum move count and whether an unstarted state contains impossible progress. A valid result is a new `GameState`; an invalid result is null. A failed decode does not partially modify the current browser game.

This validation is structural and domain-specific, not a reconstruction of every possible prior activation history. For example, the decoder checks lower bounds on moves and relationships between start state and progress; it does not replay a missing action log to prove that a particular elapsed value occurred. The format contains a state, not that history.

`saved-format.ts` uses `TextEncoder` to measure UTF-8 bytes. This is a standard facility available in both the browser and the Node environments used here. It does not read browser state, storage or the DOM. Treating every standard host-provided constructor as a browser effect would obscure the actual independence these modules need.

## Invalid arguments have explicit outcomes

Different APIs serve different callers. `boardCode` and `generateBoard` throw on invalid board descriptions because their constructors expect a valid input. `parseBoardCode` returns null, providing a nonthrowing validation boundary. `decodeSnapshot` and `replayGame` return null for invalid text, while `readReplay` exposes a structured problem.

`activateCard` instead ignores invalid indices and illegal attempts by returning its input state. That is suitable for the activation path, where stale or repeated input should not corrupt progress. `advanceGame` similarly ignores unsuitable amounts and inactive states.

These are existing contracts, not a universal rule that pure functions never throw. A function can be deterministic and still reject an argument with an exception. The important review question is whether its caller expects an exception, a null result, a problem value or unchanged state.

## Small shared helpers have real clients

`saved-format.ts` holds object narrowing, safe nonnegative integer checks, exact-key matching, byte measurement and JSON parsing. Snapshot, replay and preference validation actually share those operations. Their domain checks remain in their own modules.

A helper such as `isNonnegativeSafeInteger` cannot by itself decide whether a number is a legal move count. Snapshot adds the move cap and consistency lower bound; preferences add the board's minimum completed moves; replay uses it for timestamps and positions before applying its own range checks.

Keeping those checks explicit prevents a superficially reusable “validate number” abstraction from hiding different meanings. The architecture specification asks for shared support when two real behaviors need the same meaning, and the current helper file is small enough to inspect against its callers.

## Rendering consumes outcomes

Components derive visible state from the returned game rather than reading classes back into the rules. Focus stays in the board, and storage writes follow preference decisions through a hook. [React boundaries](react-boundaries.md) and [Session module](session-module.md) explain those adapters.

## Evidence made possible by this shape

Literal decks, direct transition tests, malformed-format cases and numerical clock steps can be checked without rendering. Browser journeys then address native input, focus, storage and delivery. [Test policy](test-policy.md) explains why these are complementary forms of evidence.

## Reviewing an accidental effect

A rule that imports a component, reads a DOM element or performs storage access would bring environment state into a computation currently driven by arguments. The source audit scans selected core filenames for known effect markers, but its list and regular expressions are limited. Reading the imports and operations remains part of review.

A less obvious problem is mutating an input array while returning a new outer object. That can preserve or corrupt references in ways memoized consumers do not expect. The existing transitions instead create changed collections where their meanings change and keep stable collections where they do not.

A useful explanation of a core change can therefore state its input, output, ignored cases and retained references. If that explanation requires a mounted component to define the result, it is probably describing an adapter concern or an incomplete rule boundary. [Module layout policy](module-layout-policy.md) connects that distinction to file placement.
# Corrupt data policy

This page explains how Neon Pairs handles unreadable or invalid stored data and how read rejection relates to a later save.

Browser storage contains strings outside the type system. A value may have been written by an older build, edited by a person, truncated by a debugging experiment or replaced by another script on the origin. The current preference reader accepts only a usable preference aggregate and otherwise returns its default. It does not try to repair individual score entries.

## Rejection at the read boundary

A failed decode produces empty application data rather than a partially interpreted value. The read path can abandon unusable content without deleting the browser string as part of that read. A stored value that fails to parse or validate is treated as empty, without any error, and stays untouched until the next save replaces it. The distinction between reading and saving matters because a save can follow immediately during application initialization.

For current preferences, “empty” is the complete fallback `{ size: DEFAULT_SIZE, bestMoves: {} }`. `DEFAULT_SIZE` is 4. The result is therefore a fresh default-size game with no known bests, rather than an empty board or a blocked screen. `readPreferences` makes that fallback before entering its `try` block and returns it from each rejection branch.

The reader has no write or removal call. However, `useSavedPreferences` runs an effect on mounting with the preferences obtained during initialization. That effect can overwrite the rejected string with valid fallback preferences after rendering. The original text remains available only until a save occurs, and the ordinary mount effect is such a save.

## Parsing is only the first filter

`parseJson` in `src/game/saved-format.ts` catches `JSON.parse` errors and returns `undefined`. A string such as `{` therefore fails without throwing an uncaught exception from the preference reader. Valid JSON can still be unusable: `null`, an array, a string, a boolean or a number does not provide the required preference object.

`isJsonObject` rejects null and arrays. After that narrowing, the reader checks `schemaVersion === PREFERENCES_VERSION` and requires `size` to have JavaScript type `number`. It then checks that size against `isValidSize` and requires `bestMoves` to be an object. A string value such as `"6"` is not accepted as a selected size even though the UI select ultimately uses string option values.

The empty string is handled even earlier. `if (!text) return fallback` covers a missing key returned as `null`, an empty stored string and a null store's absent result. It avoids parsing text that cannot represent the preference object. Whitespace-only text is truthy, reaches the parser and fails there.

These branches are worth keeping separate in a test log. They converge on the same application state, but one shows absent data, another shows malformed syntax and another shows a structural mismatch. No error copy is rendered for these preference cases.

## Whole-value validation

The reader builds a fresh `bestMoves` object and iterates through `Object.entries(value.bestMoves)`. For each entry it converts the key with `Number(size)`, then compares `String(numberSize)` with the original key. That round trip requires the canonical size spelling. It rejects `04`, `4.0`, `4e0` and strings padded with whitespace, even when numerical conversion would produce 4.

The numeric key must then be supported by `isValidSize`. Each move count must be a nonnegative safe integer, no greater than `MOVES_MAX`, and no smaller than the number of pairs for its size. `MOVES_MAX` is 999999. The lower bound is `numberSize ** 2 / 2`, because completing the board takes at least one move for each pair.

| Side length | Lowest accepted completed move count |
| --- | ---: |
| 4 | 8 |
| 6 | 18 |
| 8 | 32 |
| 10 | 50 |
| 12 | 72 |
| 14 | 98 |
| 16 | 128 |

A failure at any entry returns the fallback for the entire preference value. A valid selected size of 6 does not survive alongside an invalid 4x4 score of 1. Likewise, valid score entries are not salvaged around one bad entry. The local object being assembled is never returned on that failure path.

This behavior is observable after reload: both the size preference and all previously accepted bests can appear reset when one map entry becomes invalid. It does not indicate that the size failed its own check. [Preferences store](preferences-store.md) explains why the aggregate is read as a unit.

## Examples with different failure causes

This value parses, but its version discriminator is unsupported:

```json
{"schemaVersion":2,"size":6,"bestMoves":{}}
```

This value has the expected version and size, but the score field has the wrong shape:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":6,"bestMoves":[]}
```

This value has a valid map shape and an invalid key spelling:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":6,"bestMoves":{"04":8}}
```

This value uses a canonical supported key but an impossible completed score:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":6,"bestMoves":{"4":7}}
```

All four produce the same preference fallback. The reader does not emit different messages or a machine-readable rejection reason. A diagnostic harness can identify the failed condition by choosing one changed field at a time. The production API does not expose those distinctions to components.

By contrast, this is a valid value with no score for the selected size:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":6,"bestMoves":{"4":8}}
```

The 4x4 record is retained, the board starts at 6x6, and the 6x6 best display is `none`. Absence of a current-size best is not evidence of corruption.

## Extra properties and normalization

The preference reader does not enforce an exact property count at the top level. A value with valid expected fields and an additional property can be accepted. The returned application value includes only the selected size and the newly built score map. A normal subsequent write serializes those known fields and the schema discriminator, omitting the extra property.

This is different from the snapshot parser, which rejects unknown fields according to its own format. A shared JSON helper does not make all parsers equally strict. Tests that copy a snapshot rejection case into preferences without checking the reader could accidentally demand behavior the game does not implement.

The current reader also does not coerce score strings to numbers, round fractions or clamp out-of-range scores. A value of `"8"` is not accepted as a move count. A fraction is rejected rather than rounded. A number above the move cap invalidates the aggregate rather than being reduced to the cap. Validation produces a known state or the fallback, not a best-effort approximation of the edited input.

## The timeline of replacement

There are three useful points in a corruption test. Before initialization, the raw store contains the original text. After `readPreferences`, the caller has either accepted preferences or fallback preferences, and the raw store is still unchanged by that function. After `writePreferences`, the store may contain a valid serialized replacement if the write succeeded.

In the browser, those latter two stages are separated by React's render and effect cycle rather than by a player's explicit action. `useGame` initializes session state from the read result, then `useSavedPreferences` writes that state after mounting. A test inspecting storage only after the UI has settled can see valid defaults and miss the original corrupt text entirely.

The simplest way to prove read nonmutation is a store double whose `setItem` records calls. Invoke only `readPreferences`, inspect the original string and check that no write occurred. A separate browser test can demonstrate mount replacement. Combining both assertions into a single post-navigation observation loses the distinction this policy depends on.

## Silent rejection is local to stored preferences

Invalid input typed into the board-code and snapshot controls follows another interaction. Those controls keep the current game, preserve the draft for correction and show their defined validation status. They do not silently replace the active game with a default board. That feedback is appropriate because the person has just requested an explicit load operation.

Stored preference rejection happens during initialization with no draft to correct in the game UI. It returns a playable state quietly. There is no recovery dialog, corrupted-data banner or download of rejected text. Browser access failure also returns defaults, but concerns operation availability rather than text acceptance; see [Storage failure policy](storage-failure-policy.md).

None of these parsers establishes authenticity. A manually edited score of 8 for 4x4 is accepted if the surrounding value is valid, even without evidence that eight pairs were played. The constraints establish a plausible stored aggregate, not a verified score history.

## Evidence and useful extensions to a diagnosis

`storage.test.ts` already covers malformed JSON, null, an empty object, unsupported size, scores below the pair count, negative and fractional values, and a noncanonical key. It separately checks that a score at the move cap round-trips and one beyond it is rejected. The browser persistence contract test seeds malformed text before navigation and checks for a playable 16-card default board.

Those tests are focused evidence, not an exhaustive enumeration of every possible JSON string. A new bug report is easiest to isolate with its exact raw value and one field changed at a time. Comparing an independently written valid baseline with the failing value exposes whether the issue concerns syntax, object shape, selected size, key spelling or score bounds. [Storage testing guide](storage-testing-guide.md) gives the browser setup and store doubles for doing that without modifying the source.

# Native controls guide

This page explains the native HTML elements used by Neon Pairs and the behavior they supply to the interface.

The source combines React event wiring with browser controls. It does not draw input controls on canvas or implement a replacement select menu. The resulting code leaves common editing, activation and disclosure behavior with the browser while keeping game decisions in the session and core.

## The current element choices

| Element | Use in the game | Application responsibility around it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `button` | Cards and actions | Decide what the activation changes |
| `select` with `option` | Grid size | Supply supported sizes and start a deal |
| `label` | Grid size and text fields | Associate visible names with field ids |
| `input` | Board-code draft | Read and validate the submitted code |
| `textarea` | Snapshot draft and export | Hold text and pass it to the snapshot decoder |
| `form` | Board-code submission | Prevent navigation and handle the result |
| `details` with `summary` | Reproduction disclosure | Supply content and layout |
| `dl` with `dt` and `dd` | Current game statistics | Derive the displayed values |

These choices describe the current DOM. Policies for other kinds of content are documented in [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) and [Tables policy](tables-policy.md), without implying that those elements already appear in Game.

## Buttons unify activation

Card renders a native button with `type="button"`. Its `onClick` sends an index to the shared activation path. Enter and Space can activate the same control through normal button behavior, so there is no separate keydown implementation of reveal.

The board's keydown handler only handles plain arrows with a navigation target. It does not call activation for Enter or Space and then also allow a native click. That avoids two paths processing one keyboard action. The game's pure activation guard still decides whether the card is eligible.

Action buttons outside the board use explicit types too. The Board code loader is `type="submit"` inside its form. New Game, Restart, Export snapshot, Load snapshot and Resume are `type="button"`. This makes submission intent visible in JSX rather than relying on where the browser happens to find an enclosing form.

A native button's semantics do not automatically implement ARIA-disabled behavior. Card uses `aria-disabled={matched}` while remaining focusable, and the game ignores matched activations. [Disabled state guide](disabled-state-guide.md) explains that deliberate split.

## The select keeps its native interaction

Controls renders a labeled select whose value comes from `game.size`. Each option comes from `GRID_SIZES` and has a numeric side length value with `NxN` display text. The browser supplies its dropdown interaction and option-selection behavior.

The component handles change by converting the selected value to a number and calling `newGame`. There is no local menu-open flag, active-option state or custom pointer hit testing. The controller still checks supported sizes, because native options are an interface aid rather than the only trust boundary.

The select inherits the shared font and panel colors through `.control`. Styling the border and background does not replace its role or its label relationship. The current CSS does not remove it in favor of an invisible field beneath a separately focusable drawn menu.

A successful board-code or snapshot load changes the actual game size, which flows back into this controlled select. The visible selected option therefore follows the model rather than a second UI-only size state. [Control bar](control-bar.md) covers that data flow.

## Text editing remains text editing

Board code is an input, and Snapshot JSON is a textarea. They retain selection, caret movement and browser editing operations. The textarea can resize vertically and receives readable export text without a clipboard permission dependency.

The card's `user-select: none` styling is scoped to `.card`. It does not disable selecting an exported snapshot. The code-field spell-check and autocomplete settings reflect its format-oriented use; the snapshot field disables spell checking as well. None of those attributes validates the entered data.

BoardCodeForm uses FormData and prevents the form's default navigation in `onSubmit`. Pressing Enter in the input reaches that same submission path. The snapshot tools instead use local React state and explicit action buttons, preserving multiline Enter behavior in the textarea.

Controlled and uncontrolled fields both appear here. Reproduction controls the textarea value with state. BoardCodeForm uses `defaultValue` on an input keyed by generation. Native element choice does not determine which React state pattern is appropriate. The intended draft lifecycle does; see [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md).

## A disclosure is already an interaction

The reproduction panel uses details with a summary, starts collapsed and relies on native expansion. There is no handler toggling an `expanded` variable or emulating summary key activation. The CSS styles the panel and summary without changing their source order.

The summary's visible text supplies its purpose. The load notice and Resume live outside the collapsible body, so closing it does not hide the pause continuation action. This is a layout and component-boundary decision around the native disclosure, not a custom disclosure implementation.

A disclosure leaves the surrounding document operable and expands in flow. It is not equivalent to a modal overlay. That distinction matters when reading a feature description: choosing a different native element changes more than a border shape or animation.

## DOM cards and artwork

Board is a CSS grid of DOM buttons, and each visible face is an inline SVG child. Hidden cards omit the face component entirely. The button name comes from position, state and, when available, face description; the SVG is hidden from accessibility and cannot receive focus.

The face drawing is therefore not the input surface's semantic replacement. A user activates the button, not an independently focusable path inside the SVG. This keeps the artwork and interaction connected without requiring canvas coordinate mapping or an invisible parallel button list.

The matched check mark is also an aria-hidden, nonfocusable SVG. It reinforces state visually while the button name and disabled property express it through the control. [Card artwork](../visuals/card-artwork.md) and [Screen reader notes](screen-reader-notes.md) describe those channels more fully.

## Native elements still need application work

The browser does not know that a pair matches, that a snapshot import is paused or that a game replacement invalidates an old timer. Those decisions remain in `game.ts`, `session.ts` and `use-game.ts`. A correct native element can still call the wrong controller action.

Nor does a button automatically implement the board's remembered entry point. `useBoardFocus` supplies the tab-index pattern and arrows, while the browser supplies basic focus and activation. The scroll helper addresses a specific Chromium centering behavior rather than replacing all browser scrolling.

Labels and descriptions also need correct associations. A visible label next to an input is not sufficient if its `htmlFor` points elsewhere. A load notice remains useful because the buttons reference its actual id. Native semantics reduce custom behavior, but they do not excuse checking the JSX relationships.

The same applies to CSS. Minimum height, shrinking fields, wrapping rows and visible outlines are explicit styles. A native input can still overflow a narrow page if its sizing constraints are wrong. [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md) and [Target size policy](target-size-policy.md) cover those aspects.

## Why alternatives would carry more work

Replacing the select with a drawn menu would move option navigation, expansion, selection and focus handling into application code. Replacing summary with a styled generic container would require recreating its activation and expanded-state exposure. Those are concrete costs even if the replacement initially resembles the current design.

A canvas board would also need a separate way to expose each card's position, name, state and focus behavior. The current DOM makes those properties inspectable directly. This is the benefit behind the existing choice, not a claim that native elements alone solve every accessibility issue.

The source does not contain a component library or a custom form abstraction that all new controls must use. Shared labels and CSS are small local tools. [ADR 006](../decisions/adr-006-native-controls.md) is the decision reference, while [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md) explains the separation between browser effects and pure game behavior.

## Evidence in review

The controls tests locate fields and buttons by names and roles, inspect native option values and check selectable export text. Keyboard tests rely on normal Tab exit and native button activation. The accessibility journey captures the browser's exposed control roles and states.

These checks are more informative than asserting only that a div has the right class. They verify the interaction surface that the player receives. At the same time, they remain browser and tree evidence, with spoken confirmation assigned to user acceptance in the repository README.

For a refactor, compare element type, explicit button type, field association, key handling and callback as a connected path. If a visual wrapper is the only intended change, those details reveal whether it also changed submission, tab order or mobile flex behavior. The native structure makes the comparison concrete.
# Purity guide

This page explains the data-oriented core of Neon Pairs and the practical value of keeping rules independent of rendering and browser effects.

The core receives a board code, state, activation index, logical time amount or serialized text. Its results depend on those inputs. React, storage, event listeners and scheduling enter through adapters. This separation supports browser play and command-line replay with the same transition functions.

## Purity is about observable decisions

`createGame(code)` reconstructs the deck and initializes progress. `activateCard(state, index)` decides whether an activation is ignored, opens one card, matches a pair or creates a mismatch. `advanceGame(state, milliseconds)` applies supplied logical time. None needs to know which button was pressed or when a browser timeout was requested.

`isWon(state)` derives victory from matched and deck lengths. `faceUpCards` derives presentation positions from matched positions and selection. These functions avoid a second mutable record of facts that are already available in the state.

The session also contains pure operations. `activateSession` adds feedback and completion preferences to a core transition, while `tickSession` gates a logical advance by generation and pause. Pure does not mean “must be in the top-level game directory”; it means the decision can be evaluated from explicit data without performing an external effect.

## A concrete activation sequence

For `np1-4-1`, positions 2 and 6 both contain face 0. Starting from `createGame`, activating 2 returns a game with `started: true` and a one-card selection. Moves remain zero. Activating 6 returns a game with both positions appended to `matched`, selection closed and moves equal to one.

Activating position 0 and then 1 instead opens a mismatch because the example deck has faces 6 and 7 there. The second activation adds one move and sets `remainingMs` to 800. Activating another position while that mismatch is pending returns the same object.

The same sequence can be used by a pointer journey, a keyboard journey or replay. Their input acquisition differs, but the rule decision does not. A UI-only correction to the move text would leave these other clients inconsistent; a correction in the transition reaches them all.

## Local mutation can produce a pure result

`generateBoard` constructs a local array and swaps elements while generating the seeded deck. That local mutation does not mutate an input deck or expose intermediate state. The completed board description and deck are frozen before return.

Similarly, `readMatched` constructs a local array and map while validating input. Its decision depends on supplied data, and callers do not observe the intermediate accumulation. Purity here does not require expressing every loop as a chain of array combinators.

What matters for shared game state is that transitions do not mutate the state given to them. A new match creates a new matched array; a new selection creates a new selection object. An ignored activation returns the old state. These reference relationships are meaningful to the session commit function and board memoization.

## Readonly types and runtime behavior

The `Board` and `GameState` interfaces expose readonly fields, and arrays are typed readonly. This prevents ordinary TypeScript callers from assigning into them. The generator adds runtime freezing for the board description and deck.

Not every returned progress object is recursively frozen. The code's immutability discipline is expressed through readonly types and functional transitions, with explicit freeze at the stable board boundary. Describing the whole state as deeply frozen at runtime would overstate the implementation.

`faceUpCards` returns a `ReadonlySet<number>` but constructs an ordinary Set internally. The type communicates the consumer contract. `Board` memoizes that derived set rather than storing it in the serialized game. This distinction keeps a convenient rendering index from becoming another authoritative state field.

## Logical time is an argument

`advanceGame` ignores nonfinite or nonpositive deltas and returns unchanged data before start or after victory. For active unfinished games it caps elapsed total and decreases mismatch remainder. An advance that expires a mismatch closes selection in the same call.

Replay uses this property by advancing from the previous timestamp to the next action before activating. Equal timestamps produce a zero advance and preserve array order. A timeout boundary is therefore a numerical question that can be tested without waiting for browser scheduling.

The browser controller supplies measured active deltas through the session clock. Its effect lifecycle determines which intervals are active. The core does not infer hidden periods from a timestamp history or attempt to compensate for browser throttling itself. [Clock design](clock-design.md) follows the adapter side.

## Validation is a pure boundary too

Serialized text is untrusted input even when produced by another copy of the game. `parseJson` returns unknown data or an undefined malformed marker. `isJsonObject`, integer checks and exact-key checks narrow it before any state is installed.

The snapshot decoder checks the code, bounds, matched positions and selection against a newly reconstructed deck. It checks a minimum move count and whether an unstarted state contains impossible progress. A valid result is a new `GameState`; an invalid result is null. A failed decode does not partially modify the current browser game.

This validation is structural and domain-specific, not a reconstruction of every possible prior activation history. For example, the decoder checks lower bounds on moves and relationships between start state and progress; it does not replay a missing action log to prove that a particular elapsed value occurred. The format contains a state, not that history.

`saved-format.ts` uses `TextEncoder` to measure UTF-8 bytes. This is a standard facility available in both the browser and the Node environments used here. It does not read browser state, storage or the DOM. Treating every standard host-provided constructor as a browser effect would obscure the actual independence these modules need.

## Invalid arguments have explicit outcomes

Different APIs serve different callers. `boardCode` and `generateBoard` throw on invalid board descriptions because their constructors expect a valid input. `parseBoardCode` returns null, providing a nonthrowing validation boundary. `decodeSnapshot` and `replayGame` return null for invalid text, while `readReplay` exposes a structured problem.

`activateCard` instead ignores invalid indices and illegal attempts by returning its input state. That is suitable for the activation path, where stale or repeated input should not corrupt progress. `advanceGame` similarly ignores unsuitable amounts and inactive states.

These are existing contracts, not a universal rule that pure functions never throw. A function can be deterministic and still reject an argument with an exception. The important review question is whether its caller expects an exception, a null result, a problem value or unchanged state.

## Small shared helpers have real clients

`saved-format.ts` holds object narrowing, safe nonnegative integer checks, exact-key matching, byte measurement and JSON parsing. Snapshot, replay and preference validation actually share those operations. Their domain checks remain in their own modules.

A helper such as `isNonnegativeSafeInteger` cannot by itself decide whether a number is a legal move count. Snapshot adds the move cap and consistency lower bound; preferences add the board's minimum completed moves; replay uses it for timestamps and positions before applying its own range checks.

Keeping those checks explicit prevents a superficially reusable “validate number” abstraction from hiding different meanings. The architecture specification asks for shared support when two real behaviors need the same meaning, and the current helper file is small enough to inspect against its callers.

## Rendering consumes outcomes

Components derive visible state from the returned game rather than reading classes back into the rules. Focus stays in the board, and storage writes follow preference decisions through a hook. [React boundaries](react-boundaries.md) and [Session module](session-module.md) explain those adapters.

## Evidence made possible by this shape

Literal decks, direct transition tests, malformed-format cases and numerical clock steps can be checked without rendering. Browser journeys then address native input, focus, storage and delivery. [Test policy](test-policy.md) explains why these are complementary forms of evidence.

## Reviewing an accidental effect

A rule that imports a component, reads a DOM element or performs storage access would bring environment state into a computation currently driven by arguments. The source audit scans selected core filenames for known effect markers, but its list and regular expressions are limited. Reading the imports and operations remains part of review.

A less obvious problem is mutating an input array while returning a new outer object. That can preserve or corrupt references in ways memoized consumers do not expect. The existing transitions instead create changed collections where their meanings change and keep stable collections where they do not.

A useful explanation of a core change can therefore state its input, output, ignored cases and retained references. If that explanation requires a mounted component to define the result, it is probably describing an adapter concern or an incomplete rule boundary. [Module layout policy](module-layout-policy.md) connects that distinction to file placement.
# Corrupt data policy

This page explains how Neon Pairs handles unreadable or invalid stored data and how read rejection relates to a later save.

Browser storage contains strings outside the type system. A value may have been written by an older build, edited by a person, truncated by a debugging experiment or replaced by another script on the origin. The current preference reader accepts only a usable preference aggregate and otherwise returns its default. It does not try to repair individual score entries.

## Rejection at the read boundary

A failed decode produces empty application data rather than a partially interpreted value. The read path can abandon unusable content without deleting the browser string as part of that read. A stored value that fails to parse or validate is treated as empty, without any error, and stays untouched until the next save replaces it. The distinction between reading and saving matters because a save can follow immediately during application initialization.

For current preferences, “empty” is the complete fallback `{ size: DEFAULT_SIZE, bestMoves: {} }`. `DEFAULT_SIZE` is 4. The result is therefore a fresh default-size game with no known bests, rather than an empty board or a blocked screen. `readPreferences` makes that fallback before entering its `try` block and returns it from each rejection branch.

The reader has no write or removal call. However, `useSavedPreferences` runs an effect on mounting with the preferences obtained during initialization. That effect can overwrite the rejected string with valid fallback preferences after rendering. The original text remains available only until a save occurs, and the ordinary mount effect is such a save.

## Parsing is only the first filter

`parseJson` in `src/game/saved-format.ts` catches `JSON.parse` errors and returns `undefined`. A string such as `{` therefore fails without throwing an uncaught exception from the preference reader. Valid JSON can still be unusable: `null`, an array, a string, a boolean or a number does not provide the required preference object.

`isJsonObject` rejects null and arrays. After that narrowing, the reader checks `schemaVersion === PREFERENCES_VERSION` and requires `size` to have JavaScript type `number`. It then checks that size against `isValidSize` and requires `bestMoves` to be an object. A string value such as `"6"` is not accepted as a selected size even though the UI select ultimately uses string option values.

The empty string is handled even earlier. `if (!text) return fallback` covers a missing key returned as `null`, an empty stored string and a null store's absent result. It avoids parsing text that cannot represent the preference object. Whitespace-only text is truthy, reaches the parser and fails there.

These branches are worth keeping separate in a test log. They converge on the same application state, but one shows absent data, another shows malformed syntax and another shows a structural mismatch. No error copy is rendered for these preference cases.

## Whole-value validation

The reader builds a fresh `bestMoves` object and iterates through `Object.entries(value.bestMoves)`. For each entry it converts the key with `Number(size)`, then compares `String(numberSize)` with the original key. That round trip requires the canonical size spelling. It rejects `04`, `4.0`, `4e0` and strings padded with whitespace, even when numerical conversion would produce 4.

The numeric key must then be supported by `isValidSize`. Each move count must be a nonnegative safe integer, no greater than `MOVES_MAX`, and no smaller than the number of pairs for its size. `MOVES_MAX` is 999999. The lower bound is `numberSize ** 2 / 2`, because completing the board takes at least one move for each pair.

| Side length | Lowest accepted completed move count |
| --- | ---: |
| 4 | 8 |
| 6 | 18 |
| 8 | 32 |
| 10 | 50 |
| 12 | 72 |
| 14 | 98 |
| 16 | 128 |

A failure at any entry returns the fallback for the entire preference value. A valid selected size of 6 does not survive alongside an invalid 4x4 score of 1. Likewise, valid score entries are not salvaged around one bad entry. The local object being assembled is never returned on that failure path.

This behavior is observable after reload: both the size preference and all previously accepted bests can appear reset when one map entry becomes invalid. It does not indicate that the size failed its own check. [Preferences store](preferences-store.md) explains why the aggregate is read as a unit.

## Examples with different failure causes

This value parses, but its version discriminator is unsupported:

```json
{"schemaVersion":2,"size":6,"bestMoves":{}}
```

This value has the expected version and size, but the score field has the wrong shape:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":6,"bestMoves":[]}
```

This value has a valid map shape and an invalid key spelling:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":6,"bestMoves":{"04":8}}
```

This value uses a canonical supported key but an impossible completed score:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":6,"bestMoves":{"4":7}}
```

All four produce the same preference fallback. The reader does not emit different messages or a machine-readable rejection reason. A diagnostic harness can identify the failed condition by choosing one changed field at a time. The production API does not expose those distinctions to components.

By contrast, this is a valid value with no score for the selected size:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":6,"bestMoves":{"4":8}}
```

The 4x4 record is retained, the board starts at 6x6, and the 6x6 best display is `none`. Absence of a current-size best is not evidence of corruption.

## Extra properties and normalization

The preference reader does not enforce an exact property count at the top level. A value with valid expected fields and an additional property can be accepted. The returned application value includes only the selected size and the newly built score map. A normal subsequent write serializes those known fields and the schema discriminator, omitting the extra property.

This is different from the snapshot parser, which rejects unknown fields according to its own format. A shared JSON helper does not make all parsers equally strict. Tests that copy a snapshot rejection case into preferences without checking the reader could accidentally demand behavior the game does not implement.

The current reader also does not coerce score strings to numbers, round fractions or clamp out-of-range scores. A value of `"8"` is not accepted as a move count. A fraction is rejected rather than rounded. A number above the move cap invalidates the aggregate rather than being reduced to the cap. Validation produces a known state or the fallback, not a best-effort approximation of the edited input.

## The timeline of replacement

There are three useful points in a corruption test. Before initialization, the raw store contains the original text. After `readPreferences`, the caller has either accepted preferences or fallback preferences, and the raw store is still unchanged by that function. After `writePreferences`, the store may contain a valid serialized replacement if the write succeeded.

In the browser, those latter two stages are separated by React's render and effect cycle rather than by a player's explicit action. `useGame` initializes session state from the read result, then `useSavedPreferences` writes that state after mounting. A test inspecting storage only after the UI has settled can see valid defaults and miss the original corrupt text entirely.

The simplest way to prove read nonmutation is a store double whose `setItem` records calls. Invoke only `readPreferences`, inspect the original string and check that no write occurred. A separate browser test can demonstrate mount replacement. Combining both assertions into a single post-navigation observation loses the distinction this policy depends on.

## Silent rejection is local to stored preferences

Invalid input typed into the board-code and snapshot controls follows another interaction. Those controls keep the current game, preserve the draft for correction and show their defined validation status. They do not silently replace the active game with a default board. That feedback is appropriate because the person has just requested an explicit load operation.

Stored preference rejection happens during initialization with no draft to correct in the game UI. It returns a playable state quietly. There is no recovery dialog, corrupted-data banner or download of rejected text. Browser access failure also returns defaults, but concerns operation availability rather than text acceptance; see [Storage failure policy](storage-failure-policy.md).

None of these parsers establishes authenticity. A manually edited score of 8 for 4x4 is accepted if the surrounding value is valid, even without evidence that eight pairs were played. The constraints establish a plausible stored aggregate, not a verified score history.

## Evidence and useful extensions to a diagnosis

`storage.test.ts` already covers malformed JSON, null, an empty object, unsupported size, scores below the pair count, negative and fractional values, and a noncanonical key. It separately checks that a score at the move cap round-trips and one beyond it is rejected. The browser persistence contract test seeds malformed text before navigation and checks for a playable 16-card default board.

Those tests are focused evidence, not an exhaustive enumeration of every possible JSON string. A new bug report is easiest to isolate with its exact raw value and one field changed at a time. Comparing an independently written valid baseline with the failing value exposes whether the issue concerns syntax, object shape, selected size, key spelling or score bounds. [Storage testing guide](storage-testing-guide.md) gives the browser setup and store doubles for doing that without modifying the source.
