# Control bar

This page explains how `Controls.tsx` presents the deal actions and how those actions connect to the session.

The bar is deliberately small: a labeled size selector, New Game and Restart. It sits above the statistics and board in `src/game/Game.tsx`, so the actions that replace a deal are available before entering the board. Reproduction tools have a different rhythm and occupy their own disclosure below the board; see [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md).

## Component boundary

`src/game/controls/Controls.tsx` accepts three props: `size`, `newGame(size?: number)` and `restart()`. It does not own a second copy of the selected size, choose a seed, reset a timer or update preferences. Its select is controlled by the `size` prop. That prop comes from `session.game.size`, which makes the displayed choice agree with the board after a size change, board-code load or snapshot import.

The optional argument on `newGame` explains the two call sites. The select converts `event.currentTarget.value` with `Number(...)` and calls `newGame` with that value. New Game calls `newGame()` without an argument. The default in `use-game.ts` takes the current game's size. Restart calls its separate callback. There is no DOM inspection to decide which size to use when either button is pressed.

The select and buttons are native elements. The two buttons explicitly use `type="button"`; they do not submit the reproduction form farther down the page. The wrapper is a `div` with class `controls`, not a toolbar widget with a separate keyboard model. Tab follows ordinary document order through the select, New Game and Restart. Board navigation begins after those controls, as described in [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md).

## Labels and options

`src/game/controls/control-labels.ts` exports `DealControl`. The visible strings are `Grid size`, `New Game` and `Restart`. The label is associated with `id="grid-size"` through `htmlFor="grid-size"`. A user or browser test can therefore find the select by its visible name instead of a CSS class or its position in the bar.

The options come directly from `GRID_SIZES` in `deck.ts`. Their values are the numeric side lengths rendered as native option values, and their text is the side repeated with a lowercase `x`:

| Display | Value | Cards |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4x4 | 4 | 16 |
| 6x6 | 6 | 36 |
| 8x8 | 8 | 64 |
| 10x10 | 10 | 100 |
| 12x12 | 12 | 144 |
| 14x14 | 14 | 196 |
| 16x16 | 16 | 256 |

Those are deal sizes, rather than zoom settings. Choosing 16 changes the game to a 16-row, 16-column deck; it does not squeeze the existing sixteen cards into a different arrangement. The larger boards can exceed the available width inside their scroll container. [Pointer and touch](pointer-and-touch.md) explains the consequences for reaching cards.

The component itself receives `size: number`, but the session's `newGame` function checks `isValidSize(size)` before making a replacement. That guard is outside the control and also protects callers that do not originate in the native select. The option list is not the only validation boundary.

## Desktop arrangement

`controls.css` uses flex layout with `align-items: end`, `flex-wrap: wrap`, a `12px` gap and a `16px` bottom margin. The size group is another flex row with `align-items: center` and a `12px` gap. The label sits beside its select rather than above it. The outer alignment brings the actions to the same bottom line if control heights differ.

No explicit column count or button width is needed in this layout. Labels and the browser's select affordance contribute to their natural widths. Wrapping is enabled before the phone media query applies, so the bar can also adapt to a constrained content area on a wider window. The maximum content width and page padding come from `game.css`, not the controls stylesheet.

The shared `.control` class comes from `control.css`: `min-height: 44px`, `padding: 8px 12px`, a `1px` neutral border, an `8px` radius, panel background, text color and inherited font. The select and buttons get a pointer cursor. The stylesheet does not replace the select's browser interaction with a drawn menu. Its popup remains the native control's responsibility.

## Phone arrangement

At `max-width: 599px`, `.controls` changes to `align-items: stretch`. The size group occupies the full line with `width: 100%` and `justify-content: space-between`; its label and select move to opposite ends of that row. The direct child buttons each get `flex: 1`, sharing the following row when there is room.

The media query acts on the current DOM hierarchy. Moving a button into an extra wrapper would change the effect of `.controls > button`. A review of such a refactor can compare computed widths and wrapping before deciding that it preserves the arrangement. The apparent simplicity of a wrapper change can hide a layout change on phones.

The breakpoint is not a board-size breakpoint. A 4x4 and a 16x16 game use the same control bar at the same viewport width. The board handles its own width independently. This separation keeps the controls available even when a player has scrolled to the far end of a large board.

## What the actions replace

In `use-game.ts`, `newGame` creates a code using `freshBoardCode(size, current.current.game.seed)`, constructs the new game, resets the clock adapter and commits `replaceGame(...)`. Restart constructs a game from `current.current.game.boardCode` instead. Both begin with a closed selection, no matched positions, zero moves, zero elapsed time and `started: false` because that is what `createGame` returns.

`replaceGame` increments `session.generation`. The Board in `Game.tsx` is keyed by this generation, so it mounts with a fresh remembered tab stop. The BoardCodeForm input is also keyed by generation and receives the current board code as its default value. A reset is therefore observable in several places without each component inventing its own reset event.

The size is saved through the session preferences path. The current size's best record is read independently for the statistics. Choosing a size with no stored record shows `Best: none`; returning to a size with a record displays that size's value. For the exact display boundary, see [Status bar](status-bar.md) and [Best score records](../gameplay/best-score-records.md).

A pending mismatch cannot later alter the replacement deal. Clock reset and generation checks in the session make stale updates harmless. This is why replacing a deal during its short mismatch display is a meaningful controls test, rather than merely checking that the card count changes.

## Focus and continuity

Clicking New Game or Restart leaves focus on the action button. The components do not call `.focus()` on the board after a reset. A user can press the same action again or Tab forward to the new first card. A size change likewise uses the native select interaction rather than an application focus transfer.

Initial page load also does not select a card on the user's behalf. The board's first card is ready as its tab stop, but readiness is separate from current focus. [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) describes this distinction and the different treatment needed when Resume removes its own button.

There is no confirmation step in either callback today. Pressing an action replaces the current deal immediately. Do not infer a pending dialog from the text of an action or from the fact that the old game had moves. The separate [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) records the policy for future actions that leave unfinished work.

## A useful review path

The controls checks in `tests/controls.e2e.test.ts` inspect the native option values as well as their displayed text. `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` checks the literal labels. `tests/keyboard.e2e.test.ts` checks the relationship between Restart and the remembered board entry point. Layout coverage includes a narrow `320x640` viewport in `tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` and the equivalent zoom layout in `tests/zoom.e2e.test.ts`.

These checks cover different failures. A label refactor could preserve a screenshot while breaking name-based selection. A wrapper refactor could preserve all labels while changing the mobile row. A session refactor could keep the bar visually identical while allowing an earlier timer to touch a new deal. Reading the component, CSS and callback together makes those differences visible.

For a manual check, choose a nondefault size, reveal a mismatching pair, then use Restart before it closes. The deck repeats and the counters reset. Use New Game at that same size and confirm that its code changes. Tab into the board after each action to observe the reset entry point. Finally load a valid code of another size from the reproduction panel and look back at Grid size: the controlled select follows the loaded game without another local state update.
# Screen reader notes

This page describes the information exposed during a keyboard game and the limits of the project's screen reader evidence.

The interface exposes native controls, card names, state changes and readable results. The repository README records accessibility-tree checks in Chromium 156.0.8078.4 with Playwright 1.64.1. It also explicitly records that no screen reader was run. The names and sentences below are source-backed content available to assistive technology, not a transcript of speech captured in a listening session.

## Finding the game controls

The document language is English, the browser title is Neon Pairs, and the main area contains the game's h1 and introductory text. The first interactive deal control is the native select labeled Grid size. New Game and Restart follow as native buttons.

The select's label is connected with `htmlFor="grid-size"`. Its options read 4x4 through 16x16 at the seven supported sizes. A user can find it by its visible name rather than needing to interpret an unlabeled icon. The action buttons also use visible text as their names.

The statistics are reading content in a definition list: Moves, Pairs, Time and Best. There are no custom accessible labels replacing their values. An absent best is visible as `none`. These details matter when inspecting the tree because the information is ordinary document content, not four editable fields or buttons.

Changing size creates a deal of that size. New Game creates another deal at the current size, and Restart repeats the current code. Those actions retain focus at their controls. They do not suddenly land the player deep in the card board. [Control bar](control-bar.md) describes the callbacks and layout.

## Entering the board

Board's viewport is a region named `Game board` and described by `board-help`. The help text says: `Use a pointer or Tab to enter the board. Arrow keys move between cards. Enter or Space reveals a card.` This is visible text as well as an associated description.

Tab enters at the remembered card. Before any card focus has been remembered, that is the first card. Plain arrows move one row or column with no wrapping. Tab and Shift+Tab can leave the board. Modifier combinations and unlisted keys remain browser input rather than board commands.

The native card button provides activation through Enter and Space. Screen reader interaction modes can affect which keys reach a web page, so a real spoken acceptance journey is still valuable even when the browser's keyboard tests pass. The game's documented input relies on native button activation and board arrow navigation.

Matched cards remain focusable, and navigation does not skip them. During a mismatch or paused import, movement can continue although activating another card has no game effect. This keeps exploration separate from the turn decision. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) traces the remembered tab stop and target calculation.

## A closed card reveals no hidden identity

`describeCard` builds a one-based coordinate from the zero-based deck index. Index 0 on a four-column board is named `Row 1, column 1, closed`. Index 5 is `Row 2, column 2, closed`. The pattern gives a stable spatial reference before any face is known.

Board passes `face={null}` for a hidden card. Card then renders only the neutral back span with `aria-hidden="true"`, not the Face component. The hidden face is absent from the element's label, attributes and child artwork. A screen reader cannot legitimately read a face description from that hidden DOM because it is not there.

This is stronger than hiding a face SVG with CSS while leaving a revealing title or data attribute. The browser input-contract test compares every hidden card's attributes, inner HTML and text against the expected neutral content. A visual-only inspection could miss such a leak.

The deck still exists in game state because the game must resolve matches. The DOM boundary is the important distinction for the interface: a hidden card control exposes its position and closed state, not its underlying identity. [Card artwork](../visuals/card-artwork.md) and [Pair identity](../gameplay/pair-identity.md) explain the visual and game sides.

## The first reveal

Use `np1-4-1` as a concrete source-backed example. Its index 0 contains face 6. After activation, that button's name becomes `Row 1, column 1, revealed, cyan solid plus, marker top`. The state precedes the face description in the actual string generated by `card-state.ts`.

Face names come from `faceDesign`: color, solid or outline, shape and marker position. The SVG itself is `aria-hidden="true"` and `focusable="false"`. It does not add a separate graphic description competing with the button name. The name carries the information the player needs to remember.

A first reveal starts elapsed time but leaves Moves at zero. The game has not yet completed a two-card attempt. It also does not publish a turn result merely for that first card. A user can inspect the newly focused control's name, move to another location and make the second choice.

Repeating activation on the same first card does not complete a move. That is an ignored game action, not a second reveal or a reason to read a new turn result. This is useful when interpreting a test that presses Space twice and sees no move increment.

## A match and a miss

On the same example code, index 11 is the partner of index 0. It is row 3, column 4. Activating it completes the pair immediately. Both controls' names use `matched`, retain the face description and expose `aria-disabled="true"`.

The current result text for the first match is `Pair found. 1 pair matched.` Later nonfinal matches substitute the count and plural form. The matched controls remain in the board's spatial navigation even though activating them no longer changes the game. A screen reader may verbalize their unavailable state according to its own conventions; the source exposes the ARIA disabled state.

Indices 0 and 1 are a mismatch on this code. Their faces remain revealed for the active mismatch interval, and the turn result is `No match. Cards close after a short pause.` Additional card activation during that wait is ignored. The interval pauses while the page is hidden or imported progress waits for Resume.

After closure, the two names return to their closed forms and their face artwork is removed. Closure does not publish another turn result. Moving focus while the pair waits also does not republish the mismatch sentence. [Announcements policy](announcements-policy.md) explains the event identity that makes consecutive identical misses distinct without making ordinary renders noisy.

## Completing the game

The winning match produces `Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time.`, using the final counters. GameStatus also displays the persistent completion sentence `Every pair found in N moves and time. Well played.` A reader can revisit the final statistics and summary in document content.

The time text uses the game's formatter: seconds are padded, and minutes can grow beyond 59. The values stop advancing at completion. The final card remains the active control; completion does not force focus onto the banner.

Matched cards still occupy the board, so Tab leaves it without requiring a pass through every matched position. In the collapsed page layout, the next control is the native reproduction summary. Shift+Tab can return through the remembered board location toward the deal controls. Starting another game resets board memory while leaving the action button focused.

The complete automated journey exercises this path, including a new game after completion. It checks the final summary in the accessibility tree rather than assuming that visible text is necessarily exposed as expected.

## Reproduction tools in reading order

The native summary is named `Reproduce a game`. Expanding it exposes labeled Board code and Snapshot JSON fields with Load board, Export snapshot and Load snapshot actions. The board-code form submits with Enter; the snapshot actions are ordinary buttons rather than an Enter-to-import form.

Invalid input keeps the current game and draft. The visible outcomes are `Invalid board code.` and `Invalid snapshot.`. The load buttons reference the nearby notice paragraph as a description, and the event feedback path publishes the outcome. Clicking a load button leaves focus there. An invalid Enter submission from Board code leaves focus in the input for correction.

A valid unfinished snapshot reports `Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue.` and pauses card activation. The player can still explore the board with arrows. Resume focuses the remembered card before the Resume button is removed, then continues active play. A completed snapshot reports `Loaded completed snapshot.`, shows the completed game statically and offers no Resume button.

Export fills readable JSON into the textarea. It does not require clipboard permission or make the text impossible to select. A user can move to the native field and copy its contents through their normal editing commands. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) explains draft lifetimes and the different board-code reset behavior.

## What the automated journey records

`tests/accessibility.e2e.test.ts` uses Chromium's debugging protocol to enable accessibility and capture full trees at named stages. Its helper removes ignored nodes and records role, name, scalar value, text and selected accessibility properties. This produces evidence about exposed controls and states without preserving transient browser node identifiers.

The journey finds Grid size and New Game by name, enters the board, inspects closed and revealed names, completes pairs with Enter and Space, checks matched disabled state and reads each turn result. It then checks completion, Tab exit, New Game and repeated load outcomes. The saved artifact is named `accessibility-journey.json` by the test.

The test writes that artifact as output. The source references reviewed fixtures for expected content.

## Spoken acceptance still answers a different question

Tree exposure, keyboard behavior and speech are related but distinct. A browser may expose the correct atomic result while a particular screen reader schedules or phrases it in a way that needs listening review. Consecutive identical misses and the final combined result are especially useful listening points.

The input specification assigns spoken confirmation to user acceptance. The repository README's record says `Screen reader: not run. Spoken journey: user acceptance.` That limitation belongs beside the evidence, not hidden behind a broad statement that screen reader support was tested end to end.

A useful acceptance note names the browser, screen reader and versions, the action sequence and what was heard. If a result differs, the DOM publication history and tree capture can help locate the boundary. [Accessibility audit](../quality/accessibility-audit.md) and [Browser test guide](../quality/browser-test-guide.md) provide the wider review context.
# Interface review checklist

This page is a review route through the existing controls, input behavior and related interface policies.

A useful review follows a few populated journeys and checks source at the transitions. An empty board screenshot cannot show preserved drafts, matched-card focus or a stale timer after Restart. The checks below are grounded in the current source and specifications; links identify the separate policies for feature surfaces that do not exist yet.

## Establish what changed

Start with the actual component and its callback. A control can retain its appearance while changing submission, focus or session behavior. A CSS-only change can also alter the hit area or clipping without touching an event handler.

- Identify whether the change affects `Controls`, `Reproduction`, `BoardCodeForm`, `GameStatus`, `Board`, `Card` or the focus hook.
- Follow callbacks into `use-game.ts` and `session.ts` when the change replaces a game, accepts input or publishes feedback.
- Compare element types, ids, label associations, explicit button types and source order as well as class names.
- Check mobile selectors that depend on direct children before accepting a wrapper-only refactor as behaviorally neutral.

The current page has no name editor, dialog or result table. A change introducing one has more scope than styling an existing control. Its relevant policy is linked below, and its current behavior has to be established from its own implementation.

## Deal controls

Use [Control bar](control-bar.md) and the Controls specification as the reference for these observations.

- Grid size is a labeled native select with the seven supported choices, and its selected value agrees with the current game after either successful load type.
- New Game keeps the current size and creates a fresh deal; Restart repeats the current board code.
- Both actions reset selection, pairs, moves and elapsed time, and leave their action button focused.
- Replacing a game during a mismatch does not let an old timer change the replacement.
- The board's next native entry starts at its first card after a replacement, rather than retaining an index from the old deal.

A code comparison can distinguish New Game from Restart even when the two visible decks happen to share some positions. A move-count comparison alone cannot establish that distinction. For size changes, check both card count and the controlled select value.

The current buttons act immediately. A reviewer should not claim existing confirmation coverage from the presence of a leave policy elsewhere. [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) records that separate feature boundary.

## Text tools and errors

The useful draft is one that differs from the currently displayed code, and the useful game state has some progress. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) and [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) provide the source trace.

- The native disclosure starts collapsed and is named Reproduce a game.
- Board code and Snapshot JSON retain visible, correctly associated labels and their existing native limits.
- Editing Board code, then playing a card, keeps the edited draft.
- Invalid board-code and snapshot submissions preserve the current game and the entered text, and show their exact existing load outcomes.
- Successful Board code submission refreshes the field from the accepted code and updates the selected size.
- Export fills selectable, readable JSON without replacing or pausing play.

Try Enter from Board code as well as clicking Load board. Success focuses Load board because the input is replaced. Failure from the input keeps editing focus there. A click-origin failure keeps focus on the clicked action. The distinction can be lost in a test that only inspects the final board.

The snapshot textarea is multiline and has its own local state. Enter is not an implicit import action. Its draft is not automatically rewritten on every turn or deal replacement. The visible notice sits outside the disclosure, so closing it does not hide an unfinished import's way to continue.

## Import and Resume

A valid unfinished snapshot and a valid completed snapshot exercise different paths. The current specification gives concrete examples and constraints in [Snapshot format](../sharing/snapshot-format.md).

- Unfinished progress loads paused, including an imported position that has not started its clock yet.
- Card activation is blocked while paused, but focus movement still works.
- Resume focuses the board's remembered card before its own button is removed.
- A pending mismatch continues its remaining active interval after Resume.
- Completed progress loads completed, with static completion output and no Resume button.
- Import is not treated as a newly achieved play completion for best-record updates.

A far remembered card on a large board makes the Resume check meaningful. Scroll the board away from that card before resuming and inspect both focus and nearest visibility. Merely finding any focused button afterward would not establish that the remembered destination survived.

## Board movement and activation

Use [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md), [Pointer and touch](pointer-and-touch.md) and [Disabled state guide](disabled-state-guide.md) together.

- Tab enters the remembered card and can leave the board again; reverse traversal is native too.
- Plain arrows move one row or column, stop at edges and do not reveal cards.
- Modifier combinations and unlisted keys retain browser behavior.
- Enter, Space, primary click and completed tap reach the shared card action.
- Hover, touch scrolling, pointer cancellation and context-menu interaction do not choose a card.
- Matched cards stay focusable and expose their matched state while activation leaves the turn unchanged.
- Repeated activation of the first revealed card does not add a move.

For a mismatch, attempt a third activation while the pair is visible and move focus elsewhere. The pair stays until its active wait expires; closure does not drag focus back. Hide and show the page during the interval when a lifecycle change is in scope.

Pointer checks include a card partly clipped at the viewport edge. The source intentionally avoids moving a card under a held pointer, then scrolls it after the click. A centered-card click can pass even when that edge behavior regresses.

## Names and accessible content

Inspect actual DOM and browser accessibility exposure. Visual equivalence is insufficient when hidden data or labels are involved.

- Hidden card names expose position and closed state without a face description or hidden face artwork in their DOM.
- Revealed and matched card names include the correct face description and state.
- Face and check SVGs do not introduce extra focus targets or duplicate the button's description.
- Current statistics expose their visible terms and values without alternate labels replacing the numbers.
- Completion makes the final moves and elapsed time available in the persistent summary.

[Screen reader notes](screen-reader-notes.md) records the full journey and the distinction between tree evidence and spoken review. The repository README records the browser and tool versions and says no screen reader was run. A review report should describe the evidence it actually has.

When a feature introduces name input, consult [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md), [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md). The existing code and JSON text fields do not establish those name checks. For new result content, consult [Tables policy](tables-policy.md).

## Results and repeated events

[Announcements policy](announcements-policy.md) owns the publication model. In a populated game, inspect the event output while also checking that ordinary rendering stays quiet.

- A first reveal changes the card without publishing a resolved-turn result.
- A match or miss publishes its result once per resolved turn, including consecutive identical misses.
- Focus movement, clock updates and mismatch closure do not repeat the prior result.
- The winning result combines the last match and completion information.
- Repeated invalid loads and repeated successful snapshot loads each publish their load outcome.

The session's `announcement` value and the keyed feedback span explain repeated identical text. A refactor that only compares feedback strings can accidentally remove the event distinction. A refactor that updates the identity on every render can produce the opposite failure.

## Layout and reachability

Read [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md), [Target size policy](target-size-policy.md) and [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) for their detailed scope.

The current visual contract includes a default board fitting a phone, large-board overflow confined to the board viewport and complete focus outlines when cards are brought into view. Review the first, last and an interior card. Container padding can protect corners while an interior nearest-scroll target still clips its outline.

The stated large-board views include `360x800` and `1280x800`. The equivalent zoom layout is `640x400` with device scale 2. Controls, statistics and the completion sentence remain readable in those constrained layouts, with the outer page staying within its viewport width.

Check the expanded reproduction panel as well as the collapsed game. Fields shrink within their rows, action rows wrap and the textarea remains selectable. The native select popup and summary behavior are browser interactions; the surrounding CSS should not be assessed as though they were custom drawn widgets.

## Choose evidence that matches the change

Pure geometry is covered by `keyboard.test.ts`; focus and browser default behavior are covered by browser journeys. Parser tests cover malformed data independently of field layout. The accessibility journey captures roles, names, states and result text. These are complementary forms of evidence.

A small label or spacing change does not call for inventing a new test framework. Existing contract, controls, layout and zoom checks already target many interface failures. A callback or lifecycle change needs the populated journey that can expose its effect, especially when a pending mismatch or disappearing Resume button is involved.

The review note is most useful when it names the behavior changed, the evidence observed and any remaining limit. It can say that a tree exposes the expected result without claiming speech was heard, or that a phone layout was measured without claiming every browser was exercised. [Browser test guide](../quality/browser-test-guide.md), [Accessibility audit](../quality/accessibility-audit.md) and [Acceptance](../quality/acceptance.md) connect these checks to the wider project process.
# Tables policy

This page records the markup policy for ordered result data and explains why the current game statistics use a different structure.

`TournamentBracket.tsx` presents ordered match results in a table. `GameStatus.tsx` still displays properties of one active game in a definition list. Reproduction controls use forms, and the board is a CSS grid of buttons; those structures have different meanings from the bracket records.

## Policy for result data

When the content represents records with comparable columns, its relationships need to survive reading beyond the visual arrangement. CSS alone can align text while leaving those relationships absent from the document structure. Ranked or bracket data is a table element with a caption and th scope="col" header cells. The caption identifies the collection being read, while the column headers connect each record's values to their meaning.

This is a content-specific policy. It does not make the game board a data table because it has rows and columns, and it does not require converting every compact summary to tabular markup. The distinction begins with what the content means: interactive card coordinates, a property's value and a record in an ordered result collection are different things.

The tournament bracket uses a caption and column-scoped header cells. [Tournament mode](../competition/tournament-mode.md) describes its columns and result values. [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) discusses the broader preference for native semantics without adding another result format.

## Why the statistics are a definition list

GameStatus renders Moves, Pairs, Time and Best as four `dt`/`dd` groups inside a `dl`. Each term names a property of the same current game. There are no peer result rows and no column whose meaning changes with the row being read.

The layout happens to use flex and can wrap. At a wide width, those groups may look like cells in a horizontal strip. At a narrow width, they can flow to multiple lines. Neither visual arrangement changes the definition-list relationship. Replacing the wrapper with a table solely to preserve one desktop arrangement would confuse layout with content structure.

The Best value is one saved move count selected by current size. It does not present a list of people or a comparison across many records. `session.preferences.bestMoves[String(game.size)]` chooses the value before it reaches GameStatus. A single local best is not an implemented ordered-results screen.

[Status bar](status-bar.md) documents those expressions and labels. The present statistics model has no result columns.

## Why the card board is not a table

Board renders a named region containing an inner `div.board` and native card buttons. CSS Grid places those buttons in row order. Each card has its own coordinate and state in its accessible name, and keyboard movement follows a dedicated spatial model.

The table policy does not turn that interactive surface into a data table. A card is activated, can reveal a face and participates in remembered focus. A result cell is read as part of a record. They have different purposes even if both appear in a rectangle.

There is also no ARIA grid role on the current board. Its native buttons and movement handler implement the specified interaction without declaring a separate composite widget role. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) traces that behavior. A review of result markup should not accidentally rename or restructure the card controls because the word “row” appears in both contexts.

## What the caption contributes

An ordered collection needs context. A visible title elsewhere on a page can be helpful, but a table caption directly identifies the collection associated with the table. That matters when reading the table independently or navigating between document structures.

The policy does not specify caption text. The source has no existing results title. A feature's actual subject supplies the wording. Describing that subject is different from attaching a technical explanation of table markup to product copy.

A caption also does not supply missing column meaning. A reader needs to know whether a number represents moves, a position in an ordering or another property. The required header cells carry the column relationships; the caption names the whole collection. Combining all labels into a caption would leave the row values harder to interpret.

## Column relationships and reading order

The `scope="col"` attribute makes the header's direction explicit. It communicates that the header applies to values down its column. A bold `td`, a styled `div` or text positioned above a column can look similar while having a different structure.

A reviewer can inspect the table DOM and the browser's accessibility representation separately from the screenshot. The screenshot establishes visible arrangement. The DOM establishes element choices and attributes. The accessibility view helps establish that the browser exposes a meaningful table structure. No single one of these views proves all aspects of the interface.

Row headers, column order, numeric alignment and sorting controls depend on the result feature. The current game has no result implementation with those details.

## Narrow layouts and long values

The current game already separates outer page width from board overflow. Result data would have its own content and width behavior; it cannot simply inherit the card board's scroll logic by sharing a class name. A table's relationship between headers and values remains meaningful even when its viewport is narrow.

There is no table stylesheet in the source and no prescribed responsive table transformation here. A reviewer can still observe whether a proposed layout makes values readable and associated with their headers. Changing a collection into a stack of unrelated labels solely at a breakpoint can affect more than appearance, so both DOM and visual behavior are relevant evidence.

Name text can also vary in width without changing its accepted value. Typography and wrapping are layout concerns. The name policies remain separate from table structure; accepted names retain their displayed representation. [Typography](../visuals/typography.md) and [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md) explain nearby layout decisions in the existing interface.

The existing accessibility journey covers game controls and completion, not a result table. Evidence for a future result view would identify its actual markup and readable rows; the current statistics tests cannot establish that structure. [Accessibility audit](../quality/accessibility-audit.md) provides the wider review context.
# Target size policy

This page records the control target policy and explains the size constraints already present in the interface styles.

Target size is about the area a person can activate, not the size of a glyph drawn inside it. A card's marker is small, but the native button enclosing the whole card is the target. The same distinction applies to a summary's disclosure marker and the much larger summary row.

## Policy and present coverage

The existing code already gives cards a minimum track size and shared controls a minimum height. Extending the interface calls for checking the actual rendered target in the phone layout, where flex wrapping and available width matter. Every new control is at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels at a 390 pixel wide viewport. This policy covers the rendered control area rather than enlarging only a decorative child or a focus ring.

The current styles are useful building blocks, but they are not proof of every dimension for an arbitrary new element. In particular, `.control` declares minimum height without a general minimum width. A new short-label action could be tall enough while still being too narrow. The policy check and the existing class definition therefore answer related but different questions.

This is a control policy, not a claim of complete accessibility conformance. The visuals specification makes the same distinction for its chosen card minimum. Names, keyboard operation, contrast, visible focus and error behavior still have their own evidence. [Interface review checklist](interface-review-checklist.md) gathers those areas without turning a size measurement into a blanket result.

## Size sources in the current code

| Element | Source | Existing size behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Card button | `board.css`, `card.css` | Grid tracks from 44px to 88px, square aspect ratio |
| Button, select, input, textarea using `.control` | `control.css` | Minimum height 44px, padding 8px 12px |
| Reproduction summary | `reproduction.css` | Minimum height 44px, padding 12px 16px |
| Deal action row | `controls.css` | Wrapped flex layout, phone buttons grow |
| Reproduction action row | `reproduction.css` | Wrapped flex layout, phone buttons grow |

`game.css` applies `box-sizing: border-box` globally. The declared height constraints therefore include padding and border. Looking only at text line height would underestimate the target, while adding padding to the measured border box would overestimate it.

Cards have `width: 100%`, `aspect-ratio: 1`, zero padding and a `2px` border. Their width comes from the grid track. They do not establish their minimum using the SVG's coordinates or intrinsic artwork size. The current artwork can change shape while the card target remains the same square.

## Why large boards scroll

The inner board calculates a minimum content width from side length, `--card-min` and `--card-gap`. On a sixteen-column board that is 794px before viewport padding and border. A phone cannot display that whole width at once while keeping the current card minimum.

The implementation chooses an internal scroll area. Its `overflow: auto` and `max-width: 100%` allow the board to extend inside a bounded viewport. The outer page stays within the window. This is the reason a sixteen-column board does not respond like a shrunken thumbnail of a four-column board.

A target-size review can therefore encounter two valid observations at once: every card has its intended dimensions, and some cards are outside the current visible portion of the board. Reachability is supplied by scrolling and keyboard movement. [Pointer and touch](pointer-and-touch.md) explains the touch path to the last card; [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) explains arrow access.

A partially clipped card also has a full underlying button box. Clicking the visible part can activate it, after which the current implementation scrolls it fully into view. That behavior does not mean the clipping itself should be measured as the card's intended dimensions. It is an overflow case with a separate focus and pointer timing concern.

## Phone layout affects widths

At `max-width: 599px`, the deal size group fills the row and uses space-between alignment. New Game and Restart receive `flex: 1`. This gives the actions room without hard-coding two button widths. The text and browser control still contribute their intrinsic size constraints.

The reproduction action rows also wrap, with buttons growing on the phone breakpoint. The Board code input has `flex: 1`, a preferred width of `16ch` and `min-width: 0`. The textarea fills its parent and can resize vertically. These choices keep the text tools within the available width rather than making the outer page horizontally scroll.

A visual review at a wide desktop window can miss the consequences of a new wrapper or label. Selectors such as `.controls > button` and `.control-row > button` apply to direct children. If a wrapper changes which element grows, measuring the wrapper rather than the actual button can hide a target-width problem.

The overall content has `16px` page padding and a maximum width of `1120px`. A viewport width is therefore not the same thing as a control's available row width. Panel padding, gaps and borders consume space too. Reading the size policy as a viewport measurement alone would skip the layout where the target actually lives.

## Visible content versus activation area

A native button may contain text, a shape or multiple SVG pieces. In Card, the face SVG and matched check mark are descendants of one button, and the click callback is attached to that button. Their separate geometry does not produce separate tiny controls.

The neutral back is a `12px` span with a rotated border and `aria-hidden="true"`. It is deliberately smaller than the card. Counting its bounds as the input target would describe the drawing rather than the event-handling element. Similarly, the matched check is a state mark, not a separate action with its own click listener.

Focus outlines sit outside the control border and do not add activation area. Hover border changes likewise do not expand the target. Measurements used to assess the policy concern the actual element box; measurements used to assess focus visibility include outline width and offset. The project already has separate helpers for that distinction in `tests/focus-bounds.ts`.

The reproduction summary is another useful case. Its text and disclosure marker occupy only part of a padded native summary element. The element supplies the disclosure interaction. Replacing it with a visually similar small icon could change both target size and semantics; the current source does neither.

## Zoom, density and CSS units

The policy uses CSS pixels. Device pixel ratio affects the mapping to physical pixels, not the DOM geometry reported by `getBoundingClientRect`. A test at device scale 2 can still report a 44px CSS box. Multiplying the bounding-box result by device scale would answer a different question.

The repository's equivalent zoom layout uses a `640x400` viewport with device scale 2. It checks that controls, statistics and the completion summary remain readable and that both small and large boards remain playable. This is useful complementary evidence for a layout that wraps and scrolls rather than simply shrinking every element.

The game does not disable pinch zoom. Card touch handling uses `touch-action: manipulation`, and index.html does not impose a maximum scale. A target remains part of a browser page whose visible scale can change. [Zoom behaviour](../visuals/zoom-behaviour.md) covers the visual contract in more detail.

## Existing evidence and what it establishes

`tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` checks the default board and control dimensions at `320x640`. It measures `.controls button`, `.controls select` and `.card` boxes and checks minimum width and height. The same file checks large boards at phone and desktop viewports, where the card floor, viewport height and complete focus ring are important.

Those checks establish the existing tested elements at their stated layouts. They do not automatically cover a future control merely because it shares a color or appears next to a tested button. The source selectors and actual bounding box identify the scope of evidence.

For a new feature review, a concise measurement record can identify the viewport, the control's role and name, its width and height and whether it is fully reachable. The record is most useful alongside the rendered layout, because it can reveal that a formally large button is covered by another element or forced beyond the page edge. This is observation of the target in context, not a second numerical policy.

The current game makes many of these checks straightforward by keeping interaction on native DOM elements. There is no canvas hit-map to reconcile with a drawn target. # Reproducibility
The reproducibility specification is a set of versioned formats that recreates Neon Pairs deals, progress and actions.

Status: spec version 2.2. Board codes, snapshots and replays keep format version 1.

A board code reproduces the starting cards. A snapshot restores a later position. A replay shows the actions that produced a position, so each format answers a different debugging question.

## Board code

- D01 - Use `np1-N-seed`, where `N` is a supported side length and `seed` is an integer from `1` through `2147483646`. Use decimal digits without leading zeros. The parser accepts exactly this form. Trim surrounding whitespace in the Board code control before parsing.
- D02 - Version `np1` fixes the generation algorithm below. The same code produces the same deck in every supported runtime. Changing generation requires another version. Time, animation and other random draws can't change this deck.

For example, `np1-4-1` describes a 4 by 4 board with generation version 1 and seed 1. It contains no progress.

## Generate

- D03 - Start the Park-Miller generator at `state = seed`. Each draw sets `state = (state * 16807) % 2147483647`. Use exact integer arithmetic. Seed 1 starts with states `16807`, `282475249`, `1622650073`, `984943658` and `1144108930`.
- D04 - Create the deck as `[0, 0, 1, 1, ...]` through face `N * N / 2 - 1`. Shuffle from index `N * N - 1` down to `1`. At index `i`, draw `j` in `0..i` and swap positions `i` and `j`.

For a draw with `b` possible results, set `q = 2147483646` and `limit = floor(q / b) * b`. Advance the generator and set `x = state - 1`. If `x >= limit`, draw again. Otherwise return `x % b`. This rejection step gives every result the same number of generator values.

The resulting deck for `np1-4-1` is `[6, 7, 0, 5, 2, 2, 0, 5, 3, 7, 1, 6, 4, 4, 1, 3]`.

## Snapshot

- D05 - Encode progress as a JSON object with exactly `version`, `boardCode`, `matched`, `selection`, `moves`, `elapsedMs` and `started`. `version` is `1`. `matched` is an array of matched position indices. Derive the deck, pair count and completion from these fields.

The `selection` object has one of these forms:

| `kind` | Other fields | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `closed` | None | No unmatched card is revealed |
| `one` | `index` | One unmatched card is revealed |
| `mismatch` | `first`, `second`, `remainingMs` | Two different faces await closing |

- D06 - Validate the complete object before replacing the game. Reject unknown keys. Require unique in-range matched indices containing whole face pairs. Selection indices must be in range and unmatched. A mismatch needs distinct indices with different faces and an integer `remainingMs` from `1` through `800`. Completion requires a closed selection.
- D07 - Require boolean `started` and nonnegative safe integers for `moves` and `elapsedMs`. Reject `elapsedMs` above `359999999` and `moves` above `999999`. Apply the move cap to saved best scores too. Require at least one move per matched pair and one further move for a pending mismatch. If `started` is false, require zero moves, zero elapsed time, no matches and a closed selection. A started game with zero moves requires one revealed card. Import of unfinished progress pauses the clock and pending mismatch until Resume. Completed imports stay completed without a pause.

Illustrative snapshot:

```json
{"version":1,"boardCode":"np1-4-1","matched":[0,11],"selection":{"kind":"mismatch","first":1,"second":2,"remainingMs":300},"moves":2,"elapsedMs":1500,"started":true}
```

Importing this snapshot shows one matched pair and two different faces. Resume lets those faces close after another `300` active milliseconds.

## Replay

- D08 - Encode a single deal as `{version: 1, boardCode, actions: [{atMs, index}], endMs}`. Require exactly these fields and exactly `atMs` and `index` per action. Indices must be in range. Times are nonnegative safe integers. Action times must be nondecreasing. If actions exist, `endMs` must be at least the final action time. Equal-time actions keep array order.
- D09 - Start from the code's hidden deal. Advance active time to each action's `atMs` before activating its index, then advance to `endMs`. Resolve a mismatch whose interval ends exactly at an action time before that action. Apply the game rules to ignored activation too. Cap replayed elapsed time at `359999999` milliseconds as R07 requires. Action times and `endMs` keep the nonnegative safe integer range in D08.

Illustrative replay:

```json
{"version":1,"boardCode":"np1-4-1","actions":[{"atMs":0,"index":0},{"atMs":0,"index":11}],"endMs":800}
```

This replay ends with one matched pair, one move and `800` elapsed milliseconds. Replay timestamps use a logical timeline. The game's elapsed clock still starts at its first valid activation. Replay omits hidden-page and imported-pause time. A new deal starts another replay.

## Limits

- D10 - Limit snapshot JSON to `65536` UTF-8 bytes. Limit replay JSON to `1048576` UTF-8 bytes and `10000` actions. Reject malformed JSON and unsupported format versions. For snapshots, inconsistent data means a violation of D05, D06 or D07. For replays, it means a violation of D08 or D09. For board codes, validate D01. Validation checks these stated constraints, without requiring a reconstructed history of earlier turns. Invalid board codes and snapshots keep the current browser game. Invalid replay files are rejected by the CLI and game core.

These local formats and saved scores are untrusted input. Validation checks the state rules, not a verified play history. The game has no accounts or trusted leaderboard.

Turn and clock behavior is defined in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md). Return to [Neon Pairs](../README.md) for the full specification.
# Architecture
Architecture is the code structure for Neon Pairs that keeps game rules separate from browser effects.

Status: spec version 2.2.

A card activation changes game data first. React renders that data, then the session adapter handles time and saved preferences. The same rules run in browser tests and replay without a browser.

## Game core

- A01 - Keep deck generation, card transitions, logical time, snapshot validation and replay as pure functions under `src/game`. They receive their inputs directly. They don't read the DOM, storage, external random sources or browser clocks.

- A02 - Keep the board description and deck immutable. Keep matched positions, current selection, moves, active elapsed milliseconds and whether play started in game state. Derive pair count and victory. Serialize progress using the [reproducibility formats](../sharing/reproducibility.md).

- A03 - Use direct calls and exhaustive branches for the closed, one-card and mismatch states. Keep named states, format versions, timing values and size limits beside the behavior they control.

Proposed game functions:

| Call | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `createGame(boardCode)` | Initial state for a valid board code |
| `activateCard(state, index)` | State after one card activation |
| `advanceGame(state, milliseconds)` | State after logical time advances |
| `isWon(state)` | Whether every position is matched |
| `encodeSnapshot(state)` | Version 1 snapshot JSON |
| `decodeSnapshot(text)` | Valid restored state or `null` |
| `replayGame(text)` | Final replay state or `null` |

## Browser session

- A04 - Keep React state, timer lifecycle and browser visibility handling in `src/game/session`. Use a monotonic browser clock. Clear pending work on unmount and invalidate callbacks when the deal changes. A callback from an earlier deal can't change the current one.

- A05 - Keep preference and best-score reads in the session storage module. Treat saved JSON as unknown input. Validate grid sizes and finite integer scores. Catch read, parse and write failures. Keep unrelated storage keys untouched. A failure leaves the game playable.

- A06 - Keep active game progress in memory until you export or import a snapshot. Importing a completed snapshot doesn't update best scores or play a celebration. Completing an unfinished imported game records a local best under R10.

## Components

- A07 - `Game.tsx` composes status, the board, game controls and reproduction controls. Keep board navigation in `src/game/board`, controls in `src/game/controls` and session behavior in `src/game/session`. Keep each component's props and styles beside it.

- A08 - A card mounts its face SVG only while revealed or matched. Hidden card identity stays out of DOM attributes, accessible names and diagnostic globals. Tests can know a deck from its documented board code. The app gives them no solver endpoint.

- A09 - Use native browser input and the shared card activation function. Keep focus position in the board component. Focus movement changes presentation, never the deck or move count. [Input](../interface/input.md) defines the keys and focus rules.

## Evidence

- A10 - Keep focused tests beside their behavior. Complete browser journeys live at the application test level. Check generation against independent literal vectors. Check game transitions against stated rules. Test built HTML from disk as well as served storage behavior.

- A11 - Keep development fixtures and diagnostic helpers out of the shipped game. Tests can use the documented board code, snapshot and replay formats. The shipped game exposes only its documented controls.

## Changes

- A12 - Add a new rule at its game behavior, then update its component, tests and specification. Add shared support only when two actual behaviors need the same meaning. Don't add a global store, event bus, router or generic utility folder.

The [game specification](../README.md) defines the behavior this structure implements.

# Control bar

This page explains how `Controls.tsx` presents the deal actions and how those actions connect to the session.

The bar is deliberately small: a labeled size selector, New Game and Restart. It sits above the statistics and board in `src/game/Game.tsx`, so the actions that replace a deal are available before entering the board. Reproduction tools have a different rhythm and occupy their own disclosure below the board; see [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md).

## Component boundary

`src/game/controls/Controls.tsx` accepts three props: `size`, `newGame(size?: number)` and `restart()`. It does not own a second copy of the selected size, choose a seed, reset a timer or update preferences. Its select is controlled by the `size` prop. That prop comes from `session.game.size`, which makes the displayed choice agree with the board after a size change, board-code load or snapshot import.

The optional argument on `newGame` explains the two call sites. The select converts `event.currentTarget.value` with `Number(...)` and calls `newGame` with that value. New Game calls `newGame()` without an argument. The default in `use-game.ts` takes the current game's size. Restart calls its separate callback. There is no DOM inspection to decide which size to use when either button is pressed.

The select and buttons are native elements. The two buttons explicitly use `type="button"`; they do not submit the reproduction form farther down the page. The wrapper is a `div` with class `controls`, not a toolbar widget with a separate keyboard model. Tab follows ordinary document order through the select, New Game and Restart. Board navigation begins after those controls, as described in [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md).

## Labels and options

`src/game/controls/control-labels.ts` exports `DealControl`. The visible strings are `Grid size`, `New Game` and `Restart`. The label is associated with `id="grid-size"` through `htmlFor="grid-size"`. A user or browser test can therefore find the select by its visible name instead of a CSS class or its position in the bar.

The options come directly from `GRID_SIZES` in `deck.ts`. Their values are the numeric side lengths rendered as native option values, and their text is the side repeated with a lowercase `x`:

| Display | Value | Cards |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4x4 | 4 | 16 |
| 6x6 | 6 | 36 |
| 8x8 | 8 | 64 |
| 10x10 | 10 | 100 |
| 12x12 | 12 | 144 |
| 14x14 | 14 | 196 |
| 16x16 | 16 | 256 |

Those are deal sizes, rather than zoom settings. Choosing 16 changes the game to a 16-row, 16-column deck; it does not squeeze the existing sixteen cards into a different arrangement. The larger boards can exceed the available width inside their scroll container. [Pointer and touch](pointer-and-touch.md) explains the consequences for reaching cards.

The component itself receives `size: number`, but the session's `newGame` function checks `isValidSize(size)` before making a replacement. That guard is outside the control and also protects callers that do not originate in the native select. The option list is not the only validation boundary.

## Desktop arrangement

`controls.css` uses flex layout with `align-items: end`, `flex-wrap: wrap`, a `12px` gap and a `16px` bottom margin. The size group is another flex row with `align-items: center` and a `12px` gap. The label sits beside its select rather than above it. The outer alignment brings the actions to the same bottom line if control heights differ.

No explicit column count or button width is needed in this layout. Labels and the browser's select affordance contribute to their natural widths. Wrapping is enabled before the phone media query applies, so the bar can also adapt to a constrained content area on a wider window. The maximum content width and page padding come from `game.css`, not the controls stylesheet.

The shared `.control` class comes from `control.css`: `min-height: 44px`, `padding: 8px 12px`, a `1px` neutral border, an `8px` radius, panel background, text color and inherited font. The select and buttons get a pointer cursor. The stylesheet does not replace the select's browser interaction with a drawn menu. Its popup remains the native control's responsibility.

## Phone arrangement

At `max-width: 599px`, `.controls` changes to `align-items: stretch`. The size group occupies the full line with `width: 100%` and `justify-content: space-between`; its label and select move to opposite ends of that row. The direct child buttons each get `flex: 1`, sharing the following row when there is room.

The media query acts on the current DOM hierarchy. Moving a button into an extra wrapper would change the effect of `.controls > button`. A review of such a refactor can compare computed widths and wrapping before deciding that it preserves the arrangement. The apparent simplicity of a wrapper change can hide a layout change on phones.

The breakpoint is not a board-size breakpoint. A 4x4 and a 16x16 game use the same control bar at the same viewport width. The board handles its own width independently. This separation keeps the controls available even when a player has scrolled to the far end of a large board.

## What the actions replace

In `use-game.ts`, `newGame` creates a code using `freshBoardCode(size, current.current.game.seed)`, constructs the new game, resets the clock adapter and commits `replaceGame(...)`. Restart constructs a game from `current.current.game.boardCode` instead. Both begin with a closed selection, no matched positions, zero moves, zero elapsed time and `started: false` because that is what `createGame` returns.

`replaceGame` increments `session.generation`. The Board in `Game.tsx` is keyed by this generation, so it mounts with a fresh remembered tab stop. The BoardCodeForm input is also keyed by generation and receives the current board code as its default value. A reset is therefore observable in several places without each component inventing its own reset event.

The size is saved through the session preferences path. The current size's best record is read independently for the statistics. Choosing a size with no stored record shows `Best: none`; returning to a size with a record displays that size's value. For the exact display boundary, see [Status bar](status-bar.md) and [Best score records](../gameplay/best-score-records.md).

A pending mismatch cannot later alter the replacement deal. Clock reset and generation checks in the session make stale updates harmless. This is why replacing a deal during its short mismatch display is a meaningful controls test, rather than merely checking that the card count changes.

## Focus and continuity

Clicking New Game or Restart leaves focus on the action button. The components do not call `.focus()` on the board after a reset. A user can press the same action again or Tab forward to the new first card. A size change likewise uses the native select interaction rather than an application focus transfer.

Initial page load also does not select a card on the user's behalf. The board's first card is ready as its tab stop, but readiness is separate from current focus. [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) describes this distinction and the different treatment needed when Resume removes its own button.

There is no confirmation step in either callback today. Pressing an action replaces the current deal immediately. Do not infer a pending dialog from the text of an action or from the fact that the old game had moves. The separate [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) records the policy for future actions that leave unfinished work.

## A useful review path

The controls checks in `tests/controls.e2e.test.ts` inspect the native option values as well as their displayed text. `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` checks the literal labels. `tests/keyboard.e2e.test.ts` checks the relationship between Restart and the remembered board entry point. Layout coverage includes a narrow `320x640` viewport in `tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` and the equivalent zoom layout in `tests/zoom.e2e.test.ts`.

These checks cover different failures. A label refactor could preserve a screenshot while breaking name-based selection. A wrapper refactor could preserve all labels while changing the mobile row. A session refactor could keep the bar visually identical while allowing an earlier timer to touch a new deal. Reading the component, CSS and callback together makes those differences visible.

For a manual check, choose a nondefault size, reveal a mismatching pair, then use Restart before it closes. The deck repeats and the counters reset. Use New Game at that same size and confirm that its code changes. Tab into the board after each action to observe the reset entry point. Finally load a valid code of another size from the reproduction panel and look back at Grid size: the controlled select follows the loaded game without another local state update.

The document language is English, the browser title is Neon Pairs, and the main area contains the game's h1 and introductory text. The first interactive deal control is the native select labeled Grid size. New Game and Restart follow as native buttons.

The select's label is connected with `htmlFor="grid-size"`. Its options read 4x4 through 16x16 at the seven supported sizes. A user can find it by its visible name rather than needing to interpret an unlabeled icon. The action buttons also use visible text as their names.

The statistics are reading content in a definition list: Moves, Pairs, Time and Best. There are no custom accessible labels replacing their values. An absent best is visible as `none`. These details matter when inspecting the tree because the information is ordinary document content, not four editable fields or buttons.

Changing size creates a deal of that size. New Game creates another deal at the current size, and Restart repeats the current code. Those actions retain focus at their controls. They do not suddenly land the player deep in the card board. [Control bar](control-bar.md) describes the callbacks and layout.

Board's viewport is a region named `Game board` and described by `board-help`. The help text says: `Use a pointer or Tab to enter the board. Arrow keys move between cards. Enter or Space reveals a card.` This is visible text as well as an associated description.

Tab enters at the remembered card. Before any card focus has been remembered, that is the first card. Plain arrows move one row or column with no wrapping. Tab and Shift+Tab can leave the board. Modifier combinations and unlisted keys remain browser input rather than board commands.

The native card button provides activation through Enter and Space. Screen reader interaction modes can affect which keys reach a web page, so a real spoken acceptance journey is still valuable even when the browser's keyboard tests pass. Matched cards remain focusable, and navigation does not skip them. During a mismatch or paused import, movement can continue although activating another card has no game effect. `describeCard` builds a one-based coordinate from the zero-based deck index. Index 0 on a four-column board is named `Row 1, column 1, closed`. Index 5 is `Row 2, column 2, closed`. The pattern gives a stable spatial reference before any face is known.

- D04 - Create the deck as `[0, 0, 1, 1, ...]` through face `N * N / 2 - 1`. Shuffle from index `N * N - 1` down to `1`. At index `i`, draw `j` in `0..i` and swap positions `i` and `j`.

The resulting deck for `np1-4-1` is `[6, 7, 0, 5, 2, 2, 0, 5, 3, 7, 1, 6, 4, 4, 1, 3]`.

## Snapshot

- D05 - Encode progress as a JSON object with exactly `version`, `boardCode`, `matched`, `selection`, `moves`, `elapsedMs` and `started`. `version` is `1`. `matched` is an array of matched position indices. Derive the deck, pair count and completion from these fields.

The `selection` object has one of these forms:

| `kind` | Other fields | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `closed` | None | No unmatched card is revealed |
| `one` | `index` | One unmatched card is revealed |
| `mismatch` | `first`, `second`, `remainingMs` | Two different faces await closing |

- D06 - Validate the complete object before replacing the game. Reject unknown keys. Require unique in-range matched indices containing whole face pairs. Selection indices must be in range and unmatched. A mismatch needs distinct indices with different faces and an integer `remainingMs` from `1` through `800`. Completion requires a closed selection.
- D07 - Require boolean `started` and nonnegative safe integers for `moves` and `elapsedMs`. Reject `elapsedMs` above `359999999` and `moves` above `999999`. Apply the move cap to saved best scores too. Require at least one move per matched pair and one further move for a pending mismatch. If `started` is false, require zero moves, zero elapsed time, no matches and a closed selection. A started game with zero moves requires one revealed card. Import of unfinished progress pauses the clock and pending mismatch until Resume. Completed imports stay completed without a pause.

Illustrative snapshot:

```json
{"version":1,"boardCode":"np1-4-1","matched":[0,11],"selection":{"kind":"mismatch","first":1,"second":2,"remainingMs":300},"moves":2,"elapsedMs":1500,"started":true}
```

Importing this snapshot shows one matched pair and two different faces. Resume lets those faces close after another `300` active milliseconds.

## Replay

- D08 - Encode a single deal as `{version: 1, boardCode, actions: [{atMs, index}], endMs}`. Require exactly these fields and exactly `atMs` and `index` per action. Indices must be in range. Times are nonnegative safe integers. Action times must be nondecreasing. If actions exist, `endMs` must be at least the final action time. Equal-time actions keep array order.
- D09 - Start from the code's hidden deal. Advance active time to each action's `atMs` before activating its index, then advance to `endMs`. Resolve a mismatch whose interval ends exactly at an action time before that action. Apply the game rules to ignored activation too. Cap replayed elapsed time at `359999999` milliseconds as R07 requires. Action times and `endMs` keep the nonnegative safe integer range in D08.

Illustrative replay:

```json
{"version":1,"boardCode":"np1-4-1","actions":[{"atMs":0,"index":0},{"atMs":0,"index":11}],"endMs":800}
```

This replay ends with one matched pair, one move and `800` elapsed milliseconds. Replay timestamps use a logical timeline. The game's elapsed clock still starts at its first valid activation. Replay omits hidden-page and imported-pause time. A new deal starts another replay.

## Limits

- D10 - Limit snapshot JSON to `65536` UTF-8 bytes. Limit replay JSON to `1048576` UTF-8 bytes and `10000` actions. Reject malformed JSON and unsupported format versions. For snapshots, inconsistent data means a violation of D05, D06 or D07. For replays, it means a violation of D08 or D09. For board codes, validate D01. Validation checks these stated constraints, without requiring a reconstructed history of earlier turns. Invalid board codes and snapshots keep the current browser game. Invalid replay files are rejected by the CLI and game core.

These local formats and saved scores are untrusted input. Validation checks the state rules, not a verified play history. The game has no accounts or trusted leaderboard.

Turn and clock behavior is defined in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md). Return to [Neon Pairs](../README.md) for the full specification.
# Architecture
Architecture is the code structure for Neon Pairs that keeps game rules separate from browser effects.

Status: spec version 2.2.

A card activation changes game data first. React renders that data, then the session adapter handles time and saved preferences. The same rules run in browser tests and replay without a browser.

## Game core

- A01 - Keep deck generation, card transitions, logical time, snapshot validation and replay as pure functions under `src/game`. They receive their inputs directly. They don't read the DOM, storage, external random sources or browser clocks.

- A02 - Keep the board description and deck immutable. Keep matched positions, current selection, moves, active elapsed milliseconds and whether play started in game state. Derive pair count and victory. Serialize progress using the [reproducibility formats](../sharing/reproducibility.md).

- A03 - Use direct calls and exhaustive branches for the closed, one-card and mismatch states. Keep named states, format versions, timing values and size limits beside the behavior they control.

Proposed game functions:

| Call | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `createGame(boardCode)` | Initial state for a valid board code |
| `activateCard(state, index)` | State after one card activation |
| `advanceGame(state, milliseconds)` | State after logical time advances |
| `isWon(state)` | Whether every position is matched |
| `encodeSnapshot(state)` | Version 1 snapshot JSON |
| `decodeSnapshot(text)` | Valid restored state or `null` |
| `replayGame(text)` | Final replay state or `null` |

## Browser session

- A04 - Keep React state, timer lifecycle and browser visibility handling in `src/game/session`. Use a monotonic browser clock. Clear pending work on unmount and invalidate callbacks when the deal changes. A callback from an earlier deal can't change the current one.

- A05 - Keep preference and best-score reads in the session storage module. Treat saved JSON as unknown input. Validate grid sizes and finite integer scores. Catch read, parse and write failures. Keep unrelated storage keys untouched. A failure leaves the game playable.

- A06 - Keep active game progress in memory until you export or import a snapshot. Importing a completed snapshot doesn't update best scores or play a celebration. Completing an unfinished imported game records a local best under R10.

## Components

- A07 - `Game.tsx` composes status, the board, game controls and reproduction controls. Keep board navigation in `src/game/board`, controls in `src/game/controls` and session behavior in `src/game/session`. Keep each component's props and styles beside it.

- A08 - A card mounts its face SVG only while revealed or matched. Hidden card identity stays out of DOM attributes, accessible names and diagnostic globals. Tests can know a deck from its documented board code. The app gives them no solver endpoint.

- A09 - Use native browser input and the shared card activation function. Keep focus position in the board component. Focus movement changes presentation, never the deck or move count. [Input](../interface/input.md) defines the keys and focus rules.

## Evidence

- A10 - Keep focused tests beside their behavior. Complete browser journeys live at the application test level. Check generation against independent literal vectors. Check game transitions against stated rules. Test built HTML from disk as well as served storage behavior.

- A11 - Keep development fixtures and diagnostic helpers out of the shipped game. Tests can use the documented board code, snapshot and replay formats. The shipped game exposes only its documented controls.

## Changes

- A12 - Add a new rule at its game behavior, then update its component, tests and specification. Add shared support only when two actual behaviors need the same meaning. Don't add a global store, event bus, router or generic utility folder.

The [game specification](../README.md) defines the behavior this structure implements.
