# Controls
Controls is a specification that defines the game options and reproduction tools in Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.3.

You can start another deal, repeat the current one or load saved progress. Each control keeps the same label, so you can find the same action after a game changes.

## Deal controls

The main controls are:

- C01 - Label the native size select "Grid size". Give it options `4x4`, `6x6`, `8x8`, `10x10`, `12x12`, `14x14` and `16x16`, with numeric side length `N` as each value. After a successful board-code or snapshot load, select the loaded board's size.
- C02 - Label the fresh-deal button "New Game". It creates a fresh seed and keeps the current size.
- C03 - Label the repeat-deal button "Restart". It starts the same board code again.

Changing size, starting and restarting follow the session rules in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md).

## Reproduction tools

- C04 - Put reproduction controls inside a native `details` element that starts collapsed. Give its summary the exact text "Reproduce a game".

The controls use the board-code and snapshot formats defined in [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md). A board code starts a deal. A snapshot loads progress on a deal.

## Load a board

- C05 - Label the text input "Board code" and limit it to 32 characters. Show the current board code after a new deal, Restart or a successful load. Keep an edited draft when a card action changes the game.

- C06 - Label its button "Load board". Validate the entered code before replacing the current game with that deal's starting state.

For example, loading `np1-4-1` starts its hidden four-column board. Entering that code alone keeps the current game until you select Load board.

## Snapshot tools

- C07 - Label the textarea "Snapshot JSON" and limit it to 65536 characters. The parser also applies the UTF-8 byte limit in the snapshot format.

- C08 - Label the export button "Export snapshot". Fill the textarea with readable version 1 snapshot JSON that you can select and copy manually. Export leaves the game state and clock unchanged. It requires no Clipboard API.

Export `elapsedMs` and a pending mismatch's `remainingMs` as whole milliseconds. A pending mismatch always exports at least 1ms.

- C09 - Label the import button "Load snapshot". Validate the complete draft before replacing the current game. Load unfinished progress paused and show "Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue." Load completed progress as completed without pausing and show "Loaded completed snapshot."

- C10 - Show a "Resume" button only while an imported unfinished game is paused. Selecting it clears that pause. Unfinished play continues from the loaded state. While paused, block every card activation and allow board focus movement. On Resume, move focus to the board's remembered tab stop before removing the Resume button. A loaded completed game stays completed and shows no Resume button.

- C11 - On invalid input, keep the current game and the entered draft for correction. Show the exact status for that control:

| Control | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Load board | Invalid board code. |
| Load snapshot | Invalid snapshot. |

- C12 - A loaded completed snapshot keeps the win banner static and plays no celebration. Import doesn't write a best score. Resuming an unfinished snapshot and later winning records a local best under R10.

For example, loading a completed game with fewer moves than the saved best shows that game without replacing the saved record.

## Focus

- C13 - Keep focus on the button used for starting, restarting, loading or exporting. These actions don't move focus to the board. Resume follows C10 because its button disappears. The board's remembered tab stop follows the focus rules in [Input](input.md#focus).

## Replay

- C14 - Keep replay in the developer CLI and game core. V1 has no replay controls in the game UI.

Run `npm run --silent replay -- PATH` to read a replay file. On valid input, print only the final snapshot JSON to stdout and exit 0. On invalid input, print nothing to stdout, write a message to stderr and exit nonzero.

The complete game pack starts in [Neon Pairs](../README.md).
# Screen reader notes

This page describes the information exposed during a keyboard game and the limits of the project's screen reader evidence.

The interface exposes native controls, card names, state changes and readable results. The repository README records accessibility-tree checks in Chromium 156.0.8078.4 with Playwright 1.64.1. It also explicitly records that no screen reader was run. The names and sentences below are source-backed content available to assistive technology, not a transcript of speech captured in a listening session.

## Finding the game controls

The document language is English, the browser title is Neon Pairs, and the main area contains the game's h1 and introductory text. The first interactive deal control is the native select labeled Grid size. New Game and Restart follow as native buttons.

The select's label is connected with `htmlFor="grid-size"`. Its options read 4x4 through 16x16 at the seven supported sizes. A user can find it by its visible name rather than needing to interpret an unlabeled icon. The action buttons also use visible text as their names.

The statistics are reading content in a definition list: Moves, Pairs, Time and Best. There are no custom accessible labels replacing their values. An absent best is visible as `none`. These details matter when inspecting the tree because the information is ordinary document content, not four editable fields or buttons.

Changing size creates a deal of that size. New Game creates another deal at the current size, and Restart repeats the current code. Those actions retain focus at their controls. They do not suddenly land the player deep in the card board. [Control bar](control-bar.md) describes the callbacks and layout.

## Entering the board

Board's viewport is a region named `Game board` and described by `board-help`. The help text says: `Use a pointer or Tab to enter the board. Arrow keys move between cards. Enter or Space reveals a card.` This is visible text as well as an associated description.

Tab enters at the remembered card. Before any card focus has been remembered, that is the first card. Plain arrows move one row or column with no wrapping. Tab and Shift+Tab can leave the board. Modifier combinations and unlisted keys remain browser input rather than board commands.

The native card button provides activation through Enter and Space. Screen reader interaction modes can affect which keys reach a web page, so a real spoken acceptance journey is still valuable even when the browser's keyboard tests pass. The game's documented input relies on native button activation and board arrow navigation.

Matched cards remain focusable, and navigation does not skip them. During a mismatch or paused import, movement can continue although activating another card has no game effect. This keeps exploration separate from the turn decision. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) traces the remembered tab stop and target calculation.

## A closed card reveals no hidden identity

`describeCard` builds a one-based coordinate from the zero-based deck index. Index 0 on a four-column board is named `Row 1, column 1, closed`. Index 5 is `Row 2, column 2, closed`. The pattern gives a stable spatial reference before any face is known.

Board passes `face={null}` for a hidden card. Card then renders only the neutral back span with `aria-hidden="true"`, not the Face component. The hidden face is absent from the element's label, attributes and child artwork. A screen reader cannot legitimately read a face description from that hidden DOM because it is not there.

This is stronger than hiding a face SVG with CSS while leaving a revealing title or data attribute. The browser input-contract test compares every hidden card's attributes, inner HTML and text against the expected neutral content. A visual-only inspection could miss such a leak.

The deck still exists in game state because the game must resolve matches. The DOM boundary is the important distinction for the interface: a hidden card control exposes its position and closed state, not its underlying identity. [Card artwork](../visuals/card-artwork.md) and [Pair identity](../gameplay/pair-identity.md) explain the visual and game sides.

## The first reveal

Use `np1-4-1` as a concrete source-backed example. Its index 0 contains face 6. After activation, that button's name becomes `Row 1, column 1, revealed, cyan solid plus, marker top`. The state precedes the face description in the actual string generated by `card-state.ts`.

Face names come from `faceDesign`: color, solid or outline, shape and marker position. The SVG itself is `aria-hidden="true"` and `focusable="false"`. It does not add a separate graphic description competing with the button name. The name carries the information the player needs to remember.

A first reveal starts elapsed time but leaves Moves at zero. The game has not yet completed a two-card attempt. It also does not publish a turn result merely for that first card. A user can inspect the newly focused control's name, move to another location and make the second choice.

Repeating activation on the same first card does not complete a move. That is an ignored game action, not a second reveal or a reason to read a new turn result. This is useful when interpreting a test that presses Space twice and sees no move increment.

## A match and a miss

On the same example code, index 11 is the partner of index 0. It is row 3, column 4. Activating it completes the pair immediately. Both controls' names use `matched`, retain the face description and expose `aria-disabled="true"`.

The current result text for the first match is `Pair found. 1 pair matched.` Later nonfinal matches substitute the count and plural form. The matched controls remain in the board's spatial navigation even though activating them no longer changes the game. A screen reader may verbalize their unavailable state according to its own conventions; the source exposes the ARIA disabled state.

Indices 0 and 1 are a mismatch on this code. Their faces remain revealed for the active mismatch interval, and the turn result is `No match. Cards close after a short pause.` Additional card activation during that wait is ignored. The interval pauses while the page is hidden or imported progress waits for Resume.

After closure, the two names return to their closed forms and their face artwork is removed. Closure does not publish another turn result. Moving focus while the pair waits also does not republish the mismatch sentence. [Announcements policy](announcements-policy.md) explains the event identity that makes consecutive identical misses distinct without making ordinary renders noisy.

## Completing the game

The winning match produces `Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time.`, using the final counters. GameStatus also displays the persistent completion sentence `Every pair found in N moves and time. Well played.` A reader can revisit the final statistics and summary in document content.

The time text uses the game's formatter: seconds are padded, and minutes can grow beyond 59. The values stop advancing at completion. The final card remains the active control; completion does not force focus onto the banner.

Matched cards still occupy the board, so Tab leaves it without requiring a pass through every matched position. In the collapsed page layout, the next control is the native reproduction summary. Shift+Tab can return through the remembered board location toward the deal controls. Starting another game resets board memory while leaving the action button focused.

The complete automated journey exercises this path, including a new game after completion. It checks the final summary in the accessibility tree rather than assuming that visible text is necessarily exposed as expected.

## Reproduction tools in reading order

The native summary is named `Reproduce a game`. Expanding it exposes labeled Board code and Snapshot JSON fields with Load board, Export snapshot and Load snapshot actions. The board-code form submits with Enter; the snapshot actions are ordinary buttons rather than an Enter-to-import form.

Invalid input keeps the current game and draft. The visible outcomes are `Invalid board code.` and `Invalid snapshot.`. The load buttons reference the nearby notice paragraph as a description, and the event feedback path publishes the outcome. Clicking a load button leaves focus there. An invalid Enter submission from Board code leaves focus in the input for correction.

A valid unfinished snapshot reports `Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue.` and pauses card activation. The player can still explore the board with arrows. Resume focuses the remembered card before the Resume button is removed, then continues active play. A completed snapshot reports `Loaded completed snapshot.`, shows the completed game statically and offers no Resume button.

Export fills readable JSON into the textarea. It does not require clipboard permission or make the text impossible to select. A user can move to the native field and copy its contents through their normal editing commands. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) explains draft lifetimes and the different board-code reset behavior.

## What the automated journey records

`tests/accessibility.e2e.test.ts` uses Chromium's debugging protocol to enable accessibility and capture full trees at named stages. Its helper removes ignored nodes and records role, name, scalar value, text and selected accessibility properties. This produces evidence about exposed controls and states without preserving transient browser node identifiers.

The journey finds Grid size and New Game by name, enters the board, inspects closed and revealed names, completes pairs with Enter and Space, checks matched disabled state and reads each turn result. It then checks completion, Tab exit, New Game and repeated load outcomes. The saved artifact is named `accessibility-journey.json` by the test.

The test writes that artifact as output. The source references reviewed fixtures for expected content.

## Spoken acceptance still answers a different question

Tree exposure, keyboard behavior and speech are related but distinct. A browser may expose the correct atomic result while a particular screen reader schedules or phrases it in a way that needs listening review. Consecutive identical misses and the final combined result are especially useful listening points.

The input specification assigns spoken confirmation to user acceptance. The repository README's record says `Screen reader: not run. Spoken journey: user acceptance.` That limitation belongs beside the evidence, not hidden behind a broad statement that screen reader support was tested end to end.

A useful acceptance note names the browser, screen reader and versions, the action sequence and what was heard. If a result differs, the DOM publication history and tree capture can help locate the boundary. [Accessibility audit](../quality/accessibility-audit.md) and [Browser test guide](../quality/browser-test-guide.md) provide the wider review context.
# Tables policy

This page records the markup policy for ordered result data and explains why the current game statistics use a different structure.

`TournamentBracket.tsx` presents ordered match results in a table. `GameStatus.tsx` still displays properties of one active game in a definition list. Reproduction controls use forms, and the board is a CSS grid of buttons; those structures have different meanings from the bracket records.

## Policy for result data

When the content represents records with comparable columns, its relationships need to survive reading beyond the visual arrangement. CSS alone can align text while leaving those relationships absent from the document structure. Ranked or bracket data is a table element with a caption and th scope="col" header cells. The caption identifies the collection being read, while the column headers connect each record's values to their meaning.

This is a content-specific policy. It does not make the game board a data table because it has rows and columns, and it does not require converting every compact summary to tabular markup. The distinction begins with what the content means: interactive card coordinates, a property's value and a record in an ordered result collection are different things.

The tournament bracket uses a caption and column-scoped header cells. [Tournament mode](../competition/tournament-mode.md) describes its columns and result values. [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) discusses the broader preference for native semantics without adding another result format.

## Why the statistics are a definition list

GameStatus renders Moves, Pairs, Time and Best as four `dt`/`dd` groups inside a `dl`. Each term names a property of the same current game. There are no peer result rows and no column whose meaning changes with the row being read.

The layout happens to use flex and can wrap. At a wide width, those groups may look like cells in a horizontal strip. At a narrow width, they can flow to multiple lines. Neither visual arrangement changes the definition-list relationship. Replacing the wrapper with a table solely to preserve one desktop arrangement would confuse layout with content structure.

The Best value is one saved move count selected by current size. It does not present a list of people or a comparison across many records. `session.preferences.bestMoves[String(game.size)]` chooses the value before it reaches GameStatus. A single local best is not an implemented ordered-results screen.

[Status bar](status-bar.md) documents those expressions and labels. The present statistics model has no result columns.

## Why the card board is not a table

Board renders a named region containing an inner `div.board` and native card buttons. CSS Grid places those buttons in row order. Each card has its own coordinate and state in its accessible name, and keyboard movement follows a dedicated spatial model.

The table policy does not turn that interactive surface into a data table. A card is activated, can reveal a face and participates in remembered focus. A result cell is read as part of a record. They have different purposes even if both appear in a rectangle.

There is also no ARIA grid role on the current board. Its native buttons and movement handler implement the specified interaction without declaring a separate composite widget role. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) traces that behavior. A review of result markup should not accidentally rename or restructure the card controls because the word “row” appears in both contexts.

## What the caption contributes

An ordered collection needs context. A visible title elsewhere on a page can be helpful, but a table caption directly identifies the collection associated with the table. That matters when reading the table independently or navigating between document structures.

The policy does not specify caption text. The source has no existing results title. A feature's actual subject supplies the wording. Describing that subject is different from attaching a technical explanation of table markup to product copy.

A caption also does not supply missing column meaning. A reader needs to know whether a number represents moves, a position in an ordering or another property. The required header cells carry the column relationships; the caption names the whole collection. Combining all labels into a caption would leave the row values harder to interpret.

## Column relationships and reading order

The `scope="col"` attribute makes the header's direction explicit. It communicates that the header applies to values down its column. A bold `td`, a styled `div` or text positioned above a column can look similar while having a different structure.

A reviewer can inspect the table DOM and the browser's accessibility representation separately from the screenshot. The screenshot establishes visible arrangement. The DOM establishes element choices and attributes. The accessibility view helps establish that the browser exposes a meaningful table structure. No single one of these views proves all aspects of the interface.

Row headers, column order, numeric alignment and sorting controls depend on the result feature. The current game has no result implementation with those details.

## Narrow layouts and long values

The current game already separates outer page width from board overflow. Result data would have its own content and width behavior; it cannot simply inherit the card board's scroll logic by sharing a class name. A table's relationship between headers and values remains meaningful even when its viewport is narrow.

There is no table stylesheet in the source and no prescribed responsive table transformation here. A reviewer can still observe whether a proposed layout makes values readable and associated with their headers. Changing a collection into a stack of unrelated labels solely at a breakpoint can affect more than appearance, so both DOM and visual behavior are relevant evidence.

Name text can also vary in width without changing its accepted value. Typography and wrapping are layout concerns. The name policies remain separate from table structure; accepted names retain their displayed representation. [Typography](../visuals/typography.md) and [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md) explain nearby layout decisions in the existing interface.

The existing accessibility journey covers game controls and completion, not a result table. Evidence for a future result view would identify its actual markup and readable rows; the current statistics tests cannot establish that structure. [Accessibility audit](../quality/accessibility-audit.md) provides the wider review context.
# Source layout

This page is a map of the current Neon Pairs source tree and the responsibilities of its files.

Paths here are relative to the project root. They describe authored source and configured outputs. [Module layout policy](module-layout-policy.md) explains placement decisions; this page is for finding the implementation.

## Entry and project root

`index.html` contains the document metadata, the `root` element and the development module entry `/src/main.tsx`. It declares English, a responsive viewport, the theme color `#090B14` and the title Neon Pairs. The source HTML references a module; the production HTML is assembled by Vite and the single-file plugin.

`src/main.tsx` looks up the root, throws `Missing application root.` if it is absent and renders `<Game />` under React `StrictMode`. There is no second application page or router mounted beside it. The game begins at `src/game/Game.tsx`.

The root also holds `package.json`, `package-lock.json`, four compiler configuration files, three Vite configurations and `vitest.config.ts`. `.prettierrc.json` configures formatting; `.prettierignore` and `.gitignore` identify generated or local work. The README records setup, commands, delivery, replay and the named runtime evidence.

## Game composition

`Game.tsx` calls the solo and tournament controllers and switches between their screens. The Tournament button sits beside New Game. Opening the tournament suspends the solo clock; returning focuses the Tournament button and resumes solo timing.

Its one extra coordination operation is Resume. It asks the board's imperative ref to focus the remembered card, then calls the controller's resume action. That keeps the DOM focus handoff outside the core state. `Board` is keyed by `session.generation`, so a replacement remounts the board's local state.

`game.css` defines root colors and spacing values, system typography, page geometry, global focus styling and the reserved turn-feedback area. The more specific board, control and status rules live beside their components. [CSS organization](css-organization.md) records selectors and cascade relationships.

## Core modules directly under src/game

| File | What a reader finds there |
| --- | --- |
| `deck.ts` | Supported sizes, seed bounds, board-code parser and formatter, seeded shuffle and immutable board description |
| `selection.ts` | The closed, one-card and mismatch discriminated union |
| `game.ts` | `GameState`, caps, creation, victory, face-up positions, activation and logical advancement |
| `elapsed-time.ts` | Display formatting from elapsed milliseconds |
| `saved-format.ts` | Small shared JSON, object, key, integer and byte helpers |
| `snapshot-selection.ts` | Validation of matched positions and nested selection |
| `snapshot.ts` | Snapshot version and bound, serialization and complete-state validation |
| `replay.ts` | Replay limits, structured problems, ordered actions and final state |

These files use ordinary TypeScript functions and data. The core is not a React context or reducer hook. It can be imported by the session adapter and by the replay CLI without mounting the application.

`generateBoard` returns a frozen description with a frozen deck. `GameState` extends that description. Runtime progress is returned as new objects by transitions; ignored actions can return the existing object. This pattern explains why the board's memoized sets can survive clock-only updates.

## Core test files

`game.test.ts` checks card transitions and logical advancement. `completion.test.ts` finishes every supported size. `move-cap.test.ts` exercises play and records at the maximum move count. `elapsed-time.test.ts` covers the formatter and related elapsed behavior.

`deck.test.ts` checks parsing and generation. `deck-rejection.test.ts` references independently generated vectors for rejection-sampling boundaries. `game.fixture.ts` contains the example code, literal deck, pair positions, initial generator states and shared numerical specification vectors.

`snapshot.test.ts` and `snapshot-selection.test.ts` cover the outer state and nested validation. `replay.test.ts` and `replay-order.test.ts` cover replay acceptance and ordering. These files live near the rules even when a narrow regression deserves a different test filename from the principal module.

## Session directory

`session/session.ts` defines `Session`, the import notices and the pure session operations `initialSession`, `replaceGame`, `tickSession` and `activateSession`. It connects a game transition to feedback, completion state and preferences without itself calling the browser.

`session/use-game.ts` is the React controller. It reads initial preferences, creates the initial fresh board, keeps the latest session ref in step with state, exposes actions and composes the clock and saving hooks. Successful loads replace the game; failed loads publish notices. Exports and activations synchronize the clock first.

`session/browser-clock.ts` defines the 40ms scheduling interval and arithmetic over observed timestamps. `session/use-session-clock.ts` supplies observations, maintains visibility, schedules timeouts and removes pending work on effect cleanup. `session/browser-clock.test.ts` checks the arithmetic independently.

`session/fresh-board.ts` converts browser entropy into a valid board code, rejecting out-of-range candidates and an optional previous seed. `session/storage.ts` defines the preference key, version, default size, store interface, validators and best-score update. `session/use-saved-preferences.ts` obtains browser storage safely and writes changes in an effect.

`session/session.test.ts` covers state replacement, paused input, generations, repeated feedback events and completion handling. `session/storage.test.ts` uses in-memory and throwing stores to cover persistence decisions. [Session module](session-module.md) follows the exact call paths and state fields.

## Tournament directory

`tournament/rules.ts` owns name acceptance, turn progression, advancement and result comparison. `tournament/pairing.ts` defines the opening pairings, rounds and board sizes. `tournament/validation.ts` checks tournament progression and bracket consistency; `tournament/decode.ts` validates imported records, and `tournament/format.ts` reads and writes Tournament JSON.

`tournament/use-tournament.ts` connects those rules to a separate game state, unique board-code selection and the local past-tournament list. `tournament/use-tournament-clock.ts` applies active-time rules without writing solo best scores. `TournamentScreen`, `TournamentSetup`, `TournamentPlay`, `TournamentBracket`, `TournamentExchange` and `TournamentPast` own the view and its drafts. `storage.ts` saves finished events in the feature collection; `tournament.css` styles the screen and confirmation dialog.

## Board directory

`board/Board.tsx` maps the immutable deck into cards. It derives a face-up set and a matched set, obtains the focus hook, exposes a remembered-focus method and supplies the `--grid-size` custom property. It keeps the activation callback stable while calling the latest controller action through a ref.

`board/Card.tsx` is memoized. It renders a native button, obtains its class and accessible description from `describeCard`, renders the face only when supplied and adds a matched mark for matched positions. It delegates navigation and focus to callbacks from the board.

`board/Face.tsx` converts a face design into inline SVG primitives. `board/face-design.ts` maps one of 128 face numbers to shape, marker, color, fill style, coordinates and label. `board/card-state.ts` derives a card's closed, revealed or matched description from supplied presentation data.

`board/keyboard.ts` computes arrow-navigation targets with edge stops and modifier handling. `board/use-board-focus.ts` owns the remembered position and DOM focus calls. `board/nearest-scroll.ts` remembers the viewport scroll position so focus can use nearest alignment after Chromium's automatic focus scrolling.

`board/board.css` owns the scrolling board viewport and grid tracks. `board/card.css` owns the button, concealed back, revealed/matched surfaces, corner mark and card transition. The directory's `keyboard.test.ts`, `card-state.test.ts` and `face-design.test.ts` check the numerical and descriptive helpers. Browser tests observe actual focus, artwork and scrolling.

## Controls and status

`controls/Controls.tsx` renders the grid-size select, New Game, Tournament and Restart. It reads the size options from `GRID_SIZES`. `controls/control-labels.ts` owns the exact deal and reproduction control strings consumed by components and tests.

`controls/BoardCodeForm.tsx` renders the board-code field and submit button. Its input is keyed by generation, and successful submission moves focus to the load button because the old input is replaced. An invalid submission leaves the draft available for correction.

`controls/Reproduction.tsx` holds the snapshot textarea draft in local state, renders the details disclosure and export/load buttons, and shows the load notice and conditional Resume button outside the disclosure. It uses the game code and generation passed from the parent rather than reconstructing them.

`controls/control.css` defines the common control surface. `controls/controls.css` lays out deal controls. `controls/reproduction.css` lays out the disclosure, form rows, textarea and notice region.

`status/GameStatus.tsx` renders moves, pair progress, elapsed text, optional best moves and the completion paragraph. Tournament mode omits Best. `status/status-labels.ts` owns statistic labels. `status/status.css` styles the statistic layout and completion treatment.

## Scripts directory

`scripts/replay.ts` is the command entry. It passes command-line arguments to `runReplay` and assigns the returned status to `process.exitCode`. `scripts/replay-cli.ts` handles one input path, caller-directory resolution, file reads, human-readable stderr failures and final snapshot output. `scripts/replay.test.ts` exercises the executable in child processes.

`scripts/source-files.ts` recursively reads ordinary files from a supplied folder and rejects links or special entries. `scripts/source-audit.test.ts` inspects packages, compiler settings, source length, unsafe constructs and selected effect boundaries. `scripts/source-conventions.test.ts` checks recognized exports/imports, yes-or-no naming, test names and environment reads.

These scripts are not imported by the application entry. Some import core functions because they are clients of the same public data behavior. That direction lets command-line replay reuse the rules without putting Node APIs into browser modules.

## Application-level test support

`tests/browser-test.ts` adapts Node tests to Playwright, manages browsers and contexts, records runtime versions, gathers page errors and provides artifact paths. `tests/artifact-server.ts` serves the built HTML over loopback. `tests/game-fixture.ts` contains public-control setup helpers, disk URLs and completion helpers.
# React boundaries

This page explains where React participates in Neon Pairs and where ordinary data functions remain independent of rendering.

React mounts the application, holds the session for presentation, owns local UI state and manages browser-effect lifetimes. The game rules are callable outside React. That separation lets the browser UI and replay CLI share behavior without teaching the core about components, effects or DOM events.

## The mounted tree

`src/main.tsx` calls `createRoot` after checking the `root` element and renders `Game` inside `StrictMode`. `Game.tsx` composes the solo screen or Tournament screen. It calls `useGame` and the tournament controller, showing one screen at a time. The tournament controller is a feature-local hook rather than a global store or router.

The component tree is intentionally direct. There is no React context carrying a global game store and no router coordinating separate screens. `Controls` receives size and two actions. `GameStatus` receives a game, an optional best and a celebration flag. `Board` receives the game and activation action. `Reproduction` receives current code context, exchange actions and pause-related presentation.

These props describe the existing contracts. A component can render data it does not own without gaining responsibility for deciding a turn. The core still computes matches, move counts, elapsed advancement and victory.

## The data-only side

`deck.ts`, `game.ts`, `selection.ts`, `elapsed-time.ts`, `saved-format.ts`, `snapshot.ts`, `snapshot-selection.ts` and `replay.ts` do not import React. They accept values and return values. `session/session.ts` is also a data transformation module, although it lives beside hooks that import React.

The board has data-only helpers too. `keyboard.ts` computes a target from keys and coordinates. `card-state.ts` computes a state description. `face-design.ts` maps an integer identity to design values. These helpers can be tested without rendering `Board` or building a synthetic browser tree.

This is the meaningful interpretation of the React boundary: importing a rule in a CLI does not start an effect or require a mounted component. It is not a claim that every file ending in `.ts` is independent of React. `use-board-focus.ts`, `nearest-scroll.ts` and the session hooks are TypeScript modules with hooks and browser behavior.

## React imports in application code

| Module | React mechanisms used |
| --- | --- |
| `main.tsx` | `StrictMode`; root rendering through React DOM |
| `Game.tsx` | Ref for the board's focus interface |
| `Board.tsx` | Memoized derivations, refs, stable callback, layout effect and imperative handle |
| `Card.tsx` | `memo` and a keyboard event type |
| `use-board-focus.ts` | Local state, refs and callbacks |
| `nearest-scroll.ts` | Ref, effect and callback |
| `BoardCodeForm.tsx` | Ref for the successful-load focus target |
| `Reproduction.tsx` | Local snapshot draft state |
| `use-game.ts` | Session state and current-value ref |
| `use-session-clock.ts` | Clock/visibility refs and timer effect |
| `use-saved-preferences.ts` | Persistence effect |

`Controls`, `GameStatus` and `Face` contain JSX without importing a React runtime object. The compiler uses `jsx: react-jsx`, so those files do not need the older `import React` pattern. JSX participation and explicit hook imports are related but different observations.

The diagnostic entries also use React DOM. The face sheet renders real cards, while the session harness mounts and unmounts the real game. Their entrypoints are outside `src` and built separately, so they do not become extra runtime controls in the distributed game.

## One action path for activation

`Card` renders a native button and invokes its supplied activation callback from `onClick`. Native keyboard activation and ordinary pointer activation therefore reach the same controller action. The keydown handler delegates navigation; it does not implement another matching algorithm.

The controller synchronizes active time and calls `activateSession`, which calls `activateCard`. Components receive the resulting state and render it. A class such as `matched` is an outcome of the data, not the authoritative record of a matched pair. Reading CSS classes back into the core would reverse that relationship.

Matched buttons use `aria-disabled`, keeping them in the board's focus model. The rule function still rejects activating matched positions. During a mismatch, the session does not mark every other button disabled; the core rejects new activations while that selection is pending. Semantic presentation and transition legality are both visible, with legality centralized in the rules.

## Latest values without another store

`useGame` keeps React state for rendering and a ref for immediate event-time access. `commit` updates the ref before setting React state. A clock synchronization can therefore commit a new game, and the immediately following activation can consume that new game in the same task.

The board has a similar but narrower pattern for callback identity. `Game` supplies a new activation function as it renders. `Board` stores that function in `latestActivate`, updates the ref in a layout effect and passes a stable `useCallback` wrapper to cards. Memoized cards see a stable function prop while it calls the latest controller closure.

These refs do not bypass the rules. They keep the correct data/action visible across render scheduling. The data transition still returns a new immutable description, and React still receives the committed session. [Session module](session-module.md) explains why the current ref matters for export and activation boundaries.

## Render cost on a large board

A 16 by 16 board has 256 cards. Active time can update on the 40ms observation cadence, but most ticks do not change any card's appearance. `advanceGame` retains the deck and matched array and, outside a mismatch change, retains the selection object. `Board` memoizes face-up and matched sets from those references.

`Card` is wrapped in `memo`. Its props are primitive presentation values and stable callbacks. On an elapsed-only update, face, matched, tabIndex, size and handlers stay equal, so the cards do not all need to rerender. The parent can still update the statistic.

A pending mismatch changes selection as its remainder decreases, so the face-up set can be recomputed. The resulting card props can nevertheless remain equal until the selection actually closes. This distinction explains why immutable reference stability is useful even though the board's parent renders more often than its cards.

Memoization is not a substitute for correct state ownership. Mutating the matched array in place could keep its reference stable while changing its meaning, causing derived sets to miss an update. The transition code returns a new matched array when a pair is found, matching the assumptions of the board's memoization.

## Concealed identity is a prop boundary

`Board` knows the immutable deck, but it passes `face={null}` for every position outside the derived face-up set. `Card` then renders only a decorative back. It does not mount `Face` and hide it with CSS. Its accessible description omits face design when the supplied face is null.

When revealed or matched, a card gets the face number and renders inline SVG. `Face` marks the SVG as decorative, while the button's label describes the visible design. The board can therefore hold authoritative identity without exposing concealed identity through every child element.

This behavior is also why tests use documented board codes rather than a diagnostic global. A test can reconstruct a deal independently and activate matching positions through the public interface. There is no application solver endpoint that a production user or test needs to query.

## Local focus and DOM work

`useBoardFocus` holds a focused index initialized to zero and refs to the viewport and grid. Arrow handling calls `navigationTarget`; a non-null result prevents the browser default and focuses the target button with `preventScroll: true`. Focus events update the remembered index.

`useNearestScroll` listens to the board viewport's scroll events and remembers the reported position. For keyboard focus it restores that position before calling `scrollIntoView` with nearest alignment. This accounts for Chromium's automatic centering on focus. A click scrolls after activation so the pressed card is not moved under a held pointer before release.

These browser operations belong with the board presentation, not `GameState`. A replay contains positions and logical times, not a scroll offset. A snapshot can load into a differently sized viewport. Keeping focus and scrolling local preserves that independence.

## Replacement and imperative focus

`Game` gives `Board` a ref typed as `BoardFocus`. The board exposes only `focusRemembered()` through `useImperativeHandle`. The parent does not receive the whole grid DOM or a collection of card nodes.

Resume uses that limited operation, then calls the controller's resume action. A replacement instead increments generation and changes the board key, remounting its local focus state. `BoardCodeForm` keys its uncontrolled input by that same generation, so successful loading replaces the old draft with the current code.

A generation is consequently a lifecycle boundary shared by adapters and components. It is not a reason to put DOM state in the session core. The rule functions remain unaware of keyed mounts, refs or focus methods.

## Effects and cleanup

Browser effects pair setup with cleanup: the clock removes its listener and timeout, and nearest scrolling removes its viewport listener. The separate session harness lets tests unmount the real game and measure that cleanup. [Clock design](clock-design.md) details the active flag, generation checks and scheduling lifetime.

## Keeping a change on the right side

An incorrect pair count starts in the game state and derivation, not in JSX text. An incorrect load-pause state starts in session replacement, not a disabled style. An incorrect arrow stop starts in the numerical navigation helper, while an incorrect scroll alignment starts in the DOM hook. The boundary narrows where an explanation should begin.

The architecture specification permits shared support when two actual behaviors need the same meaning. It does not introduce a generic hooks or utilities layer merely because several files use React. Current direct imports keep ownership legible, and the module policy describes feature placement. Together they make small components useful without making rendering the owner of the game rules.
# Tournament mode

Tournament mode lets four or eight people play a local knockout bracket on one device. It reuses the card rules while keeping tournament state and completed tournament records separate from solo preferences.

## Entry and play

The Tournament button beside New Game opens the Tournament screen. The Players select offers 4 and 8. The visible name inputs are labeled Player 1 through Player 4 or Player 8. Accepted names are trimmed, interior whitespace is collapsed and text is normalized to NFC. Names must contain 2 to 20 Unicode code points and be unique without regard to case. The acceptance errors are `Use 2 to 20 characters.` and `Each name must be different.`

Seeds follow entry order. Four entrants open with seeds 1 vs 4, then 2 vs 3. Eight entrants open with 1 vs 8, 4 vs 5, 3 vs 6, then 2 vs 7. An eight-player bracket proceeds through Quarterfinal, Semifinal and Final; a four-player bracket begins with Semifinal. The active screen shows `Round: NAME` and `Now playing: NAME`.

The first person starts with Start turn. After that game, Next turn selects the other player; Start turn begins their game. Both games use the match's same board code. Next match advances after both results are recorded. Quarterfinals use 4x4 boards, semifinals use 6x6 and finals use 8x8. Every match in one event gets a distinct full board code.

The match winner is decided by fewer moves, then lower active elapsed time, then the higher entry seed (seed 1 has priority). The bracket table displays the round, local match number, deal code, both players, their moves and time, and the winner. Tournament completion displays `Champion: NAME` and Back to game. Leaving an unfinished event opens a native confirmation dialog; Keep playing and Escape retain it, while Leave returns to solo play and discards the active event.

Tournament games use the same active-time and card transitions as solo games. Opening Tournament mode suspends the solo clock, and tournament turns do not change the saved solo size or best moves. There is no backend or account identity; imported tournament data is validated as a consistent record, not authenticated as proof of play.

## Past tournaments and exchange

Completed tournaments appear newest first under Past tournaments. The `np3:tournaments` key stores a version 3 feature envelope with an `items` array and keeps the newest ten records. A blocked or failed store leaves the in-memory list usable and shows `Progress won't be saved on this device.` beside the list. Active tournaments are not written automatically.

Tournament JSON is a separate exchange format with root `format: "neon-pairs/tournament"` and numeric `version: 1`. Its object keys are written alphabetically. It carries entrants, board codes, match results, the current turn and the current game position. Import checks exact fields, names, board sizes, distinct deals, result bounds, progression and winner consistency before replacing the active tournament. Input is limited to 65,536 UTF-8 bytes. Unknown fields report `Unknown field: NAME.`; other rejected input reports `Invalid tournament JSON.`

Export tournament synchronizes the active clock before filling the Tournament JSON box. With no active event it exports the newest past tournament. With neither, it leaves the box empty and reports `Start or load a tournament before exporting.` Load tournament validates the box before replacing the event. Replacing an unfinished event asks for confirmation. A valid completed import is also added to the local past list.

## Source ownership

`src/game/tournament/rules.ts` owns names, turn progression, advancement and result comparison. `pairing.ts` defines round plans; `decode.ts`, `validation.ts` and `format.ts` own the exchange boundary. `use-tournament.ts` and `use-tournament-clock.ts` connect the pure decisions to browser state, fresh deals, timing and persistence. The components under `src/game/tournament` render setup, turns, the bracket, exchange tools and past records.

The feature follows [pairing](competition-pairing.md), [rounds](competition-rounds.md), [boards](competition-boards.md), [deals](competition-deals.md), [ties](competition-ties.md) and [score isolation](competition-scores.md). The complete journey is in [Acceptance](../quality/acceptance.md#tournament).

# Controls
Controls is a specification that defines the game options and reproduction tools in Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.3.

You can start another deal, repeat the current one or load saved progress. Each control keeps the same label, so you can find the same action after a game changes.

## Deal controls

The main controls are:

- C01 - Label the native size select "Grid size". Give it options `4x4`, `6x6`, `8x8`, `10x10`, `12x12`, `14x14` and `16x16`, with numeric side length `N` as each value. After a successful board-code or snapshot load, select the loaded board's size.
- C02 - Label the fresh-deal button "New Game". It creates a fresh seed and keeps the current size.
- C03 - Label the repeat-deal button "Restart". It starts the same board code again.

Changing size, starting and restarting follow the session rules in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md).

## Reproduction tools

- C04 - Put reproduction controls inside a native `details` element that starts collapsed. Give its summary the exact text "Reproduce a game".

The controls use the board-code and snapshot formats defined in [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md). A board code starts a deal. A snapshot loads progress on a deal.

## Load a board

- C05 - Label the text input "Board code" and limit it to 32 characters. Show the current board code after a new deal, Restart or a successful load. Keep an edited draft when a card action changes the game.

- C06 - Label its button "Load board". Validate the entered code before replacing the current game with that deal's starting state.

For example, loading `np1-4-1` starts its hidden four-column board. Entering that code alone keeps the current game until you select Load board.

## Snapshot tools

# Screen reader notes

This page describes the information exposed during a keyboard game and the limits of the project's screen reader evidence.

The interface exposes native controls, card names, state changes and readable results. The repository README records accessibility-tree checks in Chromium 156.0.8078.4 with Playwright 1.64.1. It also explicitly records that no screen reader was run. The names and sentences below are source-backed content available to assistive technology, not a transcript of speech captured in a listening session.

## Finding the game controls

The document language is English, the browser title is Neon Pairs, and the main area contains the game's h1 and introductory text. The first interactive deal control is the native select labeled Grid size. New Game and Restart follow as native buttons.

The select's label is connected with `htmlFor="grid-size"`. Its options read 4x4 through 16x16 at the seven supported sizes. A user can find it by its visible name rather than needing to interpret an unlabeled icon. The action buttons also use visible text as their names.

The statistics are reading content in a definition list: Moves, Pairs, Time and Best. There are no custom accessible labels replacing their values. An absent best is visible as `none`. These details matter when inspecting the tree because the information is ordinary document content, not four editable fields or buttons.

Changing size creates a deal of that size. New Game creates another deal at the current size, and Restart repeats the current code. Those actions retain focus at their controls. They do not suddenly land the player deep in the card board. [Control bar](control-bar.md) describes the callbacks and layout.

## Entering the board

Board's viewport is a region named `Game board` and described by `board-help`. The help text says: `Use a pointer or Tab to enter the board. Arrow keys move between cards. Enter or Space reveals a card.` This is visible text as well as an associated description.

Tab enters at the remembered card. Before any card focus has been remembered, that is the first card. Plain arrows move one row or column with no wrapping. Tab and Shift+Tab can leave the board. Modifier combinations and unlisted keys remain browser input rather than board commands.

The native card button provides activation through Enter and Space. Screen reader interaction modes can affect which keys reach a web page, so a real spoken acceptance journey is still valuable even when the browser's keyboard tests pass. The game's documented input relies on native button activation and board arrow navigation.

Matched cards remain focusable, and navigation does not skip them. During a mismatch or paused import, movement can continue although activating another card has no game effect. This keeps exploration separate from the turn decision. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) traces the remembered tab stop and target calculation.

## A closed card reveals no hidden identity

`describeCard` builds a one-based coordinate from the zero-based deck index. Index 0 on a four-column board is named `Row 1, column 1, closed`. Index 5 is `Row 2, column 2, closed`. The pattern gives a stable spatial reference before any face is known.

Board passes `face={null}` for a hidden card. Card then renders only the neutral back span with `aria-hidden="true"`, not the Face component. The hidden face is absent from the element's label, attributes and child artwork. A screen reader cannot legitimately read a face description from that hidden DOM because it is not there.

This is stronger than hiding a face SVG with CSS while leaving a revealing title or data attribute. The browser input-contract test compares every hidden card's attributes, inner HTML and text against the expected neutral content. A visual-only inspection could miss such a leak.

The deck still exists in game state because the game must resolve matches. The DOM boundary is the important distinction for the interface: a hidden card control exposes its position and closed state, not its underlying identity. [Card artwork](../visuals/card-artwork.md) and [Pair identity](../gameplay/pair-identity.md) explain the visual and game sides.

## The first reveal

Use `np1-4-1` as a concrete source-backed example. Its index 0 contains face 6. After activation, that button's name becomes `Row 1, column 1, revealed, cyan solid plus, marker top`. The state precedes the face description in the actual string generated by `card-state.ts`.

Face names come from `faceDesign`: color, solid or outline, shape and marker position. The SVG itself is `aria-hidden="true"` and `focusable="false"`. It does not add a separate graphic description competing with the button name. The name carries the information the player needs to remember.

A first reveal starts elapsed time but leaves Moves at zero. The game has not yet completed a two-card attempt. It also does not publish a turn result merely for that first card. A user can inspect the newly focused control's name, move to another location and make the second choice.

Repeating activation on the same first card does not complete a move. That is an ignored game action, not a second reveal or a reason to read a new turn result. This is useful when interpreting a test that presses Space twice and sees no move increment.

## A match and a miss

On the same example code, index 11 is the partner of index 0. It is row 3, column 4. Activating it completes the pair immediately. Both controls' names use `matched`, retain the face description and expose `aria-disabled="true"`.

The current result text for the first match is `Pair found. 1 pair matched.` Later nonfinal matches substitute the count and plural form. The matched controls remain in the board's spatial navigation even though activating them no longer changes the game. A screen reader may verbalize their unavailable state according to its own conventions; the source exposes the ARIA disabled state.

Indices 0 and 1 are a mismatch on this code. Their faces remain revealed for the active mismatch interval, and the turn result is `No match. Cards close after a short pause.` Additional card activation during that wait is ignored. The interval pauses while the page is hidden or imported progress waits for Resume.

After closure, the two names return to their closed forms and their face artwork is removed. Closure does not publish another turn result. Moving focus while the pair waits also does not republish the mismatch sentence. [Announcements policy](announcements-policy.md) explains the event identity that makes consecutive identical misses distinct without making ordinary renders noisy.

## Completing the game

The winning match produces `Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time.`, using the final counters. GameStatus also displays the persistent completion sentence `Every pair found in N moves and time. Well played.` A reader can revisit the final statistics and summary in document content.

The time text uses the game's formatter: seconds are padded, and minutes can grow beyond 59. The values stop advancing at completion. The final card remains the active control; completion does not force focus onto the banner.

Matched cards still occupy the board, so Tab leaves it without requiring a pass through every matched position. In the collapsed page layout, the next control is the native reproduction summary. Shift+Tab can return through the remembered board location toward the deal controls. Starting another game resets board memory while leaving the action button focused.

The complete automated journey exercises this path, including a new game after completion. It checks the final summary in the accessibility tree rather than assuming that visible text is necessarily exposed as expected.

## Reproduction tools in reading order

The native summary is named `Reproduce a game`. Expanding it exposes labeled Board code and Snapshot JSON fields with Load board, Export snapshot and Load snapshot actions. The board-code form submits with Enter; the snapshot actions are ordinary buttons rather than an Enter-to-import form.

Invalid input keeps the current game and draft. The visible outcomes are `Invalid board code.` and `Invalid snapshot.`. The load buttons reference the nearby notice paragraph as a description, and the event feedback path publishes the outcome. Clicking a load button leaves focus there. An invalid Enter submission from Board code leaves focus in the input for correction.

A valid unfinished snapshot reports `Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue.` and pauses card activation. The player can still explore the board with arrows. Resume focuses the remembered card before the Resume button is removed, then continues active play. A completed snapshot reports `Loaded completed snapshot.`, shows the completed game statically and offers no Resume button.

Export fills readable JSON into the textarea. It does not require clipboard permission or make the text impossible to select. A user can move to the native field and copy its contents through their normal editing commands. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) explains draft lifetimes and the different board-code reset behavior.

## What the automated journey records

`tests/accessibility.e2e.test.ts` uses Chromium's debugging protocol to enable accessibility and capture full trees at named stages. Its helper removes ignored nodes and records role, name, scalar value, text and selected accessibility properties. This produces evidence about exposed controls and states without preserving transient browser node identifiers.

The journey finds Grid size and New Game by name, enters the board, inspects closed and revealed names, completes pairs with Enter and Space, checks matched disabled state and reads each turn result. It then checks completion, Tab exit, New Game and repeated load outcomes. The saved artifact is named `accessibility-journey.json` by the test.

The test writes that artifact as output. The source references reviewed fixtures for expected content.

## Spoken acceptance still answers a different question

Tree exposure, keyboard behavior and speech are related but distinct. A browser may expose the correct atomic result while a particular screen reader schedules or phrases it in a way that needs listening review. Consecutive identical misses and the final combined result are especially useful listening points.

The input specification assigns spoken confirmation to user acceptance. The repository README's record says `Screen reader: not run. Spoken journey: user acceptance.` That limitation belongs beside the evidence, not hidden behind a broad statement that screen reader support was tested end to end.

A useful acceptance note names the browser, screen reader and versions, the action sequence and what was heard. If a result differs, the DOM publication history and tree capture can help locate the boundary. [Accessibility audit](../quality/accessibility-audit.md) and [Browser test guide](../quality/browser-test-guide.md) provide the wider review context.
# Tables policy

This page records the markup policy for ordered result data and explains why the current game statistics use a different structure.

`TournamentBracket.tsx` presents ordered match results in a table. `GameStatus.tsx` still displays properties of one active game in a definition list. Reproduction controls use forms, and the board is a CSS grid of buttons; those structures have different meanings from the bracket records.

## Policy for result data

When the content represents records with comparable columns, its relationships need to survive reading beyond the visual arrangement. CSS alone can align text while leaving those relationships absent from the document structure. Ranked or bracket data is a table element with a caption and th scope="col" header cells. The caption identifies the collection being read, while the column headers connect each record's values to their meaning.

This is a content-specific policy. It does not make the game board a data table because it has rows and columns, and it does not require converting every compact summary to tabular markup. The distinction begins with what the content means: interactive card coordinates, a property's value and a record in an ordered result collection are different things.

The tournament bracket uses a caption and column-scoped header cells. [Tournament mode](../competition/tournament-mode.md) describes its columns and result values. [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) discusses the broader preference for native semantics without adding another result format.

## Why the statistics are a definition list

GameStatus renders Moves, Pa…3569 tokens truncated…sclosure. It uses the game code and generation passed from the parent rather than reconstructing them.

`controls/control.css` defines the common control surface. `controls/controls.css` lays out deal controls. `controls/reproduction.css` lays out the disclosure, form rows, textarea and notice region.

`status/GameStatus.tsx` renders moves, pair progress, elapsed text, optional best moves and the completion paragraph. Tournament mode omits Best. `status/status-labels.ts` owns statistic labels. `status/status.css` styles the statistic layout and completion treatment.

## Scripts directory

`scripts/replay.ts` is the command entry. It passes command-line arguments to `runReplay` and assigns the returned status to `process.exitCode`. `scripts/replay-cli.ts` handles one input path, caller-directory resolution, file reads, human-readable stderr failures and final snapshot output. `scripts/replay.test.ts` exercises the executable in child processes.

`scripts/source-files.ts` recursively reads ordinary files from a supplied folder and rejects links or special entries. `scripts/source-audit.test.ts` inspects packages, compiler settings, source length, unsafe constructs and selected effect boundaries. `scripts/source-conventions.test.ts` checks recognized exports/imports, yes-or-no naming, test names and environment reads.

These scripts are not imported by the application entry. Some import core functions because they are clients of the same public data behavior. That direction lets command-line replay reuse the rules without putting Node APIs into browser modules.

## Application-level test support

`tests/browser-test.ts` adapts Node tests to Playwright, manages browsers and contexts, records runtime versions, gathers page errors and provides artifact paths. `tests/artifact-server.ts` serves the built HTML over loopback. `tests/game-fixture.ts` contains public-control setup helpers, disk URLs and completion helpers.
# React boundaries

This page explains where React participates in Neon Pairs and where ordinary data functions remain independent of rendering.

React mounts the application, holds the session for presentation, owns local UI state and manages browser-effect lifetimes. The game rules are callable outside React. That separation lets the browser UI and replay CLI share behavior without teaching the core about components, effects or DOM events.

## The mounted tree

`src/main.tsx` calls `createRoot` after checking the `root` element and renders `Game` inside `StrictMode`. `Game.tsx` composes the solo screen or Tournament screen. It calls `useGame` and the tournament controller, showing one screen at a time. The tournament controller is a feature-local hook rather than a global store or router.

The component tree is intentionally direct. There is no React context carrying a global game store and no router coordinating separate screens. `Controls` receives size and two actions. `GameStatus` receives a game, an optional best and a celebration flag. `Board` receives the game and activation action. `Reproduction` receives current code context, exchange actions and pause-related presentation.

These props describe the existing contracts. A component can render data it does not own without gaining responsibility for deciding a turn. The core still computes matches, move counts, elapsed advancement and victory.

## The data-only side

`deck.ts`, `game.ts`, `selection.ts`, `elapsed-time.ts`, `saved-format.ts`, `snapshot.ts`, `snapshot-selection.ts` and `replay.ts` do not import React. They accept values and return values. `session/session.ts` is also a data transformation module, although it lives beside hooks that import React.

The board has data-only helpers too. `keyboard.ts` computes a target from keys and coordinates. `card-state.ts` computes a state description. `face-design.ts` maps an integer identity to design values. These helpers can be tested without rendering `Board` or building a synthetic browser tree.

This is the meaningful interpretation of the React boundary: importing a rule in a CLI does not start an effect or require a mounted component. It is not a claim that every file ending in `.ts` is independent of React. `use-board-focus.ts`, `nearest-scroll.ts` and the session hooks are TypeScript modules with hooks and browser behavior.

## React imports in application code

| Module | React mechanisms used |
| --- | --- |
| `main.tsx` | `StrictMode`; root rendering through React DOM |
| `Game.tsx` | Ref for the board's focus interface |
| `Board.tsx` | Memoized derivations, refs, stable callback, layout effect and imperative handle |
| `Card.tsx` | `memo` and a keyboard event type |
| `use-board-focus.ts` | Local state, refs and callbacks |
| `nearest-scroll.ts` | Ref, effect and callback |
| `BoardCodeForm.tsx` | Ref for the successful-load focus target |
| `Reproduction.tsx` | Local snapshot draft state |
| `use-game.ts` | Session state and current-value ref |
| `use-session-clock.ts` | Clock/visibility refs and timer effect |
| `use-saved-preferences.ts` | Persistence effect |

`Controls`, `GameStatus` and `Face` contain JSX without importing a React runtime object. The compiler uses `jsx: react-jsx`, so those files do not need the older `import React` pattern. JSX participation and explicit hook imports are related but different observations.

The diagnostic entries also use React DOM. The face sheet renders real cards, while the session harness mounts and unmounts the real game. Their entrypoints are outside `src` and built separately, so they do not become extra runtime controls in the distributed game.

## One action path for activation

`Card` renders a native button and invokes its supplied activation callback from `onClick`. Native keyboard activation and ordinary pointer activation therefore reach the same controller action. The keydown handler delegates navigation; it does not implement another matching algorithm.

The controller synchronizes active time and calls `activateSession`, which calls `activateCard`. Components receive the resulting state and render it. A class such as `matched` is an outcome of the data, not the authoritative record of a matched pair. Reading CSS classes back into the core would reverse that relationship.

Matched buttons use `aria-disabled`, keeping them in the board's focus model. The rule function still rejects activating matched positions. During a mismatch, the session does not mark every other button disabled; the core rejects new activations while that selection is pending. Semantic presentation and transition legality are both visible, with legality centralized in the rules.

## Latest values without another store

`useGame` keeps React state for rendering and a ref for immediate event-time access. `commit` updates the ref before setting React state. A clock synchronization can therefore commit a new game, and the immediately following activation can consume that new game in the same task.

The board has a similar but narrower pattern for callback identity. `Game` supplies a new activation function as it renders. `Board` stores that function in `latestActivate`, updates the ref in a layout effect and passes a stable `useCallback` wrapper to cards. Memoized cards see a stable function prop while it calls the latest controller closure.

These refs do not bypass the rules. They keep the correct data/action visible across render scheduling. The data transition still returns a new immutable description, and React still receives the committed session. [Session module](session-module.md) explains why the current ref matters for export and activation boundaries.

## Render cost on a large board

A 16 by 16 board has 256 cards. Active time can update on the 40ms observation cadence, but most ticks do not change any card's appearance. `advanceGame` retains the deck and matched array and, outside a mismatch change, retains the selection object. `Board` memoizes face-up and matched sets from those references.

`Card` is wrapped in `memo`. Its props are primitive presentation values and stable callbacks. On an elapsed-only update, face, matched, tabIndex, size and handlers stay equal, so the cards do not all need to rerender. The parent can still update the statistic.

A pending mismatch changes selection as its remainder decreases, so the face-up set can be recomputed. The resulting card props can nevertheless remain equal until the selection actually closes. This distinction explains why immutable reference stability is useful even though the board's parent renders more often than its cards.

Memoization is not a substitute for correct state ownership. Mutating the matched array in place could keep its reference stable while changing its meaning, causing derived sets to miss an update. The transition code returns a new matched array when a pair is found, matching the assumptions of the board's memoization.

## Concealed identity is a prop boundary

`Board` knows the immutable deck, but it passes `face={null}` for every position outside the derived face-up set. `Card` then renders only a decorative back. It does not mount `Face` and hide it with CSS. Its accessible description omits face design when the supplied face is null.

When revealed or matched, a card gets the face number and renders inline SVG. `Face` marks the SVG as decorative, while the button's label describes the visible design. The board can therefore hold authoritative identity without exposing concealed identity through every child element.

This behavior is also why tests use documented board codes rather than a diagnostic global. A test can reconstruct a deal independently and activate matching positions through the public interface. There is no application solver endpoint that a production user or test needs to query.

## Local focus and DOM work

`useBoardFocus` holds a focused index initialized to zero and refs to the viewport and grid. Arrow handling calls `navigationTarget`; a non-null result prevents the browser default and focuses the target button with `preventScroll: true`. Focus events update the remembered index.

`useNearestScroll` listens to the board viewport's scroll events and remembers the reported position. For keyboard focus it restores that position before calling `scrollIntoView` with nearest alignment. This accounts for Chromium's automatic centering on focus. A click scrolls after activation so the pressed card is not moved under a held pointer before release.

These browser operations belong with the board presentation, not `GameState`. A replay contains positions and logical times, not a scroll offset. A snapshot can load into a differently sized viewport. Keeping focus and scrolling local preserves that independence.

## Replacement and imperative focus

`Game` gives `Board` a ref typed as `BoardFocus`. The board exposes only `focusRemembered()` through `useImperativeHandle`. The parent does not receive the whole grid DOM or a collection of card nodes.

Resume uses that limited operation, then calls the controller's resume action. A replacement instead increments generation and changes the board key, remounting its local focus state. `BoardCodeForm` keys its uncontrolled input by that same generation, so successful loading replaces the old draft with the current code.

A generation is consequently a lifecycle boundary shared by adapters and components. It is not a reason to put DOM state in the session core. The rule functions remain unaware of keyed mounts, refs or focus methods.

## Effects and cleanup

Browser effects pair setup with cleanup: the clock removes its listener and timeout, and nearest scrolling removes its viewport listener. The separate session harness lets tests unmount the real game and measure that cleanup. [Clock design](clock-design.md) details the active flag, generation checks and scheduling lifetime.

## Keeping a change on the right side

An incorrect pair count starts in the game state and derivation, not in JSX text. An incorrect load-pause state starts in session replacement, not a disabled style. An incorrect arrow stop starts in the numerical navigation helper, while an incorrect scroll alignment starts in the DOM hook. The boundary narrows where an explanation should begin.

The architecture specification permits shared support when two actual behaviors need the same meaning. It does not introduce a generic hooks or utilities layer merely because several files use React. Current direct imports keep ownership legible, and the module policy describes feature placement. Together they make small components useful without making rendering the owner of the game rules.
# Tournament mode

Tournament mode lets four or eight people play a local knockout bracket on one device. It reuses the card rules while keeping tournament state and completed tournament records separate from solo preferences.

## Entry and play

The Tournament button beside New Game opens the Tournament screen. The Players select offers 4 and 8. The visible name inputs are labeled Player 1 through Player 4 or Player 8. Accepted names are trimmed, interior whitespace is collapsed and text is normalized to NFC. Names must contain 2 to 20 Unicode code points and be unique without regard to case. The acceptance errors are `Use 2 to 20 characters.` and `Each name must be different.`

Seeds follow entry order. Four entrants open with seeds 1 vs 4, then 2 vs 3. Eight entrants open with 1 vs 8, 4 vs 5, 3 vs 6, then 2 vs 7. An eight-player bracket proceeds through Quarterfinal, Semifinal and Final; a four-player bracket begins with Semifinal. The active screen shows `Round: NAME` and `Now playing: NAME`.

The first person starts with Start turn. After that game, Next turn selects the other player; Start turn begins their game. Both games use the match's same board code. Next match advances after both results are recorded. Quarterfinals use 4x4 boards, semifinals use 6x6 and finals use 8x8. Every match in one event gets a distinct full board code.

The match winner is decided by fewer moves, then lower active elapsed time, then the higher entry seed (seed 1 has priority). The bracket table displays the round, local match number, deal code, both players, their moves and time, and the winner. Tournament completion displays `Champion: NAME` and Back to game. Leaving an unfinished event opens a native confirmation dialog; Keep playing and Escape retain it, while Leave returns to solo play and discards the active event.

Tournament games use the same active-time and card transitions as solo games. Opening Tournament mode suspends the solo clock, and tournament turns do not change the saved solo size or best moves. There is no backend or account identity; imported tournament data is validated as a consistent record, not authenticated as proof of play.

## Past tournaments and exchange

Completed tournaments appear newest first under Past tournaments. The `np3:tournaments` key stores a version 3 feature envelope with an `items` array and keeps the newest ten records. A blocked or failed store leaves the in-memory list usable and shows `Progress won't be saved on this device.` beside the list. Active tournaments are not written automatically.

Tournament JSON is a separate exchange format with root `format: "neon-pairs/tournament"` and numeric `version: 1`. Its object keys are written alphabetically. It carries entrants, board codes, match results, the current turn and the current game position. Import checks exact fields, names, board sizes, distinct deals, result bounds, progression and winner consistency before replacing the active tournament. Input is limited to 65,536 UTF-8 bytes. Unknown fields report `Unknown field: NAME.`; other rejected input reports `Invalid tournament JSON.`

Export tournament synchronizes the active clock before filling the Tournament JSON box. With no active event it exports the newest past tournament. With neither, it leaves the box empty and reports `Start or load a tournament before exporting.` Load tournament validates the box before replacing the event. Replacing an unfinished event asks for confirmation. A valid completed import is also added to the local past list.

## Source ownership

`src/game/tournament/rules.ts` owns names, turn progression, advancement and result comparison. `pairing.ts` defines round plans; `decode.ts`, `validation.ts` and `format.ts` own the exchange boundary. `use-tournament.ts` and `use-tournament-clock.ts` connect the pure decisions to browser state, fresh deals, timing and persistence. The components under `src/game/tournament` render setup, turns, the bracket, exchange tools and past records.

The feature follows [pairing](competition-pairing.md), [rounds](competition-rounds.md), [boards](competition-boards.md), [deals](competition-deals.md), [ties](competition-ties.md) and [score isolation](competition-scores.md). The complete journey is in [Acceptance](../quality/acceptance.md#tournament).
