# React boundaries

This page explains where React participates in Neon Pairs and where ordinary data functions remain independent of rendering.

React mounts the application, holds the session for presentation, owns local UI state and manages browser-effect lifetimes. The game rules are callable outside React. That separation lets the browser UI and replay CLI share behavior without teaching the core about components, effects or DOM events.

## The mounted tree

`src/main.tsx` calls `createRoot` after checking the `root` element and renders `Game` inside `StrictMode`. `Game.tsx` composes the solo screen or Tournament screen. It calls `useGame` and the tournament controller, showing one screen at a time. The tournament controller is a feature-local hook rather than a global store or router.

The component tree is intentionally direct. There is no React context carrying a global game store and no router coordinating separate screens. `Controls` receives size, solo actions, a Tournament action and its button ref. `GameStatus` receives a game, an optional best and a celebration flag. `Board` receives the game and activation action. `Reproduction` receives current code context, exchange actions and pause-related presentation. `TournamentScreen` receives tournament state and actions from its feature-local hook.

These props describe the existing contracts. A component can render data it does not own without gaining responsibility for deciding a turn. The core still computes matches, move counts, elapsed advancement and victory.

## The data-only side

`deck.ts`, `game.ts`, `selection.ts`, `elapsed-time.ts`, `saved-format.ts`, `snapshot.ts`, `snapshot-selection.ts` and `replay.ts` do not import React. They accept values and return values. `session/session.ts` is also a data transformation module, although it lives beside hooks that import React.

The board has data-only helpers too. `keyboard.ts` computes a target from keys and coordinates. `card-state.ts` computes a state description. `face-design.ts` maps an integer identity to design values. These helpers can be tested without rendering `Board` or building a synthetic browser tree.

This is the meaningful interpretation of the React boundary: importing a rule in a CLI does not start an effect or require a mounted component. It is not a claim that every file ending in `.ts` is independent of React. `use-board-focus.ts`, `nearest-scroll.ts` and the session hooks are TypeScript modules with hooks and browser behavior.

## React imports in application code

| Module | React mechanisms used |
| --- | --- |
| `main.tsx` | `StrictMode`; root rendering through React DOM |
| `Game.tsx` | Board and Tournament refs, screen selection and return focus |
| `Board.tsx` | Memoized derivations, refs, stable callback, layout effect and imperative handle |
| `Card.tsx` | `memo` and a keyboard event type |
| `use-board-focus.ts` | Local state, refs and callbacks |
| `nearest-scroll.ts` | Ref, effect and callback |
| `BoardCodeForm.tsx` | Ref for the successful-load focus target |
| `Reproduction.tsx` | Local snapshot draft state |
| `use-game.ts` | Session state and current-value ref |
| `use-session-clock.ts` | Clock/visibility refs and timer effect |
| `use-saved-preferences.ts` | Persistence effect |
| `tournament/TournamentScreen.tsx` | Local dialog/load state and heading focus |
| `tournament/TournamentPlay.tsx` | Board focus and match/player handoff focus |
| `tournament/use-tournament.ts` | Tournament state, actions and completed-record archive |
| `tournament/use-tournament-clock.ts` | Tournament timer and visibility lifecycle |

`Controls`, `GameStatus` and `Face` contain JSX without importing a React runtime object. The compiler uses `jsx: react-jsx`, so those files do not need the older `import React` pattern. JSX participation and explicit hook imports are related but different observations.

The diagnostic entries also use React DOM. The face sheet renders real cards, while the session harness mounts and unmounts the real game. Their entrypoints are outside `src` and built separately, so they do not become extra runtime controls in the distributed game.

## One action path for activation

`Card` renders a native button and invokes its supplied activation callback from `onClick`. Native keyboard activation and ordinary pointer activation therefore reach the same controller action. The keydown handler delegates navigation; it does not implement another matching algorithm.

The controller synchronizes active time and calls `activateSession`, which calls `activateCard`. Components receive the resulting state and render it. A class such as `matched` is an outcome of the data, not the authoritative record of a matched pair. Reading CSS classes back into the core would reverse that relationship.

Matched buttons use `aria-disabled`, keeping them in the board's focus model. The rule function still rejects activating matched positions. During a mismatch, the session does not mark every other button disabled; the core rejects new activations while that selection is pending. Semantic presentation and transition legality are both visible, with legality centralized in the rules.

## Latest values without another store

`useGame` keeps React state for rendering and a ref for immediate event-time access. `commit` updates the ref before setting React state. A clock synchronization can therefore commit a new game, and the immediately following activation can consume that new game in the same task.

The board has a similar but narrower pattern for callback identity. `Game` supplies a new activation function as it renders. `Board` stores that function in `latestActivate`, updates the ref in a layout effect and passes a stable `useCallback` wrapper to cards. Memoized cards see a stable function prop while it calls the latest controller closure.

These refs do not bypass the rules. They keep the correct data/action visible across render scheduling. The data transition still returns a new immutable description, and React still receives the committed session. [Session module](session-module.md) explains why the current ref matters for export and activation boundaries.

## Render cost on a large …5880 tokens truncated…code plus an action sequence can distinguish a bad card layout from a bad state transition. The appropriate artifact depends on whether the disputed behavior is generation, state, time or presentation.

## What the exchange formats carry

A board code carries generation version, supported side length and seed. `generateBoard` derives the immutable deck. The result contains face identifiers in position order; the code does not carry artwork, card names or a language setting. Loading it creates a fresh hidden state with no moves and no elapsed time. The algorithm and literal example are documented in [Board code format](board-code-format.md).

A snapshot carries `boardCode`, matched position indices, a tagged selection, moves, elapsed milliseconds and the `started` flag, alongside its format version. It does not duplicate the deck. Pair count and completion are derived after loading. Omitting those derived values avoids accepting a record in which the supplied pair total disagrees with the matched positions. [Snapshot format](snapshot-format.md) gives the complete field and validation reference.

A replay carries `boardCode`, an ordered array of `{atMs, index}` actions and `endMs`, alongside its version. It starts from the hidden deal rather than from an imported snapshot. The action timeline advances game time before each activation. The final time is advanced even when no action occurs there. This is how a replay can describe a mismatch closing after the final click. [Replay format](replay-format.md) covers the timeline and diagnostic result.

Tournament JSON contains player names and seeds, a fixed list of unique board codes, match attempts, winners and the current game position. It validates bracket progression and completion consistency before replacing the current event. Its maximum input size is 65,536 UTF-8 bytes. It is a local transfer format, not a signed record of who played. See [Tournament mode](../competition/tournament-mode.md).

None of these objects contains a browser storage key, a saved size preference, a per-size best record, a focus location or an animation flag. Those values have different lifetimes and authorities. A loaded board's size becomes the chosen size through session replacement; that is a browser consequence of loading, not a separate field in the artifact. A completed import is displayed without recording an import as a new played result.

## Browser text is an explicit boundary

The reproduction panel is a native `details` element with the summary “Reproduce a game”. It contains the Board code input and Snapshot JSON textarea. Editing either field only edits a draft. `Load board` or `Load snapshot` performs the actual load. This separation lets a player inspect and correct copied text without replacing a running game on each keystroke.

`Export snapshot` fills the textarea with a point-in-time representation. The player can select and copy that text manually. There is no dependency on the Clipboard API, no upload step and no account exchange. Export does not put the live session into the imported pause state. If the source game keeps running while the text is copied, the later source position may differ from the exported one.

The Board code control permits 32 characters and trims surrounding whitespace in `useGame.loadBoard`. The parser used inside JSON does not perform that trim. The Snapshot JSON control permits 65536 characters, while decoding separately enforces 65536 UTF-8 bytes. These are different measurements. A text field limit is an input affordance; the decoder remains the format boundary for programmatically supplied text too.

Successful load resets the board's remembered tab stop to its first position through a new session generation. Load and export buttons retain focus, with Resume handling its own disappearing-button focus transition. Focus is not serialized, so sharing a position cannot restore where the sender last tabbed. See [Reproduction panel](../interface/reproduction-panel.md) and [Focus policy](../interface/focus-policy.md) for interface details.

## Core functions and effectful adapters

The pure format functions operate on strings and game data. `parseBoardCode` returns size and seed or `null`; `decodeSnapshot` returns a reconstructed state or `null`; `readReplay` returns a final state or a classified problem. They do not operate browser controls, write storage or read files.

The browser adapter in `session/use-game.ts` decides when accepted data replaces a session. The CLI adapter in `scripts/replay-cli.ts` reads UTF-8 text and converts accepted replay results through `encodeSnapshot`. Pasting that output into the browser adds normal snapshot import behavior, including a pause for unfinished progress. The replay evaluator itself has no pause field.

## Trust and interpretation

All copied or loaded data is untrusted. “Valid snapshot” means that the object satisfies the documented state constraints, not that its claimed result has a verified play history. A hand-edited object can be accepted if its fields remain consistent. That is useful for debugging and does not provide evidence of a person's performance.

Replays give a more explicit history, but they still contain author-supplied actions and times. The evaluator applies normal rules, including ignored activations, and does not attest who supplied the file. There is no authentication or signed result in the current exchange model. Local best moves are local game records, not a remote ranking service.

A board code also reveals enough information for a developer to regenerate the whole deck. That is its purpose. The browser still keeps hidden face identity out of hidden-card DOM content. Those facts are compatible: the shareable deterministic deal is a debugging tool, while the ordinary board presents the information available during play. [Import safety](import-safety-policy.md) describes validation and replacement behavior in more detail.

## Following a reported disagreement

For a generation mismatch, begin in `src/game/deck.ts` and compare the literal vector. For a rejected position, follow `snapshot.ts` into `snapshot-selection.ts` and `saved-format.ts`. For an unexpected action result, follow `replay.ts` into `advanceGame` and `activateCard` in `game.ts`.

A useful report preserves the original artifact and says which boundary was exercised. “The CLI rejected this replay” and “the browser rejected the CLI's output” refer to different decoders. Keeping that distinction often removes an entire round of reproduction work.
# Native controls guide

This page explains the native HTML elements used by Neon Pairs and the behavior they supply to the interface.

The source combines React event wiring with browser controls. It does not draw input controls on canvas or implement a replacement select menu. The resulting code leaves common editing, activation and disclosure behavior with the browser while keeping game decisions in the session and core.

## The current element choices

| Element | Use in the game | Application responsibility around it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `button` | Cards and actions | Decide what the activation changes |
| `select` with `option` | Grid size | Supply supported sizes and start a deal |
| `label` | Grid size and text fields | Associate visible names with field ids |
| `input` | Board-code draft | Read and validate the submitted code |
| `textarea` | Snapshot draft and export | Hold text and pass it to the snapshot decoder |
| `form` | Board-code submission | Prevent navigation and handle the result |
| `details` with `summary` | Reproduction disclosure | Supply content and layout |
| `dl` with `dt` and `dd` | Current game statistics | Derive the displayed values |
| `dialog` | Tournament leave or replacement confirmation | Preserve the current event when canceled |
| `table` | Tournament bracket | Associate match values with column headings |

These choices describe the current DOM. The dialog and table appear in Tournament mode; [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) and [Tables policy](tables-policy.md) describe their interaction and content structure.

## Buttons unify activation

Card renders a native button with `type="button"`. Its `onClick` sends an index to the shared activation path. Enter and Space can activate the same control through normal button behavior, so there is no separate keydown implementation of reveal.

The board's keydown handler only handles plain arrows with a navigation target. It does not call activation for Enter or Space and then also allow a native click. That avoids two paths processing one keyboard action. The game's pure activation guard still decides whether the card is eligible.

Action buttons outside the board use explicit types too. The Board code loader is `type="submit"` inside its form. New Game, Restart, Export snapshot, Load snapshot and Resume are `type="button"`. This makes submission intent visible in JSX rather than relying on where the browser happens to find an enclosing form.

A native button's semantics do not automatically implement ARIA-disabled behavior. Card uses `aria-disabled={matched}` while remaining focusable, and the game ignores matched activations. [Disabled state guide](disabled-state-guide.md) explains that deliberate split.

## The select keeps its native interaction

Controls renders a labeled select whose value comes from `game.size`. Each option comes from `GRID_SIZES` and has a numeric side length value with `NxN` display text. The browser supplies its dropdown interaction and option-selection behavior.

The component handles change by converting the selected value to a number and calling `newGame`. There is no local menu-open flag, active-option state or custom pointer hit testing. The controller still checks supported sizes, because native options are an interface aid rather than the only trust boundary.

The select inherits the shared font and panel colors through `.control`. Styling the border and background does not replace its role or its label relationship. The current CSS does not remove it in favor of an invisible field beneath a separately focusable drawn menu.

A successful board-code or snapshot load changes the actual game size, which flows back into this controlled select. The visible selected option therefore follows the model rather than a second UI-only size state. [Control bar](control-bar.md) covers that data flow.

## Text editing remains text editing

Board code is an input, and Snapshot JSON is a textarea. They retain selection, caret movement and browser editing operations. The textarea can resize vertically and receives readable export text without a clipboard permission dependency.

The card's `user-select: none` styling is scoped to `.card`. It does not disable selecting an exported snapshot. The code-field spell-check and autocomplete settings reflect its format-oriented use; the snapshot field disables spell checking as well. None of those attributes validates the entered data.

BoardCodeForm uses FormData and prevents the form's default navigation in `onSubmit`. Pressing Enter in the input reaches that same submission path. The snapshot tools instead use local React state and explicit action buttons, preserving multiline Enter behavior in the textarea.

Controlled and uncontrolled fields both appear here. Reproduction controls the textarea value with state. BoardCodeForm uses `defaultValue` on an input keyed by generation. Native element choice does not determine which React state pattern is appropriate. The intended draft lifecycle does; see [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md).

## A disclosure is already an interaction

The reproduction panel uses details with a summary, starts collapsed and relies on native expansion. There is no handler toggling an `expanded` variable or emulating summary key activation. The CSS styles the panel and summary without changing their source order.

The summary's visible text supplies its purpose. The load notice and Resume live outside the collapsible body, so closing it does not hide the pause continuation action. This is a layout and component-boundary decision around the native disclosure, not a custom disclosure implementation.

A disclosure leaves the surrounding document operable and expands in flow. It is not equivalent to a modal overlay. That distinction matters when reading a feature description: choosing a different native element changes more than a border shape or animation.

## DOM cards and artwork

Board is a CSS grid of DOM buttons, and each visible face is an inline SVG child. Hidden cards omit the face component entirely. The button name comes from position, state and, when available, face description; the SVG is hidden from accessibility and cannot receive focus.

The face drawing is therefore not the input surface's semantic replacement. A user activates the button, not an independently focusable path inside the SVG. This keeps the artwork and interaction connected without requiring canvas coordinate mapping or an invisible parallel button list.

The matched check mark is also an aria-hidden, nonfocusable SVG. It reinforces state visually while the button name and disabled property express it through the control. [Card artwork](../visuals/card-artwork.md) and [Screen reader notes](screen-reader-notes.md) describe those channels more fully.

## Native elements still need application work

The browser does not know that a pair matches, that a snapshot import is paused or that a game replacement invalidates an old timer. Those decisions remain in `game.ts`, `session.ts` and `use-game.ts`. A correct native element can still call the wrong controller action.

Nor does a button automatically implement the board's remembered entry point. `useBoardFocus` supplies the tab-index pattern and arrows, while the browser supplies basic focus and activation. The scroll helper addresses a specific Chromium centering behavior rather than replacing all browser scrolling.

Labels and descriptions also need correct associations. A visible label next to an input is not sufficient if its `htmlFor` points elsewhere. A load notice remains useful because the buttons reference its actual id. Native semantics reduce custom behavior, but they do not excuse checking the JSX relationships.

The same applies to CSS. Minimum height, shrinking fields, wrapping rows and visible outlines are explicit styles. A native input can still overflow a narrow page if its sizing constraints are wrong. [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md) and [Target size policy](target-size-policy.md) cover those aspects.

## Why alternatives would carry more work

Replacing the select with a drawn menu would move option navigation, expansion, selection and focus handling into application code. Replacing summary with a styled generic container would require recreating its activation and expanded-state exposure. Those are concrete costs even if the replacement initially resembles the current design.

A canvas board would also need a separate way to expose each card's position, name, state and focus behavior. The current DOM makes those properties inspectable directly. This is the benefit behind the existing choice, not a claim that native elements alone solve every accessibility issue.

The source does not contain a component library or a custom form abstraction that all new controls must use. Shared labels and CSS are small local tools. [ADR 006](../decisions/adr-006-native-controls.md) is the decision reference, while [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md) explains the separation between browser effects and pure game behavior.

## Evidence in review

The controls tests locate fields and buttons by names and roles, inspect native option values and check selectable export text. Keyboard tests rely on normal Tab exit and native button activation. The accessibility journey captures the browser's exposed control roles and states.

- Hover, touch scrolling, pointer cancellation and context-menu interaction do not choose a card.
- Matched cards stay focusable and expose their matched state while activation leaves the turn unchanged.
- Repeated activation of the first revealed card does not add a move.

For a mismatch, attempt a third activation while the pair is visible and move focus elsewhere. The pair stays until its active wait expires; closure does not drag focus back. Hide and show the page during the interval when a lifecycle change is in scope.

## Names and accessible content

Inspect actual DOM and browser accessibility exposure. Visual equivalence is insufficient when hidden data or labels are involved.

- Hidden card names expose position and closed state without a face description or hidden face artwork in their DOM.
- Revealed and matched card names include the correct face description and state.
- Face and check SVGs do not introduce extra focus targets or duplicate the button's description.
- Current statistics expose their visible terms and values without alternate labels replacing the numbers.
- Completion makes the final moves and elapsed time available in the persistent summary.

[Screen reader notes](screen-reader-notes.md) records the full journey and the distinction between tree evidence and spoken review. The repository README records the browser and tool versions and says no screen reader was run. A review report should describe the evidence it actually has.

When a feature introduces name input, consult [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md), [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md). The existing code and JSON text fields do not establish those name checks. For new result content, consult [Tables policy](tables-policy.md).

## Results and repeated events

[Announcements policy](announcements-policy.md) owns the publication model. In a populated game, inspect the event output while also checking that ordinary rendering stays quiet.

- A first reveal changes the card without publishing a resolved-turn result.
- A match or miss publishes its result once per resolved turn, including consecutive identical misses.
- Focus movement, clock updates and mismatch closure do not repeat the prior result.
- The winning result combines the last match and completion information.
- Repeated invalid loads and repeated successful snapshot loads each publish their load outcome.

The session's `announcement` value and the keyed feedback span explain repeated identical text. A refactor that only compares feedback strings can accidentally remove the event distinction. A refactor that updates the identity on every render can produce the opposite failure.

## Layout and reachability

Read [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md), [Target size policy](target-size-policy.md) and [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) for their detailed scope.

The current visual contract includes a default board fitting a phone, large-board overflow confined to the board viewport and complete focus outlines when cards are brought into view. Review the first, last and an interior card. Container padding can protect corners while an interior nearest-scroll target still clips its outline.

The stated large-board views include `360x800` and `1280x800`. The equivalent zoom layout is `640x400` with device scale 2. Controls, statistics and the completion sentence remain readable in those constrained layouts, with the outer page staying within its viewport width.

Check the expanded reproduction panel as well as the collapsed game. Fields shrink within their rows, action rows wrap and the textarea remains selectable. The native select popup and summary behavior are browser interactions; the surrounding CSS should not be assessed as though they were custom drawn widgets.

## Choose evidence that matches the change

Pure geometry is covered by `keyboard.test.ts`; focus and browser default behavior are covered by browser journeys. Parser tests cover malformed data independently of field layout. The accessibility journey captures roles, names, states and result text. These are complementary forms of evidence.

A small label or spacing change does not call for inventing a new test framework. Existing contract, controls, layout and zoom checks already target many interface failures. A callback or lifecycle change needs the populated journey that can expose its effect, especially when a pending mismatch or disappearing Resume button is involved.

The review note is most useful when it names the behavior changed, the evidence observed and any remaining limit. It can say that a tree exposes the expected result without claiming speech was heard, or that a phone layout was measured without claiming every browser was exercised. [Browser test guide](../quality/browser-test-guide.md), [Accessibility audit](../quality/accessibility-audit.md) and [Acceptance](../quality/acceptance.md) connect these checks to the wider project process.
# Acceptance
Acceptance is a set of journeys that checks whether Neon Pairs meets its product requirements.

Status: spec version 2.3.

Finish a game, then start another one during a mismatch. The first journey checks play and completion. The second checks that an earlier timer can't change a new game.

## Play

Use these journeys with the requirements in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md):

- Finish every supported size with complete pairs.
- Reveal one card twice, then reveal a different card. Check the exact move count.
- Match a pair, then miss a pair. Check the immediate match and the 800ms active mismatch interval.
- Hide the page during a mismatch, then return and finish its remaining interval.
- Start and restart during a mismatch. Check the cleared state and later timer updates.
- Finish games with better, equal and worse move counts. Reload and check the current size's best.

## Controls

Use pointer, touch and keyboard to follow [Input](../interface/input.md) and [Controls](../interface/controls.md). Check control labels, row movement, edge stops, native Tab exit and focus after each action. Check that hidden cards reveal no identity in the DOM.

Follow the keyboard journey in I17 and check its accessibility tree. During user acceptance, confirm spoken results with a screen reader, including consecutive identical results and the final match with its win.

## Appearance

Measure the layout and review all 128 faces against [Visuals](../visuals/visuals.md). Use a 44px grayscale face sheet to distinguish shape, marker and fill. Check 16x16 boards at both stated viewport sizes, full focus outlines and the equivalent zoom layout. Check reduced motion and the static completion banner after its single pulse.

Play through completion and reset while checking [Sound](../sound/sound.md). Every action stays silent.

## Reproduction

Check [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) with its example deck and replay. Check snapshot round trips and malformed input. Check the exact mismatch timeout before an equal-time replay action.

Load an unfinished snapshot, attempt input while paused, then Resume. Check its remaining active time and focus. Load a completed snapshot and check its static banner and unchanged best score.

## Tournament

Start four-player and eight-player tournaments with distinct names. Check the opening pairings, round labels, board sizes and unique board codes. For each match, play both turns and confirm both boards use the same code. Check that the lower move count wins; equal moves use active time, then entry seed.

Finish a tournament and reload the page. Check its champion remains in Past tournaments while the ordinary saved size and best scores are unchanged. Export and load an active tournament, then repeat with malformed JSON and an unknown field. Leave an unfinished tournament and keep playing in the confirmation dialog; repeat and leave it.

## Delivery

Use a locked install, type check, unit tests and a fresh browser build as defined in [Technology](../architecture/technology.md). Open the resulting HTML directly from disk with network access blocked. Use a local HTTP origin for saved preferences.

Review the pure game functions, browser effects, file sizes and behavior placement against [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md).

Back to [Neon Pairs](../README.md).

docs/gameplay/selection-state.md:45:There is no deadline attached to closed selection. Waiting before a first reveal leaves the game unstarted; waiting between turns of a started game adds elapsed time. The `started` flag, completion result, and browser session determine that distinction.
docs/gameplay/selection-state.md:63:A one-card selection does not expire on its own. `advanceGame` updates elapsed time but leaves this selection in place. docs/gameplay/selection-state.md:75:Equal deck values move both positions into `matched` and close selection immediately. There is no temporary matching alternative or 800-millisecond wait before the next turn.
docs/gameplay/mismatch-interval.md:56:There is no fixed number of ticks defining a mismatch. docs/quality/browser-support.md:74:The technology specification explicitly notes that disk-origin storage varies among browsers. docs/competition/competition-boards.md:9:Competition uses a subset of the sizes already supported by the solo game. Quarterfinals are played on 4x4, semifinals on 6x6 and finals on 8x8. docs/competition/competition-ties.md:23:The examples deliberately separate efficiency from speed. An implementation that adds moves and seconds together, or sorts by time first, would produce a different comparison. There is no weighted combined score in the existing core or in the decision above.
docs/quality/release-checklist.md:64:There is no configured automatic browser retry policy or trace-on-every-failure mechanism in the local wrapper. docs/competition/competition-pairing.md:30:In this scope, the seed identifies a place derived from entry. It is not an estimate of memory skill. docs/quality/performance-budget.md:4:There is no numeric first-render, input-latency, frame-rate, bundle-byte or memory budget in the specification or test configuration. Browser-test timeouts are automation allowances.
docs/quality/performance-budget.md:62:A focus change updates tab indices for the remembered old and new card. A reveal changes the face prop of the newly exposed position. There is no global state library, worker-based board renderer or canvas layer in this implementation.
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:9:A shared device may already contain records from someone who is not taking part in the event. docs/competition/competition-scores.md:36:[Preferences store](../persistence/preferences-store.md) and [best score records](../gameplay/best-score-records.md) explain the ordinary mechanism. docs/competition/tournament-mode.md:15:Tournament games use the same active-time and card transitions as solo games. docs/competition/competition-overview.md:11:Tournament turns reuse the card transitions but do not call the solo session's best-score or size replacement paths. The bracket, persistence and exchange boundaries are described in [Tournament mode](tournament-mode.md).
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:17:A shared screen makes the activity visible. People can talk about the artwork, remember a near miss and recognize the effort behind another person's finish. There is no remote opponent waiting behind a network connection, and no account setup between the group and the game. The game already has a compact delivery model: the built game can be opened from one HTML file.
docs/sharing/import-safety-policy.md:12:The snapshot and replay implementations do not define a traversal order, object-path syntax or combined-error format for a field-specific diagnostic. docs/sharing/import-safety-policy.md:16:`useGame.loadSnapshot(text)` calls `decodeSnapshot(text)` first. A failed result calls the notice helper and returns `false`. docs/sharing/data-exchange-policy.md:39:Tournament JSON contains player names and seeds, a fixed list of unique board codes, match attempts, winners and the current game position. It is a local transfer format, not a signed record of who played. See [Tournament mode](../competition/tournament-mode.md).
docs/sharing/data-exchange-policy.md:47:`Export snapshot` fills the textarea with a point-in-time representation. The player can select and copy that text manually. docs/sharing/data-exchange-policy.md:63:Replays give a more explicit history, but they still contain author-supplied actions and times. docs/persistence/preferences-store.md:79:`useSavedPreferences` invokes `writePreferences` in a `useEffect` dependent on `[preferences, store]`. Effects run after rendering, including the initial mount. There is no debounce interval, end-of-page listener or pending-save object. The hook has no cleanup because it schedules no continuing background operation.
docs/persistence/preferences-store.md:89:There is no `storage` event listener in this adapter. A tab reads at initialization, keeps its own preference snapshot and writes that aggregate later. Multiple-tab reconciliation is outside the current supported specification. A second tab's newer value is not automatically reflected in the first tab's displayed best.
docs/sharing/format-versioning-guide.md:18:This is why replacing a JSON `version` with a product release string fails. The current readers compare the parsed value directly with their numeric constant. The string `"1"` is also different from number `1`. There is no negotiation, version range or “closest supported version” branch.
docs/persistence/persistence-envelope.md:51:There is no migration chain in the preference store. An unsupported discriminator produces the same fallback as a malformed value. No code attempts to guess an older shape, rename its fields or convert a saved sequence into a best map. A migration requires a code change with observable effects.
docs/persistence/persistence-envelope.md:59:An envelope serves a similar boundary role for its own record collection, but there is no existing generic persistence framework to extend. The source uses direct imports and a two-method store interface. There is no registry, adapter hierarchy or global storage coordinator.
docs/sharing/snapshot-format.md:97:Elapsed time is independently bounded. There is no rule that a certain move count requires a minimum positive number of milliseconds. Multiple eligible activations can occur at the same logical replay time, so zero elapsed time can accompany completed moves. Likewise, the decoder does not compare elapsed time against the age of a pending mismatch to reconstruct exactly when it began.
docs/persistence/retention-policy.md:11:This rule concerns a saved list. It does not turn the existing `bestMoves` object into a history or add a timestamp to it. Tournament history keeps the newest ten completed events. Record types, sort fields and tie-breaking conventions are separate from the amount retained. The preference store still implements the solo best-score aggregate.
docs/persistence/retention-policy.md:27:The preference format contains no creation date, last-played time or expiry value. `readPreferences` does not inspect the current time. It cannot tell whether a valid best was written a minute ago or on a much earlier visit. There is no scheduled cleanup effect, idle purge or age-based deletion in `use-saved-preferences.ts`.
docs/persistence/retention-policy.md:35:The preference writer runs from a React effect whose dependencies are the preferences object and store. This is not a page-exit flush. On initial mounting, the effect writes the current preference state. Later, a new preference object causes another effect run. There is no dependency on active elapsed milliseconds or every move in the game.
docs/persistence/retention-policy.md:41:For list work, the save event named by the retention rule should be understood in the feature's own operation. The existing preference effect has no generic event log or timer that scans all browser keys. There is no central list manager in this source tree.
docs/sharing/snapshot-selection-notes.md:50:A closed selection is accepted only with the key `kind`. There is no `index`, no empty array of selected cards and no remaining-time field. The returned value is a new `{kind: SelectionKind.closed}` object.
docs/sharing/snapshot-selection-notes.md:60:There is no minimum positive move count at this point. A first reveal starts the clock and sets `started`, but a move is counted on the next different eligible reveal. A full snapshot with no matches, `started: true`, zero moves and index `2` revealed is therefore valid. A full snapshot with the same fields and `started: false` is invalid.
docs/sharing/snapshot-selection-notes.md:88:There is no generic recursive object validator here. Each selection branch knows its own key list and semantics. That makes the relationship to `activateCard` direct: closed opens one card; one either matches and closes or becomes a mismatch; mismatch closes after active time. If a format change affects one of those meanings, review the transition functions as well as these read helpers. [Turn resolution](../gameplay/turn-resolution.md), [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) and [Format versioning](format-versioning-guide.md) provide the adjacent context.
docs/persistence/storage-failure-policy.md:5:The current game isolates storage failures from the active game. It catches errors while obtaining the browser store, reading the preference key and writing its replacement. The session can hold its selected size and best results in memory even when no durable write succeeds. There is no current preference-storage warning in the rendered game.
docs/persistence/storage-failure-policy.md:29:After a denied startup read, the game starts at the default size with no saved bests. Choosing another supported size updates the active session. Completing a game can produce a best for that size in memory. New Game and Restart preserve those in-memory preferences because `replaceGame` copies the session preference object rather than rereading the browser store.
docs/persistence/storage-failure-policy.md:45:There is no queue, timer-driven retry, backoff or unload handler. Another dependency change can cause another attempt, but the code does not poll for a browser setting to change. A returned `null` store is captured in state for the lifetime of that mounted game; enabling storage later does not replace that state value automatically.
docs/persistence/corrupt-data-policy.md:101:Stored preference rejection happens during initialization with no draft to correct in the game UI. It returns a playable state quietly. There is no recovery dialog, corrupted-data banner or download of rejected text. Browser access failure also returns defaults, but concerns operation availability rather than text acceptance; see [Storage failure policy](storage-failure-policy.md).

## Names and accessible content

Inspect actual DOM and browser accessibility exposure. Visual equivalence is insufficient when hidden data or labels are involved.

- Hidden card names expose position and closed state without a face description or hidden face artwork in their DOM.
- Revealed and matched card names include the correct face description and state.
- Face and check SVGs do not introduce extra focus targets or duplicate the button's description.
- Current statistics expose their visible terms and values without alternate labels replacing the numbers.
- Completion makes the final moves and elapsed time available in the persistent summary.

[Screen reader notes](screen-reader-notes.md) records the full journey and the distinction between tree evidence and spoken review. The repository README records the browser and tool versions and says no screen reader was run. A review report should describe the evidence it actually has.

When a feature introduces name input, consult [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md), [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md). The existing code and JSON text fields do not establish those name checks. For new result content, consult [Tables policy](tables-policy.md).

## Results and repeated events

[Announcements policy](announcements-policy.md) owns the publication model. In a populated game, inspect the event output while also checking that ordinary rendering stays quiet.

- A first reveal changes the card without publishing a resolved-turn result.
- A match or miss publishes its result once per resolved turn, including consecutive identical misses.
- Focus movement, clock updates and mismatch closure do not repeat the prior result.
- The winning result combines the last match and completion information.
- Repeated invalid loads and repeated successful snapshot loads each publish their load outcome.

The session's `announcement` value and the keyed feedback span explain repeated identical text. A refactor that only compares feedback strings can accidentally remove the event distinction. A refactor that updates the identity on every render can produce the opposite failure.

## Layout and reachability

Read [Form layout guide](form-layout-guide.md), [Target size policy](target-size-policy.md) and [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) for their detailed scope.

The current visual contract includes a default board fitting a phone, large-board overflow confined to the board viewport and complete focus outlines when cards are brought into view. Review the first, last and an interior card. Container padding can protect corners while an interior nearest-scroll target still clips its outline.

The stated large-board views include `360x800` and `1280x800`. The equivalent zoom layout is `640x400` with device scale 2. Controls, statistics and the completion sentence remain readable in those constrained layouts, with the outer page staying within its viewport width.

Check the expanded reproduction panel as well as the collapsed game. Fields shrink within their rows, action rows wrap and the textarea remains selectable. The native select popup and summary behavior are browser interactions; the surrounding CSS should not be assessed as though they were custom drawn widgets.

## Choose evidence that matches the change

Pure geometry is covered by `keyboard.test.ts`; focus and browser default behavior are covered by browser journeys. Parser tests cover malformed data independently of field layout. The accessibility journey captures roles, names, states and result text. These are complementary forms of evidence.

A small label or spacing change does not call for inventing a new test framework. Existing contract, controls, layout and zoom checks already target many interface failures. A callback or lifecycle change needs the populated journey that can expose its effect, especially when a pending mismatch or disappearing Resume button is involved.

The review note is most useful when it names the behavior changed, the evidence observed and any remaining limit. It can say that a tree exposes the expected result without claiming speech was heard, or that a phone layout was measured without claiming every browser was exercised. [Browser test guide](../quality/browser-test-guide.md), [Accessibility audit](../quality/accessibility-audit.md) and [Acceptance](../quality/acceptance.md) connect these checks to the wider project process.
# Acceptance
Acceptance is a set of journeys that checks whether Neon Pairs meets its product requirements.

Status: spec version 2.3.

Finish a game, then start another one during a mismatch. The first journey checks play and completion. The second checks that an earlier timer can't change a new game.

## Play

Use these journeys with the requirements in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md):

- Finish every supported size with complete pairs.
- Reveal one card twice, then reveal a different card. Check the exact move count.
- Match a pair, then miss a pair. Check the immediate match and the 800ms active mismatch interval.
- Hide the page during a mismatch, then return and finish its remaining interval.
- Start and restart during a mismatch. Check the cleared state and later timer updates.
- Finish games with better, equal and worse move counts. Reload and check the current size's best.

## Controls

Use pointer, touch and keyboard to follow [Input](../interface/input.md) and [Controls](../interface/controls.md). Check control labels, row movement, edge stops, native Tab exit and focus after each action. Check that hidden cards reveal no identity in the DOM.

Follow the keyboard journey in I17 and check its accessibility tree. During user acceptance, confirm spoken results with a screen reader, including consecutive identical results and the final match with its win.

## Appearance

Measure the layout and review all 128 faces against [Visuals](../visuals/visuals.md). Use a 44px grayscale face sheet to distinguish shape, marker and fill. Check 16x16 boards at both stated viewport sizes, full focus outlines and the equivalent zoom layout. Check reduced motion and the static completion banner after its single pulse.

Play through completion and reset while checking [Sound](../sound/sound.md). Every action stays silent.

## Reproduction

Check [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) with its example deck and replay. Check snapshot round trips and malformed input. Check the exact mismatch timeout before an equal-time replay action.

Load an unfinished snapshot, attempt input while paused, then Resume. Check its remaining active time and focus. Load a completed snapshot and check its static banner and unchanged best score.

## Tournament

Start four-player and eight-player tournaments with distinct names. Check the opening pairings, round labels, board sizes and unique board codes. For each match, play both turns and confirm both boards use the same code. Check that the lower move count wins; equal moves use active time, then entry seed.

Finish a tournament and reload the page. Check its champion remains in Past tournaments while the ordinary saved size and best scores are unchanged. Export and load an active tournament, then repeat with malformed JSON and an unknown field. Leave an unfinished tournament and keep playing in the confirmation dialog; repeat and leave it.

## Delivery

Use a locked install, type check, unit tests and a fresh browser build as defined in [Technology](../architecture/technology.md). Open the resulting HTML directly from disk with network access blocked. Use a local HTTP origin for saved preferences.

Review the pure game functions, browser effects, file sizes and behavior placement against [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md).

Back to [Neon Pairs](../README.md).

# Persistence overview

This page explains the small amount of browser data Neon Pairs saves and the boundary between remembered preferences and an active game.

Solo play uses `neon-pairs.preferences.v1` for the selected board size and per-size best moves. Tournament mode uses a separate `np3:tournaments` feature collection for the newest ten finished tournaments. Neither value restores an active game after reload; tournament progress can be transferred explicitly through Tournament JSON.

## The durable part of a visit

`src/game/session/storage.ts` defines the persistence data and its reader and writer. The in-memory `Preferences` interface has two properties: `size`, a number, and `bestMoves`, a read-only mapping from size strings to move counts. The writer adds `schemaVersion: 1` when serializing it. A representative stored value is:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":6,"bestMoves":{"4":9,"6":20}}
```

Here the next page load starts a new 6x6 game. The best displayed while playing that size is 20. Choosing 4x4 exposes the independent best of 9. There is no record for 8x8, so the status displays `none` for that size. The selected size does not have to be the only size represented in the score map.

The list of supported side lengths comes from `GRID_SIZES` in `src/game/deck.ts`: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16. `DEFAULT_SIZE` uses the first entry, currently 4. A missing or rejected preference value therefore produces a playable 4x4 start with an empty score map. Storage is useful for continuity between visits, but the game does not depend on it to construct a board or resolve a turn.

# Retention policy

This page explains retention for saved feature lists and contrasts it with solo play's compact best-score aggregate.

Retention describes how much accepted data remains after a save. It is separate from parsing a malformed value, clearing site data in browser settings or losing a private browsing session. Solo play remembers one best move count per supported size rather than preserving each attempt. Tournament mode separately retains a bounded list of completed events.

## Saved lists

A list can grow as a feature saves additional records, even when every individual record is small. Its retention boundary applies during saving, rather than acting as an expiration clock while the player is idle. A stored list keeps its newest 10 records and drops older ones when a new record is saved. This bounds the retained collection while leaving the active interaction independent of an ever-growing history.

This rule concerns a saved list. It does not turn the existing `bestMoves` object into a history or add a timestamp to it. Tournament history keeps the newest ten completed events. Record types, sort fields and tie-breaking conventions are separate from the amount retained. The preference store still implements the solo best-score aggregate.

The list representation is discussed in [Persistence envelope](persistence-envelope.md). Parsing and validation failures are covered in [Corrupt data policy](corrupt-data-policy.md), because retention of accepted records and recovery from rejected input are different operations.

## The current aggregate retains outcomes, not attempts

`Preferences.bestMoves` is a `Readonly<Record<string, number>>`. The key is the canonical decimal side length, such as `4` or `12`, and the value is the best completed move count for that size. The selected board size lives separately in `Preferences.size`. Selecting another size does not discard the previous size's best.

The supported set has seven entries. Once read validation has succeeded, the score map can therefore contain at most seven different supported size keys. It can also contain fewer, including none. # Persistence envelope

This page describes the feature storage envelope and distinguishes it from the preference format already implemented in Neon Pairs.

Solo preferences serialize as an aggregate under `neon-pairs.preferences.v1` with discriminator `schemaVersion: 1`. Tournament history is the first feature collection and uses a distinct `np3:tournaments` key with the version 3 envelope. The existing preference reader and writer retain their original format.

## The feature value boundary

A feature's stored collection has an outer representation and a collection of domain records inside it. The envelope carries the format identity at that outer boundary, before any individual record can be interpreted. Every value a feature adds to browser storage is a JSON object with exactly two keys: "v", the number 3, and "items", the array of records. The records carry the feature's data, while the outer object identifies the representation used to hold that collection.

This makes a feature value inspectable without relying on the name of a variable in the UI. A reader can distinguish an outer format mismatch from a problem in a particular record. The envelope is separate from the record schema, storage key, ordering field and identity scheme. The current preferences implementation stores a selected size and a best-score map rather than feature records.

The envelope also does not change board-code, snapshot or replay formats. Those are interchange representations with their own version identifiers and validation. A snapshot copied by the player is not a preference save, and a replay read by the developer command is not a browser collection. See [Format versioning guide](../sharing/format-versioning-guide.md) and [Data exchange policy](../sharing/data-exchange-policy.md) when following a value across those boundaries.

## The existing aggregate, precisely

The current storage writer does this:

```ts
JSON.stringify({ schemaVersion: PREFERENCES_VERSION, ...preferences })
```

`PREFERENCES_VERSION` is 1. With the ordinary session value, this produces `schemaVersion`, `size` and `bestMoves`. For example:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":8,"bestMoves":{"4":8,"8":40}}
```

This object remembers a selected 8x8 size, a 4x4 best of 8 moves and an 8x8 best of 40. The score map is keyed by board size rather than represented as a sequence of attempts. It has no recency information. Its version number is not inferred from the suffix on the storage key: the reader checks the numeric discriminator inside the value as well.

The feature-envelope reader and writer live in `src/game/tournament/storage.ts`, separate from `src/game/session/storage.ts`. `readPreferences` expects the existing aggregate, and feeding it a feature-shaped collection returns the default preference state. Tournament records are validated by the tournament decoder and never converted into the preference map. The two representations have different jobs and are not interchangeable encodings of the same object.

[Preferences store](preferences-store.md) documents the complete aggregate reader. [Persistence overview](persistence-overview.md) explains why active progress is absent from that value.

# Format versioning guide
This page explains which versions Neon Pairs exposes and how to assess compatibility when its exchange behavior changes.

The current product specification is version 2.3. Board generation, snapshots and replays still use their original format versions, and Tournament JSON has its own version 1 format. A product release and an exchange format answer different questions: the release says which application behavior was delivered; the format says how an artifact is interpreted. The package's `1.0.0` version is another independent value and does not select a decoder.

## The version map today

| Surface | Version marker | Source authority |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starting deal | `np1` prefix inside the board code | `BOARD_VERSION` in `deck.ts` |
| Progress position | Numeric root `version: 1` | `SNAPSHOT_VERSION` in `snapshot.ts` |
| Action timeline | Numeric root `version: 1` | `REPLAY_VERSION` in `replay.ts` |
| Tournament state | `format: "neon-pairs/tournament"`, numeric root `version: 1` | `TOURNAMENT_FORMAT` and `TOURNAMENT_VERSION` |
| Product behavior | Specification status 2.3 | Current game and Tournament requirements |

The JSON version does not absorb the board generation version. A snapshot is version 1 and contains a separately parsed board code. A replay has the same layering. Its action semantics and its starting arrangement both matter, but they are represented by different fields.

This is why replacing a JSON `version` with a product release string fails. The current readers compare the parsed value directly with their numeric constant. The string `"1"` is also different from number `1`. There is no negotiation, version range or “closest supported version” branch.

## Compatibility follows the reader

An existing snapshot reader accepts exactly seven root fields and three exact selection shapes. An existing replay reader accepts exactly four root fields and two action fields. Adding an optional annotation may look harmless to its writer, but an unchanged reader rejects it. In these formats, an additive field is not automatically a compatible change.

Property order and whitespace are different. Both readers parse JSON before checking key sets, so a reordered object with the same values is accepted. Formatting can still cross the byte limit. An export style change can therefore be semantically neutral for small files and affect acceptance near a size boundary.

Accepted array order depends on the field. A snapshot's matched list is validated by membership and whole-face counts; export sorts it numerically. A replay's action list is chronological data with stable ordering at equal times. Sorting a replay action list to make output look tidy can change its result even if no timestamp changes.

The general policies for future exchange objects and field diagnostics are in [Data exchange policy](data-exchange-policy.md) and [Import safety](import-safety-policy.md). They are separate from the accepted version 1 wire definitions. Reading a policy page does not make the current decoder accept fields absent from its exact-key lists.

## A board prefix fixes more than a seed

The reproducibility specification explicitly ties `np1` to the generation algorithm and says that a generation change requires another version. That includes initial paired-face ordering, Park-Miller constants, rejection sampling and backward shuffle order. A different unbiased shuffle is still a different meaning for the same seed.

An implementation refactor that preserves every generated deck leaves that meaning intact. A change that silently produces different cards for an existing code breaks the artifact even if the code still parses. This is the most direct compatibility promise in the exchange model because a short board code appears inside both JSON formats too.

The current `parseBoardCode` supports one prefix. No older-prefix dispatch table, migration helper or multi-version generation registry exists. Future support cannot be assumed from the fact that the prefix contains a digit. [Board code format](board-code-format.md) documents the actual parser and vectors.

## Semantic changes can matter without a new key

A replay's meaning includes advancing time before activation, preserving equal-time array order and resolving a mismatch at its exact closing boundary. Reversing one of those operations would change a version 1 result without changing its object shape. Comparing field lists alone would miss the compatibility effect.
# Acceptance
Acceptance is a set of journeys that checks whether Neon Pairs meets its product requirements.

Status: spec version 2.3.

Finish a game, then start another one during a mismatch. The first journey checks play and completion. The second checks that an earlier timer can't change a new game.

## Play

Use these journeys with the requirements in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md):

- Finish every supported size with complete pairs.
- Reveal one card twice, then reveal a different card. Check the exact move count.
- Match a pair, then miss a pair. Check the immediate match and the 800ms active mismatch interval.
- Hide the page during a mismatch, then return and finish its remaining interval.
- Start and restart during a mismatch. Check the cleared state and later timer updates.
- Finish games with better, equal and worse move counts. Reload and check the current size's best.

## Controls

Use pointer, touch and keyboard to follow [Input](../interface/input.md) and [Controls](../interface/controls.md). Check control labels, row movement, edge stops, native Tab exit and focus after each action. Check that hidden cards reveal no identity in the DOM.

Follow the keyboard journey in I17 and check its accessibility tree. During user acceptance, confirm spoken results with a screen reader, including consecutive identical results and the final match with its win.

## Appearance

Measure the layout and review all 128 faces against [Visuals](../visuals/visuals.md). Use a 44px grayscale face sheet to distinguish shape, marker and fill. Check 16x16 boards at both stated viewport sizes, full focus outlines and the equivalent zoom layout. Check reduced motion and the static completion banner after its single pulse.

Play through completion and reset while checking [Sound](../sound/sound.md). Every action stays silent.

## Reproduction

Check [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) with its example deck and replay. Check snapshot round trips and malformed input. Check the exact mismatch timeout before an equal-time replay action.

Load an unfinished snapshot, attempt input while paused, then Resume. Check its remaining active time and focus. Load a completed snapshot and check its static banner and unchanged best score.

## Tournament

Start four-player and eight-player tournaments with distinct names. Check the opening pairings, round labels, board sizes and unique board codes. For each match, play both turns and confirm both boards use the same code. Check that the lower move count wins; equal moves use active time, then entry seed.

Finish a tournament and reload the page. Check its champion remains in Past tournaments while the ordinary saved size and best scores are unchanged. Export and load an active tournament, then repeat with malformed JSON and an unknown field. Leave an unfinished tournament and keep playing in the confirmation dialog; repeat and leave it.

## Delivery

Use a locked install, type check, unit tests and a fresh browser build as defined in [Technology](../architecture/technology.md). Open the resulting HTML directly from disk with network access blocked. Use a local HTTP origin for saved preferences.

Review the pure game functions, browser effects, file sizes and behavior placement against [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md).

Back to [Neon Pairs](../README.md).
# Form layout guide

This page explains the label, field and action arrangements used by the current controls.

Solo play has the always-visible deal bar and text tools inside Reproduce a game. Tournament mode adds its player fields and Tournament JSON text area. They share native elements and the `.control` style, but their DOM and layout differ.

## A map of the current groups

| Group | Markup and layout | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grid size | Label and select in a flex row | `Controls.tsx`, `controls.css` |
| Deal actions | Two buttons in the outer wrapped flex row | `Controls.tsx` |
| Board code | Form with label above a field/action row | `BoardCodeForm.tsx`, `reproduction.css` |
| Snapshot JSON | Label and textarea in the panel's body grid | `Reproduction.tsx` |
| Snapshot actions | Two buttons in a wrapped flex row | `Reproduction.tsx` |
| Load outcome | Paragraph and conditional Resume in a wrapped row | `Reproduction.tsx` |
| Tournament players | Players select and labeled inputs in a responsive grid | `TournamentSetup.tsx`, `tournament.css` |
| Tournament JSON | Labeled textarea and export/load actions | `TournamentExchange.tsx`, `tournament.css` |

Only Board code is wrapped in a form element. The snapshot field is controlled React state in Reproduction, and its buttons explicitly call callbacks. Enter in a multiline textarea remains text editing rather than submitting the snapshot. Enter in Board code invokes the form's submit path.

## Labels are visible and associated

Grid size uses `htmlFor="grid-size"` and a select with that id. Board code uses `htmlFor="board-code"`, and Snapshot JSON uses `htmlFor="snapshot-json"`. The visible text supplies the fields' names; placeholders do not stand in for labels.

Board code also has `name="boardCode"` because its form reads that field through FormData. Its id serves label association; its name serves native form data lookup. Those are different roles, and changing one does not automatically update the other.

The snapshot textarea has no need for a FormData name in its current path because its value is held in React state and passed directly to `loadSnapshot`. Adding a name attribute alone would not turn its surrounding buttons into a form submission. [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) explains the behavioral value of the current element choices.

Solo deal labels come from `control-labels.ts`; Tournament labels are rendered by its setup and exchange components. Keeping visible text in constants or component markup does not change the label/field relationship. A review can inspect both the displayed label and actual id association, because a correct label string next to the wrong id is still a broken field relationship.

## Deal bar: horizontal until it wraps

The outer `.controls` container uses `display: flex`, bottom alignment, wrapping and a `12px` gap. The nested `.size-control` is a centered flex row with its own `12px` gap. On a wide layout, label, select and action buttons appear in one compact band above the statistics.

[Preferences store](preferences-store.md) documents the complete aggregate reader. [Persistence overview](persistence-overview.md) explains why active progress is absent from that value.

## What the preference reader actually checks
# Format versioning guide
This page explains which versions Neon Pairs exposes and how to assess compatibility when its exchange behavior changes.

The current product specification is version 2.3. Board generation, snapshots and replays still use their original format versions, and Tournament JSON has its own version 1 format. A product release and an exchange format answer different questions: the release says which application behavior was delivered; the format says how an artifact is interpreted. The package's `1.0.0` version is another independent value and does not select a decoder.

## The version map today

| Surface | Version marker | Source authority |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starting deal | `np1` prefix inside the board code | `BOARD_VERSION` in `deck.ts` |
| Progress position | Numeric root `version: 1` | `SNAPSHOT_VERSION` in `snapshot.ts` |
| Action timeline | Numeric root `version: 1` | `REPLAY_VERSION` in `replay.ts` |
| Tournament state | `format: "neon-pairs/tournament"`, numeric root `version: 1` | `TOURNAMENT_FORMAT` and `TOURNAMENT_VERSION` |
| Product behavior | Specification status 2.3 | Current game and Tournament requirements |

The JSON version does not absorb the board generation version. A snapshot is version 1 and contains a separately parsed board code. A replay has the same layering. Its action semantics and its starting arrangement both matter, but they are represented by different fields.

This is why replacing a JSON `version` with a product release string fails. The current readers compare the parsed value directly with their numeric constant. The string `"1"` is also different from number `1`. There is no negotiation, version range or “closest supported version” branch.

## Compatibility follows the reader

An existing snapshot reader accepts exactly seven root fields and three exact selection shapes. An existing replay reader accepts exactly four root fields and two action fields. Adding an optional annotation may look harmless to its writer, but an unchanged reader rejects it. In these formats, an additive field is not automatically a compatible change.

Property order and whitespace are different. Both readers parse JSON before checking key sets, so a reordered object with the same values is accepted. Formatting can still cross the byte limit. An export style change can therefore be semantically neutral for small files and affect acceptance near a size boundary.

Accepted array order depends on the field. A snapshot's matched list is validated by membership and whole-face counts; export sorts it numerically. A replay's action list is chronological data with stable ordering at equal times. Sorting a replay action list to make output look tidy can change its result even if no timestamp changes.

The general policies for future exchange objects and field diagnostics are in [Data exchange policy](data-exchange-policy.md) and [Import safety](import-safety-policy.md). They are separate from the accepted version 1 wire definitions. Reading a policy page does not make the current decoder accept fields absent from its exact-key lists.

## A board prefix fixes more than a seed

The reproducibility specification explicitly ties `np1` to the generation algorithm and says that a generation change requires another version. That includes initial paired-face ordering, Park-Miller constants, rejection sampling and backward shuffle order. A different unbiased shuffle is still a different meaning for the same seed.

An implementation refactor that preserves every generated deck leaves that meaning intact. A change that silently produces different cards for an existing code breaks the artifact even if the code still parses. This is the most direct compatibility promise in the exchange model because a short board code appears inside both JSON formats too.

The current `parseBoardCode` supports one prefix. No older-prefix dispatch table, migration helper or multi-version generation registry exists. Future support cannot be assumed from the fact that the prefix contains a digit. [Board code format](board-code-format.md) documents the actual parser and vectors.

## Semantic changes can matter without a new key

A replay's meaning includes advancing time before activation, preserving equal-time array order and resolving a mismatch at its exact closing boundary. Reversing one of those operations would change a version 1 result without changing its object shape. Comparing field lists alone would miss the compatibility effect.
# Acceptance
Acceptance is a set of journeys that checks whether Neon Pairs meets its product requirements.

Status: spec version 2.3.

Finish a game, then start another one during a mismatch. The first journey checks play and completion. The second checks that an earlier timer can't change a new game.

## Play

Use these journeys with the requirements in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md):

- Finish every supported size with complete pairs.
- Reveal one card twice, then reveal a different card. Check the exact move count.
- Match a pair, then miss a pair. Check the immediate match and the 800ms active mismatch interval.
- Hide the page during a mismatch, then return and finish its remaining interval.
- Start and restart during a mismatch. Check the cleared state and later timer updates.
- Finish games with better, equal and worse move counts. Reload and check the current size's best.

## Controls

Use pointer, touch and keyboard to follow [Input](../interface/input.md) and [Controls](../interface/controls.md). Check control labels, row movement, edge stops, native Tab exit and focus after each action. Check that hidden cards reveal no identity in the DOM.

Follow the keyboard journey in I17 and check its accessibility tree. During user acceptance, confirm spoken results with a screen reader, including consecutive identical results and the final match with its win.

## Appearance

Measure the layout and review all 128 faces against [Visuals](../visuals/visuals.md). Use a 44px grayscale face sheet to distinguish shape, marker and fill. Check 16x16 boards at both stated viewport sizes, full focus outlines and the equivalent zoom layout. Check reduced motion and the static completion banner after its single pulse.

Play through completion and reset while checking [Sound](../sound/sound.md). Every action stays silent.

## Reproduction

Check [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) with its example deck and replay. Check snapshot round trips and malformed input. Check the exact mismatch timeout before an equal-time replay action.

Load an unfinished snapshot, attempt input while paused, then Resume. Check its remaining active time and focus. Load a completed snapshot and check its static banner and unchanged best score.

## Tournament

Start four-player and eight-player tournaments with distinct names. Check the opening pairings, round labels, board sizes and unique board codes. For each match, play both turns and confirm both boards use the same code. Check that the lower move count wins; equal moves use active time, then entry seed.

Finish a tournament and reload the page. Check its champion remains in Past tournaments while the ordinary saved size and best scores are unchanged. Export and load an active tournament, then repeat with malformed JSON and an unknown field. Leave an unfinished tournament and keep playing in the confirmation dialog; repeat and leave it.

## Delivery

Use a locked install, type check, unit tests and a fresh browser build as defined in [Technology](../architecture/technology.md). Open the resulting HTML directly from disk with network access blocked. Use a local HTTP origin for saved preferences.

Review the pure game functions, browser effects, file sizes and behavior placement against [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md).

Back to [Neon Pairs](../README.md).
# Form layout guide

This page explains the label, field and action arrangements used by the current controls.

Solo play has the always-visible deal bar and text tools inside Reproduce a game. Tournament mode adds its player fields and Tournament JSON text area. They share native elements and the `.control` style, but their DOM and layout differ.

## A map of the current groups

| Group | Markup and layout | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grid size | Label and select in a flex row | `Controls.tsx`, `controls.css` |
| Deal actions | Two buttons in the outer wrapped flex row | `Controls.tsx` |
| Board code | Form with label above a field/action row | `BoardCodeForm.tsx`, `reproduction.css` |
| Snapshot JSON | Label and textarea in the panel's body grid | `Reproduction.tsx` |
| Snapshot actions | Two buttons in a wrapped flex row | `Reproduction.tsx` |
| Load outcome | Paragraph and conditional Resume in a wrapped row | `Reproduction.tsx` |
| Tournament players | Players select and labeled inputs in a responsive grid | `TournamentSetup.tsx`, `tournament.css` |
| Tournament JSON | Labeled textarea and export/load actions | `TournamentExchange.tsx`, `tournament.css` |

Only Board code is wrapped in a form element. The snapshot field is controlled React state in Reproduction, and its buttons explicitly call callbacks. Enter in a multiline textarea remains text editing rather than submitting the snapshot. Enter in Board code invokes the form's submit path.

## Labels are visible and associated

Grid size uses `htmlFor="grid-size"` and a select with that id. Board code uses `htmlFor="board-code"`, and Snapshot JSON uses `htmlFor="snapshot-json"`. The visible text supplies the fields' names; placeholders do not stand in for labels.

Board code also has `name="boardCode"` because its form reads that field through FormData. Its id serves label association; its name serves native form data lookup. Those are different roles, and changing one does not automatically update the other.

The snapshot textarea has no need for a FormData name in its current path because its value is held in React state and passed directly to `loadSnapshot`. Adding a name attribute alone would not turn its surrounding buttons into a form submission. [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) explains the behavioral value of the current element choices.

Solo deal labels come from `control-labels.ts`; Tournament labels are rendered by its setup and exchange components. Keeping visible text in constants or component markup does not change the label/field relationship. A review can inspect both the displayed label and actual id association, because a correct label string next to the wrong id is still a broken field relationship.

## Deal bar: horizontal until it wraps

The outer `.controls` container uses `display: flex`, bottom alignment, wrapping and a `12px` gap. The nested `.size-control` is a centered flex row with its own `12px` gap. On a wide layout, label, select and action buttons appear in one compact band above the statistics.
